A **compact Jordan parameter region** is a compact Jordan measurable set $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ that is the closure of its nonempty connected interior $D^\circ$ ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]). Its boundary has content zero ([[thm-jordan-boundary-criterion]]).

A regular parametrized surface patch is the image of a $C^1$ map from a compact Jordan parameter region whose parameter cross product is nonzero on the region's interior and for which no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of the whole region. Seam identifications and rank failures may occur only on the boundary. Here $C^1$ is the Euclidean componentwise class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. More precisely, the parametrization $\varphi$ is defined on an open neighbourhood of $D$, $\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\ne0$ on $D^\circ$, and no point of $D^\circ$ has the same image as a distinct point of $D$. The chosen pair $(D,\varphi)$ is part of the patch data.

For a regular patch $(D,\varphi)$, the parametrization induces on its interior the unit normal
$$N_\varphi=\frac{\varphi_u\times\varphi_v}{\|\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\|_2}.$$
The denominator is positive there by regularity and [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]], and the vector is orthogonal to the tangent plane ([[def-tangent-plane-of-a-regular-surface-patch]]). Choosing $N_\varphi$ rather than $-N_\varphi$ is an **orientation**.

For a continuous vector field $F$, the flux in the orientation induced by $\varphi$ is $\int_D(F\circ\varphi)\cdot(\varphi_u\times\varphi_v)$. This is the scalar Riemann integral of a continuous function on $D$ ([[def-surface-area-and-scalar-surface-integral-of-a-patch]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); replacing the orientation by its negative negates the integrand.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $j:S\hookrightarrow M$ be an oriented embedded smooth $k$-submanifold, with boundary allowed. For a smooth $k$-form $\omega$ on $M$ such that $j^*\omega$ has compact support on $S$, define $\int_S\omega:=\int_Sj^*\omega$. If $F:T\to S$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism, this equals $\int_T(jF)^*\omega$. Compact support is required on $S$ itself.

Let $n\geq1$, let $M^n$ be oriented, and let $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$. For $1\leq i\leq m$ let $D_i\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded open Jordan domains and $F_i:\overline D_i\to M$ continuous and smooth up to the boundary in target coordinates: near each parameter point, a target coordinate representative extends smoothly to a Euclidean neighborhood. Suppose $F_i|_{D_i}$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism onto an open $W_i\subset M$, the $W_i$ are pairwise disjoint, and $\operatorname{supp}\omega\subset\bigcup_i\overline W_i$. Then
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{i=1}^m\int_{D_i}F_i^*\omega.$$
An empty family is allowed when the support is empty. No nonsingularity of $DF_i$ on $\partial D_i$, and no $M$-valued extension across a genuine target boundary, is assumed.

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}$ be a bounded Jordan set and let $g:E\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Suppose that for all $x$ outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, the section $E_x$ is Jordan measurable and $g_x$ is integrable over it. Put $h(x)=\int_{E_x}g_x$ there and assign arbitrary bounded values to $h$ on $N$, with empty-section integral equal to $0$. Then $h$ is integrable on any rectangle containing the projection of $E$, its integral is independent of that rectangle and of the values on $N$, and
$$\int_Eg=\int h(x)\,dx.$$
The symmetric assertion holds for the other coordinate block.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded and Jordan measurable, let $f,g:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded, and suppose $\{x\in E:f(x)\ne g(x)\}$ has content zero. Then $f$ is Riemann integrable over $E$ if and only if $g$ is, and when they are integrable their integrals are equal.

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its boundary $\partial E$ is null, equivalently has content zero.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

derivations.claim: The rectangle $D$ is a compact Jordan parameter region, and $\Phi$ is smooth on all of $\mathbb R^2$. Every point of $S^2$ is in its image: choose $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ with $\cos\theta=p_3$; when $\sin\theta>0$, the pair $(p_1/\sin\theta,p_2/\sin\theta)$ is a unit-circle point and [F7] supplies $\phi\in[0,2\pi]$, while at a pole any $\phi$ works. More precisely, the interior image is $W=S^2\setminus\Phi(\partial D)$: for every point not on the poles or the longitude seam, the latitude is unique by strict decrease of cosine on $(0,\pi)$, and the longitude is unique by the bijection in [F7]. Direct differentiation gives $\Phi_\theta=(\cos\theta\cos\phi,\cos\theta\sin\phi,-\sin\theta)$ and $\Phi_\phi=(-\sin\theta\sin\phi,\sin\theta\cos\phi,0)$; substituting into the coordinate cross-product formula [F3] yields $\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_\phi=(\sin^2\theta\cos\phi,\sin^2\theta\sin\phi,\sin\theta\cos\theta)=\sin\theta\,\Phi$. [F7] makes this nonzero for $0<\theta<\pi$, and its direction is outward because $\Phi$ is the unit radial vector. In any smooth chart on $S^2$, the coordinate derivative of $\Phi$ is therefore invertible; [F6] gives a smooth local inverse. The bijection onto $W$ and these local inverses make $\Phi|_{D^\circ}$ an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism onto the open set $W$. Thus [F1] applies, including the permitted seam and pole degeneracy on $\partial D$.

By [F2] and step 1.1, the flux integrand is $f(\theta,\phi)=\Phi\cdot(\sin\theta\,\Phi)=\sin\theta$, and the same coefficient is $\omega(\Phi_\theta,\Phi_\phi)$. This function is continuous on the compact Jordan rectangle $D$, so [F11] makes it Riemann integrable there; [F7] gives $0\le f\le1$. The bounded open rectangle $D^\circ$ has boundary $\partial D$, which has two-dimensional content zero by [F1], so [F10] makes $D^\circ$ Jordan measurable. Define $g:D\to\mathbb R$ by $g=f$ on $D^\circ$ and $g=0$ on $\partial D$. The functions $f,g$ are bounded and differ only on the content-zero set $\partial D$; [F9] therefore gives that $g$ is Riemann integrable on $D$ and $\int_Dg=\int_Df$. By the zero-extension definition in [F10], $\int_Dg=\int_{D^\circ}f$. This supplies the Riemann-integral consequence of the null boundary explicitly. [F4] defines the oriented-sphere integral and ensures compact support, and [F5] identifies it with $\int_{D^\circ}f$. Therefore [F8] gives $\int_D (X\circ\Phi)\cdot(\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_\phi)\,d\theta\,d\phi=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=2\pi\bigl(-\cos\theta\bigr)\big|_0^\pi=4\pi$. The vanishing cross product at the poles and the repeated longitude seam occur only on $\partial D$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n\geq1$, let $M^n$ be oriented, and let $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$. For $1\leq i\leq m$ let $D_i\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded open Jordan domains and $F_i:\overline D_i\to M$ continuous and smooth up to the boundary in target coordinates: near each parameter point, a target coordinate representative extends smoothly to a Euclidean neighborhood. Suppose $F_i|_{D_i}$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism onto an open $W_i\subset M$, the $W_i$ are pairwise disjoint, and $\operatorname{supp}\omega\subset\bigcup_i\overline W_i$. Then
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{i=1}^m\int_{D_i}F_i^*\omega.$$
An empty family is allowed when the support is empty. No nonsingularity of $DF_i$ on $\partial D_i$, and no $M$-valued extension across a genuine target boundary, is assumed.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}$ be a bounded Jordan set and let $g:E\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Suppose that for all $x$ outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, the section $E_x$ is Jordan measurable and $g_x$ is integrable over it. Put $h(x)=\int_{E_x}g_x$ there and assign arbitrary bounded values to $h$ on $N$, with empty-section integral equal to $0$. Then $h$ is integrable on any rectangle containing the projection of $E$, its integral is independent of that rectangle and of the values on $N$, and
$$\int_Eg=\int h(x)\,dx.$$
The symmetric assertion holds for the other coordinate block.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Use the finite Lorentz oscillator closure in its homogeneous material rest frame. Let $N\ge1$ be finite, with $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ in F m$^{-1}$, $a_\ell>0$ in F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $\omega_\ell>0$ in s$^{-1}$ and $\gamma_\ell\ge0$ in s$^{-1}$ as in that model. Assume Countable Choice; for the strictly damped integrable-kernel dispersion clause also assume Dependent Choice, as required by the causal-response supplier. For the time convention $e^{-i\omega t}$, let $z$ denote complex angular frequency in s$^{-1}$ and define the absolute oscillator susceptibility, with units F m$^{-1}$, by

$$\chi_{\mathrm{abs}}(z):=\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}\frac{a_\ell}{\omega_\ell^2-z^2-i\gamma_\ell z},\qquad \varepsilon(z):=\varepsilon_\infty+\chi_{\mathrm{abs}}(z).$$

The dimensionless transfer function in the causal-response theorem is $\chi_{\mathrm{norm}}(z):=\chi_{\mathrm{abs}}(z)/\varepsilon_0$, so that it has the theorem's convention $P=\varepsilon_0\chi_{\mathrm{norm}}E$ for harmonic histories.

The function $\chi_{\mathrm{abs}}$ is analytic for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$ for every $\gamma_\ell\ge0$. For real angular frequency $\omega>0$ in s$^{-1}$ away from undamped poles, $\chi_{\mathrm{abs}}(\omega)$ is the scalar multiplier for a harmonic particular solution: if $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$ and $P_\ell(t)=\operatorname{Re}(p_\ell e^{-i\omega t})$, then $p_\ell=a_\ell e/(\omega_\ell^2-\omega^2-i\gamma_\ell\omega)$ and $p=\sum_\ell p_\ell=\chi_{\mathrm{abs}}(\omega)e$. This coefficient calculation is not by itself a zero-past response to an eternal harmonic input. In the undamped branch the retarded onset solution is specified by initial data and the real poles are excluded; when every $\gamma_\ell>0$, the separately stated integrable retarded kernels realize the same harmonic multiplier.

$$\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon(\omega)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}\frac{a_\ell\gamma_\ell\omega}{(\omega_\ell^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma_\ell^2\omega^2}\ge0.$$

When every $\gamma_\ell>0$, each causal impulse-response kernel is exponentially decaying, satisfies the integrable-kernel hypotheses of the causal-response theorem, and $\varepsilon-\varepsilon_\infty$ obeys its unsubtracted Hilbert-transform relations. When $\gamma_\ell=0$, that oscillator's poles lie at $z=\pm\omega_\ell$ on the real boundary; the transfer function has no pointwise value at those poles, and no pointwise dispersion formula there is asserted. The theorem makes no universal group-velocity bound.

Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]: fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ jointly of class $C^1$ with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and continuous source densities $\rho,J$ of [[def-em-sources]]. Let $P,M$ and the derived objects $\rho_b,J_b,\rho_f,J_f,D,H$ be those of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], with $P,M$ of class $C^2$, and use the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Then:

**(a) [Bound-source conservation]** $\partial_t\rho_b+\operatorname{div}J_b=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the regular-distribution and classical-compatibility interfaces below. Identify continuous sources with their regular distributions using [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. Then

$$\partial_t\rho_f+\operatorname{div}J_f=\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J$$

as distributions on $U$, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]: the free pair is distributionally conserved exactly when the total pair is. Under the adopted four vacuum equations both sides are zero distributions, by [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]. These statements do not require classical derivatives of $\rho,J$. Where the partial derivatives $\partial_t\rho$ and $\partial_{x_i}J_i$ exist, the same identity holds pointwise by differentiating the free/bound decomposition; in particular, if these derivatives are continuous on $U$, both pairs satisfy the classical pointwise continuity equation. The bound-source conservation equation remains classical and uses only $P,M\in C^2$.

**(b) [Macroscopic equations]** On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD.$$

**(c) [Interpretation and scope]** Equations (b) are an exact rewriting of the adopted vacuum equations under the decomposition of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]]: the two equations written in $E$ and $B$ are unchanged, and the $D$ and $H$ equations hold for every $C^2$ pair $(P,M)$, independently of any constitutive law. The classical bound identity of (a) uses the exchange of $\partial_t$ with $\operatorname{div}$ for $C^2$ data; the free/total identity is distributional in the stated continuous-source class, with its classical interpretation only under the additional derivatives stated in (a). The distributional conservation conclusion embeds the adopted smooth solution only; no macroscopic field-equation claim is made for the weak branch of the Maxwell postulate, for singular or sheet sources or for discontinuous $(P,M)$; no constitutive relation and no empirical statement is made.

Adopt as a modelling postulate of this framework the following constitutive branches for the material described by the macroscopic fields of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]].

**(a) [Material rest frame]** The relations below are stated in a material rest frame: an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the Minkowski model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$, hence history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$ on the declared time interval. When this is the laboratory frame, the components below are laboratory components. Boosting the material changes both the fields and the rest observer; this postulate does not assert that the relations below hold with the same constants in every frame.

**(b) [Elementary inertial-rest branch]** In the rest frame, with constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (the isotropic scalar cases $\varepsilon=\varepsilon\mathbf 1$, $\mu=\mu\mathbf 1$ with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ included), the model takes

$$D=\varepsilon E,\qquad B=\mu H,\qquad J_c=\sigma E,$$

where $\sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and $J_c$ is the conduction part of the free current, $J_f=J_c+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. For a real matrix $T$, symmetric means $T^{\mathsf T}=T$, positive definite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^3$, and positive semidefinite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv\ge0$ for every $v$. Entries of $\varepsilon,\mu,\sigma$ carry respectively $\mathrm F\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\mathrm H\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\mathrm S\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, where $\mathrm F=\mathrm C/\mathrm V$, $\mathrm H=\mathrm T\,\mathrm m^2/\mathrm A$ and $\mathrm S=\mathrm A/\mathrm V$; these make the three displayed relations dimensionally consistent. Local, linear and nondispersive (instantaneous) response is part of this restricted assumption. In the isotropic case an exact broadband interpretation of the constant-coefficient law additionally requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$, so that the characteristic speed $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$ does not exceed the vacuum speed $c$; without that condition, and in the anisotropic branch, the constant-coefficient law is a declared finite-band effective phase-response model and carries no universal front-speed claim.

**(c) [Causal memory branch]** Alternatively, at each fixed material position $x$, declare a bounded continuous full history $E_x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and its response $P_x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. Write $E(t)=E_x(t)$ and $P(t)=P_x(t)$ in the following formula; any field on a smaller time interval uses a declared full-history extension, not unspecified past values. The polarisation response is the causal convolution

$$P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)\,E(t-s)\,ds$$

for a declared real matrix kernel $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ with entries in $L^1(0,\infty)$ ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and units $\mathrm s^{-1}$; the integral then converges absolutely because $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$. The convolution uses only the past history; its continuity and causality are proved in `pthm-em-causal-dispersive-response`, while passivity is an additional model condition. Spatial or temporal differentiability of the resulting fields requires separate hypotheses when used. A finitely-subtracted analytic response may instead be declared by a dimensionless scalar transfer function $\chi$ that is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, continuous on its closure, of class $C^1$ on the real boundary away from a real subtraction point $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ in $\mathbb C$, and satisfies $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ outside a compact set for some integer $n\ge1$ and constant $C>0$ ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). Here $z,\omega_0$ are numerical angular frequencies in $\mathrm s^{-1}$ and the growth bound uses those SI numerical coordinates. Require also $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for every real $\omega$, hence $\chi(0)\in\mathbb R$, so that the response is defined on real harmonic histories independently of their representation. For $\omega\ne0$ the amplitude at that frequency is unique and reversing frequency conjugates it; the symmetry gives the same real output. At $\omega=0$ only $\operatorname{Re}e$ determines the input, and real $\chi(0)$ makes the output depend only on that input. For $e\in\mathbb C^3$, real $\omega$, and componentwise real part, declaring this transfer means adopting the harmonic relation $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})\mapsto P(t)=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e e^{-i\omega t})$; upper-half-plane holomorphy alone does not construct a time-domain response for arbitrary histories.

**(d) [Status]** These are adopted model assumptions, one branch at a time; the framework does not derive them from the vacuum equations or from coarse graining, and no microscopic mechanism, material data or empirical validity is claimed. Ferroelectric and ferromagnetic response, hysteresis, nonlinear response and general nonlocal response lie outside the branches declared here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

For the Lebesgue branches (a) and (b) assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the exact measure interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); the finite sums in branch (c) are defined and computed without Choice. Let the laboratory region, its chart, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\delta_{ij}$ be the Kronecker symbol in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame, with $|y|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This definition assigns **source moments** to a static charge distribution in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d) and (e). Three branches are declared.

(a) [Absolutely continuous branch] Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $\overline B_a(0)=\{y:|y|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are

$$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\ (l\ge1),$$

$$M^{(0)}:=Q,\qquad M_i:=p_i,\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$

with $l\ge1$ and indices in $\{1,2,3\}$; units are C for $Q$, C m for $p$, C m$^l$ for the degree-$l$ Cartesian moment and C m$^2$ for $Q_{ij}$, and all integrals are in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Each integral is absolutely convergent: since $\rho=0$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, and the maps $y\mapsto y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}$ and $y\mapsto 3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}$ are bounded $\lambda_3$-a.e. on that ball by $a^l$ and by $4a^2$ respectively, the integrands are dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $a^l|\rho|$ and $4a^2|\rho|$, which lie in $L^1$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). The traceless quadrupole is traceless,

$$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$

because $\sum_{i=1}^3(3y_i^2-|y|^2)=0$ pointwise, and summing the three integrable functions $3y_i^2\rho-|y|^2\rho$ and applying finite linearity of the integral on $L^1$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]) evaluates the sum as the integral of the pointwise-zero function; replacing $\rho$ by an equal $\lambda_3$-a.e. density changes no moment ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]).

(b) [General locally integrable branch] If instead $\rho\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ is real and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^l|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)<\infty$ for a given integer $l\ge0$, then the degree-$l$ Cartesian moments of the same formula are absolutely convergent and defined; if the absolute weighted moment $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^L|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)$ is finite for some real $L\ge0$, then every integer Cartesian degree $0\le l\le L$ is defined, and in particular $Q=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$ is absolutely convergent, so that $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ is a conclusion of this branch and not an added hypothesis. Here $\rho$ is restricted to the closed unit ball, where it is integrable by local integrability, and outside it $|y|^l\le|y|^L$; splitting the nonnegative integral over these two measurable sets and applying monotonicity and additivity of the integral gives $\int|y|^l|\rho|\le\int_{\overline B_1(0)}|\rho|+\int_{\{|y|>1\}}|y|^L|\rho|<\infty$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-metric-ball]]). The convention $|y|^0=1$ includes the origin, no compact support and no $L^1$-membership is assumed in this branch, and Cartesian monomials of degree $l$ have modulus at most $|y|^l$, so all lower moments, including $Q$, exist together with the degree-$l$ moment.

(c) [Finite system of stationary point charges] Let $N\ge0$, let $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $q_1,\dots,q_N\in\mathbb R$ be charge parameters ([[def-em-sources]] (a)), read as the stationary point charges $q_k\delta_{x_k}$ in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e); for $N=0$ the lists are empty and every sum below is the empty sum $0$. Define

$$Q:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k,\qquad p:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_kx_k,\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\,x_{k,i_1}\cdots x_{k,i_l}\ (l\ge1),\qquad M^{(0)}:=Q,$$

$$Q_{ij}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\bigl(3x_{k,i}x_{k,j}-|x_k|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr),$$

finite sums in the sense of [[def-finite-sum]] ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]); again

$$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$

by finite distributivity. The points need not be distinct; charges at a common point add in every sum.

(d) [Reference point and scope] Every moment of (a)-(c) is computed about the chart origin of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; this origin is part of the definition. These are source moments of a prescribed static distribution, not momenta, rest masses, intrinsic spins, self-energies or dynamical quantities, and no field, force, equation of motion, equilibrium or empirical claim is made here; the static regime in which the source is read is the adopted idealisation of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (f). Every Cartesian degree $l$ in this definition is a nonnegative integer (the number of Cartesian indices); only the absolute weighted exponent $L$ in (b) may be any nonnegative real number.

Assume Countable Choice and the source, SI and retarded-field hypotheses of the preceding transverse-radiation theorem on a nondegenerate compact retarded-time interval $K$. Fix an integer $N\ge0$. Define the $N$th finite retarded-current Taylor coefficient by

$$\mathcal J_N(n,u):=\sum_{k=0}^{N}\frac{1}{k!\,c^k}\int_{B_a}(n\cdot y)^k\,\partial_t^{k+1}J(y,u)\,dy,$$

and define the source-scale remainder

$$\mathcal R_N(u):=\frac{a^{N+1}}{(N+1)!\,c^{N+1}}\int_{B_a}\sup_{|s-u|\le a/c}\left|\partial_t^{N+2}J(y,s)\right|\,dy.$$

The coefficient $\mathcal J_N$ and the remainder $\mathcal R_N$ both have units $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$. The supremum is finite and integrable in $y$. Let

$$A_N(u):=\sup_{n\in S^2}|\mathcal J_N(n,u)|,\qquad P(u):=\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot S(rn,u+r/c)\,d\Omega(n),$$

where $P(u)$ exists by the preceding theorem. Then uniformly for $n\in S^2$ and $u\in K$,

$$|V(n,u)-\mathcal J_N(n,u)|\le\mathcal R_N(u),$$

$$\left|E(rn,u+r/c)-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times\mathcal J_N(n,u))\right|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2}+\frac{\mu_0\mathcal R_N(u)}{4\pi r}\qquad(r\ge2a),$$

$$\left|P(u)-\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}|n\times\mathcal J_N(n,u)|^2\,d\Omega(n)\right|\le\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi c}\bigl(2A_N(u)+\mathcal R_N(u)\bigr)\mathcal R_N(u).$$

For $N=0$, $\mathcal J_0(n,u)=p''(u)$ for the time-dependent electric dipole moment $p(u):=\int_{B_a}y\rho(y,u)\,dy$, and $\mathcal R_0(u)=\frac ac\int_{B_a}\sup_{|s-u|\le a/c}|J_{tt}(y,s)|\,dy$. Consequently

$$\left|P(u)-\frac{\mu_0}{6\pi c}|p''(u)|^2\right|\le\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi c}\left(2|p''(u)|\mathcal R_0(u)+\mathcal R_0(u)^2\right).$$

Every finite truncation has its own explicit derivative remainder. No convergence of the infinite Taylor series and no relative error at an angular node are asserted.
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the SI laboratory chart and source conventions: $\rho:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ has units $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-3}$ and $J:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ has units $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. Let $a,c,\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, and let $\rho,J$ be jointly $C^\infty$, vanish for $|y|>a$, and satisfy $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_yJ=0$. Let $K=[u_-,u_+]\subset\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate compact interval, $u_-<u_+$, and put $K^\sharp=[u_--2a/c,u_++2a/c]$. For $j=0,1,2$, define

$$M_{\rho,j}:=\sup_{\overline B_a\times K^\sharp}|\partial_t^j\rho|,\qquad M_{J,j}:=\sup_{\overline B_a\times K^\sharp}|\partial_t^jJ|.$$

For $n\in S^2$ and $u\in K$, define the retarded current moment and its derivative by

$$I(n,u):=\int_{B_a}J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy,\qquad V(n,u):=\partial_u I(n,u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy.$$

Let $E,B$ be the selected retarded fields of the preceding theorem, set $S=E\times B/\mu_0$, and define

$$\Gamma_E:=\frac{\mu_0\lambda_3(B_a)}{4\pi}\left(4c^2M_{\rho,0}+13caM_{\rho,1}+a^2M_{\rho,2}+3aM_{J,1}+\frac{a^2}{c}M_{J,2}\right),$$

$$\Gamma_B:=\frac{\mu_0\lambda_3(B_a)}{4\pi}\left(4M_{J,0}+\frac{13a}{c}M_{J,1}+\frac{a^2}{c^2}M_{J,2}\right).$$

Then for every $n\in S^2$, $u\in K$ and $r\ge2a$, with $E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times V(n,u))$,

$$\left|E(rn,u+r/c)-E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)\right|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2},\qquad \left|B(rn,u+r/c)-\frac{n\times E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)}{c}\right|\le\frac{\Gamma_B}{r^2}.$$

Consequently the radiation data of the preceding definition exist uniformly on $S^2\times K$ and equal

$$E_{\mathrm{rad}}(n,u)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}n\times(n\times V(n,u)),\qquad B_{\mathrm{rad}}(n,u)=\frac{n\times E_{\mathrm{rad}}(n,u)}{c}.$$

For each fixed retarded time $u$, the outward retarded-time flux has the exact limit

$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot S(rn,u+r/c)\,d\Omega(n)=\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}|n\times V(n,u)|^2\,d\Omega(n).$$

derivations.claim: Choose $0<r_0<R_0<a$ and apply [F1] to obtain $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ with $0\le f\le1$, $f=1$ on $\overline B_{r_0}(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}f\subset B_{R_0}(0)$. By [F5], $F:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(y)\,dy\ge\lambda_3(B_{r_0})>0$. By [F2], choose $\chi_G,\chi_H\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\chi_G=1$ near $u$ and $\chi_H=1$ on a neighborhood of $[u-a/c,u+a/c]$. Define $G(t):=\chi_G(t)(t-u)^2$ and $H(t):=\chi_H(t)(t-u)^3$. Then $G''(u)=2$ and $H'''(s)=6$ for every $s\in[u-a/c,u+a/c]$.

Let $e_1=(1,0,0)$ and $e_3=(0,0,1)$, and define $\displaystyle \rho(y,t):=-G(t)\partial_3f(y),\qquad J(y,t):=G'(t)f(y)e_3+H'(t)\bigl(-\partial_3f(y)e_1+\partial_1f(y)e_3\bigr).$ These maps are jointly smooth and supported in $\operatorname{supp}f\times(\operatorname{supp}G\cup\operatorname{supp}G'\cup\operatorname{supp}H')$, a compact subset of $B_a\times\mathbb R$. Their derivatives satisfy $\displaystyle \partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_yJ=-G'(t)\partial_3f+G'(t)\partial_3f+H'(t)(-\partial_1\partial_3f+\partial_3\partial_1f)=0$ by [F4], so the source is admissible for the controlled multipole theorem.

The current derivative is $J_t=G''f e_3+H''(-\partial_3f\,e_1+\partial_1f\,e_3)$. Each integral $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\partial_i f\,dy$ is zero by the divergence theorem applied to $f e_i$ on a ball containing $\operatorname{supp}f$, since its boundary flux vanishes. Thus [F3] gives $p''(u)=\int J_t(y,u)\,dy=G''(u)F e_3=2F e_3$, which is nonzero and parallel to $n=e_3$. Therefore $n\times(n\times p''(u))=0$.

For $n=e_3$, the $e_1$ component of the exact shifted current moment is $\displaystyle V_1(e_3,u)=-\int_{B_a}H''(u+y_3/c)\partial_3f(y)\,dy=\frac1c\int_{B_a}f(y)H'''(u+y_3/c)\,dy=\frac{6F}{c}>0.$ The middle equality is integration by parts in $y_3$; the boundary term vanishes because $f$ has compact support, and $|y_3|\le a$ on its support, so $H'''=6$ there by step 1.1. The term $G''f e_3$ contributes no $e_1$ component. Hence $V(e_3,u)$ has a nonzero component perpendicular to $e_3$.

By [F6], $E_{\mathrm{rad}}(e_3,u)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}e_3\times(e_3\times V(e_3,u))\ne0$, whereas the dipole coefficient $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}e_3\times(e_3\times p''(u))$ is zero by step 3.1. Therefore the absolute multipole remainder is nonzero at a direction where the dipole reference amplitude vanishes; no finite uniform relative-error bound with that dipole amplitude as denominator can hold.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For the Lebesgue branches (a) and (b) assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the exact measure interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); the finite sums in branch (c) are defined and computed without Choice. Let the laboratory region, its chart, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\delta_{ij}$ be the Kronecker symbol in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame, with $|y|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This definition assigns **source moments** to a static charge distribution in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d) and (e). Three branches are declared.

(a) [Absolutely continuous branch] Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $\overline B_a(0)=\{y:|y|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are

$$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\ (l\ge1),$$

$$M^{(0)}:=Q,\qquad M_i:=p_i,\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$

with $l\ge1$ and indices in $\{1,2,3\}$; units are C for $Q$, C m for $p$, C m$^l$ for the degree-$l$ Cartesian moment and C m$^2$ for $Q_{ij}$, and all integrals are in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Each integral is absolutely convergent: since $\rho=0$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$, and the maps $y\mapsto y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}$ and $y\mapsto 3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}$ are bounded $\lambda_3$-a.e. on that ball by $a^l$ and by $4a^2$ respectively, the integrands are dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $a^l|\rho|$ and $4a^2|\rho|$, which lie in $L^1$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). The traceless quadrupole is traceless,

$$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$

because $\sum_{i=1}^3(3y_i^2-|y|^2)=0$ pointwise, and summing the three integrable functions $3y_i^2\rho-|y|^2\rho$ and applying finite linearity of the integral on $L^1$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]) evaluates the sum as the integral of the pointwise-zero function; replacing $\rho$ by an equal $\lambda_3$-a.e. density changes no moment ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]).

(b) [General locally integrable branch] If instead $\rho\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ is real and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^l|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)<\infty$ for a given integer $l\ge0$, then the degree-$l$ Cartesian moments of the same formula are absolutely convergent and defined; if the absolute weighted moment $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^L|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)$ is finite for some real $L\ge0$, then every integer Cartesian degree $0\le l\le L$ is defined, and in particular $Q=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$ is absolutely convergent, so that $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ is a conclusion of this branch and not an added hypothesis. Here $\rho$ is restricted to the closed unit ball, where it is integrable by local integrability, and outside it $|y|^l\le|y|^L$; splitting the nonnegative integral over these two measurable sets and applying monotonicity and additivity of the integral gives $\int|y|^l|\rho|\le\int_{\overline B_1(0)}|\rho|+\int_{\{|y|>1\}}|y|^L|\rho|<\infty$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-metric-ball]]). The convention $|y|^0=1$ includes the origin, no compact support and no $L^1$-membership is assumed in this branch, and Cartesian monomials of degree $l$ have modulus at most $|y|^l$, so all lower moments, including $Q$, exist together with the degree-$l$ moment.

(c) [Finite system of stationary point charges] Let $N\ge0$, let $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $q_1,\dots,q_N\in\mathbb R$ be charge parameters ([[def-em-sources]] (a)), read as the stationary point charges $q_k\delta_{x_k}$ in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e); for $N=0$ the lists are empty and every sum below is the empty sum $0$. Define

$$Q:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k,\qquad p:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_kx_k,\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\,x_{k,i_1}\cdots x_{k,i_l}\ (l\ge1),\qquad M^{(0)}:=Q,$$

$$Q_{ij}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\bigl(3x_{k,i}x_{k,j}-|x_k|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr),$$

finite sums in the sense of [[def-finite-sum]] ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]); again

$$\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ii}=0,$$

by finite distributivity. The points need not be distinct; charges at a common point add in every sum.

(d) [Reference point and scope] Every moment of (a)-(c) is computed about the chart origin of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; this origin is part of the definition. These are source moments of a prescribed static distribution, not momenta, rest masses, intrinsic spins, self-energies or dynamical quantities, and no field, force, equation of motion, equilibrium or empirical claim is made here; the static regime in which the source is read is the adopted idealisation of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (f). Every Cartesian degree $l$ in this definition is a nonnegative integer (the number of Cartesian indices); only the absolute weighted exponent $L$ in (b) may be any nonnegative real number.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice and the source, SI and retarded-field hypotheses of the preceding transverse-radiation theorem on a nondegenerate compact retarded-time interval $K$. Fix an integer $N\ge0$. Define the $N$th finite retarded-current Taylor coefficient by

$$\mathcal J_N(n,u):=\sum_{k=0}^{N}\frac{1}{k!\,c^k}\int_{B_a}(n\cdot y)^k\,\partial_t^{k+1}J(y,u)\,dy,$$

and define the source-scale remainder

$$\mathcal R_N(u):=\frac{a^{N+1}}{(N+1)!\,c^{N+1}}\int_{B_a}\sup_{|s-u|\le a/c}\left|\partial_t^{N+2}J(y,s)\right|\,dy.$$

The coefficient $\mathcal J_N$ and the remainder $\mathcal R_N$ both have units $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$. The supremum is finite and integrable in $y$. Let

$$A_N(u):=\sup_{n\in S^2}|\mathcal J_N(n,u)|,\qquad P(u):=\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot S(rn,u+r/c)\,d\Omega(n),$$

where $P(u)$ exists by the preceding theorem. Then uniformly for $n\in S^2$ and $u\in K$,

$$|V(n,u)-\mathcal J_N(n,u)|\le\mathcal R_N(u),$$

$$\left|E(rn,u+r/c)-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times\mathcal J_N(n,u))\right|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2}+\frac{\mu_0\mathcal R_N(u)}{4\pi r}\qquad(r\ge2a),$$

$$\left|P(u)-\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}|n\times\mathcal J_N(n,u)|^2\,d\Omega(n)\right|\le\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi c}\bigl(2A_N(u)+\mathcal R_N(u)\bigr)\mathcal R_N(u).$$

For $N=0$, $\mathcal J_0(n,u)=p''(u)$ for the time-dependent electric dipole moment $p(u):=\int_{B_a}y\rho(y,u)\,dy$, and $\mathcal R_0(u)=\frac ac\int_{B_a}\sup_{|s-u|\le a/c}|J_{tt}(y,s)|\,dy$. Consequently

$$\left|P(u)-\frac{\mu_0}{6\pi c}|p''(u)|^2\right|\le\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi c}\left(2|p''(u)|\mathcal R_0(u)+\mathcal R_0(u)^2\right).$$

Every finite truncation has its own explicit derivative remainder. No convergence of the infinite Taylor series and no relative error at an angular node are asserted.
