citations.quote:
Use a fixed positively oriented inertial laboratory chart with spatial coordinate
$x\in\mathbb R^3$, time $t\in\mathbb R$, Euclidean dot and cross products, and
the SI vacuum speed $c>0$. A smooth amplitude is a map
$a:\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb C^3$ whose coordinate partial
derivatives of every order exist and are continuous. Require its support
$K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ to be compact and require the bilinear
transversality condition
$k\cdot a(k):=\sum_{j=1}^3 k_j a_j(k)=0$ for every $k\ne0$. The dot in this
condition is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. The zero extension of $a$
to $k=0$ is understood.

For $R>0$, put $Q_R=[-R,R]^3$. Integrals of continuous real scalar functions on
$Q_R$ are the ordinary real Riemann integrals, defined as the common lower and
upper Darboux value. For a continuous
$F:Q_R\to\mathbb C^m$, define its Riemann integral componentwise by
$$\left(\int_{Q_R}F\,d^3y\right)_j:=\int_{Q_R}\operatorname{Re}F_j\,d^3y+i\int_{Q_R}\operatorname{Im}F_j\,d^3y\qquad(1\le j\le m),$$
where $y$ denotes the cube coordinates.
This also defines integrals of real vector fields by taking their imaginary
components to be zero; a real scalar is the case $m=1$. For a continuous real
scalar or finite-dimensional real/complex vector field $F$ on $\mathbb R^3$, write
$\int_{\mathbb R^3}F\,d^3x$ for the finite componentwise limit
$\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{Q_R}F\,d^3x$ when each real-valued component
$\operatorname{Re}F_j$ and $\operatorname{Im}F_j$ has a finite limit. For
$F:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^m$, say that $F$ is absolutely
integrable when the nonnegative real cube integrals
$$\int_{Q_R}\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(|\operatorname{Re}F_j|+|\operatorname{Im}F_j|\bigr)\,d^3x$$
have a finite limit as $R\to\infty$. For a real scalar integrand this means
that the cube integrals of its absolute value have a finite limit. If this
absolute-integral limit is finite, every real or imaginary component integral
has a finite cube-exhaustion limit. For one such component $h$, set
$I_R:=\int_{Q_R}h$ and let $A_R$ denote the absolute component-sum cube integral
in the preceding display. Finite coordinate-slice additivity and the
absolute-value estimate give $|I_S-I_R|\le A_S-A_R$ for $S>R$. Since $A_R$
is nondecreasing by nonnegativity and additivity, if its limit is $A$ then
$0\le A_S-A_R\le A-A_R\to0$ uniformly for $S\ge R$. Thus these component
integrals are Cauchy as $R\to\infty$. The
integer-radius values form a Cauchy sequence and converge in $\mathbb R$; the
uniform tail bound then gives the same limit for all real radii, because an
integer radius can be chosen above any fixed real threshold. The argument uses
finite coordinate-slice additivity, the Riemann absolute-value estimate, and
completeness of $\mathbb R$. If $F$ is
continuous and compactly supported, its whole-space integral agrees with the
componentwise Riemann integral over any sufficiently large cube containing its
support and is independent of that cube. Every complex- or real-vector
integral below uses this convention. Define
the complex vector potential and its associated real fields by

$$A_+(x,t):=(2\pi)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}a(k)\exp\!\bigl(i(k\cdot x-c|k|t)\bigr)\,d^3k,\qquad A:=2\operatorname{Re}A_+,\qquad \varphi:=0,\qquad E:=-\partial_tA,\qquad B:=\operatorname{curl}A.$$

Here $k$ is a spatial wavevector with units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $|k|$ is its
Euclidean norm, $t$ is in seconds, and $i^2=-1$; thus the phase is
dimensionless and real part is taken componentwise.
If $a$ carries units $\mathrm{T\,m^4}$, then $A$ carries $\mathrm{T\,m}$,
$E$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and $B$ carries $\mathrm T$. These fields are
real and jointly smooth on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$; at each fixed time
$A,E,B$ are Schwartz functions of $x$, and their spatial Schwartz seminorms are
bounded on every compact time interval. They satisfy the smooth source-free
vacuum Maxwell equations and the Coulomb condition
$\operatorname{div}A=0$ with the stated scalar potential $\varphi=0$. Their
total field energy
$W(t):=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{[-R,R]^3}u(x,t)\,d^3x$, with $u$ the vacuum
energy density, is finite for every $t$. The amplitudes are a classical Fourier
description; no photon state is defined.

Retain the fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of [[def-em-fields]], the
energy density $u$ and Poynting vector $S$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]],
the laboratory region, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and its spatial
Euclidean structure of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the constants and units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and the partial derivatives $\partial_j$ of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Write $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ for the
position in the spatial chart, $\delta_{ij}$ for the Kronecker symbol
($\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise), $\lvert E\rvert^2=\langle E,E\rangle$
with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and
$\times$ for the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] in the frame
basis. Let $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\mu_0>0$ be the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Momentum density] The **electromagnetic momentum density** is the map
$g:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ defined by

$$g:=\frac{S}{c^2}=\varepsilon_0\,E\times B,$$

in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm s^{-1}$; the second equality uses
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

(b) [Maxwell stress tensor] The **Maxwell stress tensor** is the spatial
tensor field $\sigma$ on $\Omega\times I$ with components

$$\sigma_{ij}:=\varepsilon_0\Bigl(E_iE_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert E\rvert^2\Bigr)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\Bigl(B_iB_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert B\rvert^2\Bigr),$$

in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$; the indices range over
$\{1,2,3\}$ and repeated symbols are not summed here, every sum being written
explicitly. The tensor is **symmetric**, $\sigma_{ij}=\sigma_{ji}$ for all
$i,j$, by inspection of the displayed expression. Its divergence is the vector
field with components
$(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$, the partial
derivatives being taken at fixed $t$.

(c) [Momentum flux] The **momentum flux tensor** is $\Pi:=-\sigma$, with
$(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\Pi_{ij}$; then
$\operatorname{div}\Pi=-\operatorname{div}\sigma$ componentwise.

(d) [Orbital angular momentum density and its flux] Relative to the origin of
the spatial chart, the **orbital angular momentum density** is
$\ell:=x\times g$, with components $\ell_i=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}x_jg_k$,
and its **flux tensor** is the spatial tensor field $x\times\Pi$ with
components

$$(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}\,x_j\,\Pi_{k\ell}.$$

Here $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the Levi-Civita symbol, defined by
$\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ if $(i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(1,2,3)$,
$\epsilon_{ijk}=-1$ if it is an odd permutation, and $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$ if two
indices coincide, in the positively oriented basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The object
$\ell$ carries $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-1}$ and the components
of $x\times\Pi$ carry $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-2}=\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-1}$.

(e) [Origin] Both $\ell$ and $x\times\Pi$ depend on the origin of the spatial
chart: under a shift $x\mapsto x+a$ of the origin by a constant $a\in\mathbb R^3$
their values become $\ell+a\times g$ and $x\times\Pi+a\times\Pi$ respectively,
so the definition fixes one origin in the laboratory frame and every statement
about $\ell$ or $x\times\Pi$ is relative to that fixed origin.

(f) [Status] This item fixes objects and index conventions only. No balance
identity and no interpretation of $\sigma$ or $\Pi$ as force or momentum flux
is asserted here; every balance identity involving these objects is the content
of the separate theorem items of this page.

(g) [Quadratic character and singular support] All five objects are quadratic
in the fields $E,B$. For a locally integrable branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] the exclusions recorded in
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] apply to each of them: the products
$E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally
integrable, no product of distributions is defined, and the displayed formulas
then define the objects pointwise almost everywhere, the framework using them
only where the local integrability of the products is separately established.
No value is assigned at a point of singular source support.

(h) [No covariant object] No four-dimensional or covariant interpretation of
$(u,S,g,\sigma)$ is defined here; in particular $g$ is not identified with the
spatial components of a covariant momentum density.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with The reals form a totally ordered field,
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)).

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.

derivations.claim: For every Schwartz component $f$ and every integer $N$, the finite expansion of $\prod_{j=1}^3(1+|x_j|)^N$ is controlled term-by-term by the seminorms in [F1], so $|f(x)|\le C_N\prod_j(1+|x_j|)^{-N}$; the same holds for its derivatives. Choose $N=4$. Each component of each vector integrand defining $J_{\mathrm{kin}}$, $L_{\mathrm{can}}$, and $S_{\mathrm{can}}$ is a sum of products of two Schwartz components, with at most one coordinate factor. Therefore, for each such vector integrand $V$, $\sum_{j=1}^3|V_j(x)|\le C_VG(x)$ for some $C_V\ge0$, where $G(x):=\prod_{j=1}^3(1+|x_j|)^{-7}$. By [F5], for $R>0$ the one-dimensional factor satisfies $\int_{-R}^{R}(1+|s|)^{-7}\,ds=\frac13(1-(1+R)^{-6})\le\frac13$ and tends to $1/3$. Riemann-Fubini [F4] gives $\int_{Q_R}G\,d^3x=\left(\frac13(1-(1+R)^{-6})\right)^3\le1/27$. Thus the nonnegative cube integrals $A_R(V):=\int_{Q_R}\sum_{j=1}^3|V_j(x)|\,d^3x$ are bounded above by $C_V/27$ and are nondecreasing in $R$ by finite-slice additivity and monotonicity [F6]. The set $\{A_R(V):R>0\}$ is nonempty (take $R=1$) and bounded above, so its finite real supremum $A(V)$ exists by [F7]. For every $\varepsilon>0$, choose $R_0$ with $A_{R_0}(V)>A(V)-\varepsilon$; then $A(V)-\varepsilon<A_R(V)\le A(V)$ for all $R\ge R_0$, proving that $A_R(V)$ has a finite limit. Hence each $V$ is absolutely integrable in the preceding Definition's sense, and its signed component integrals have finite cube-exhaustion limits by the proved absolute-tail implication in [F1]. This proves that all three functionals are well-defined finite vectors.

The integrand of $J_{\mathrm{kin}}$ is $x$ (metres) crossed with the momentum density $g$ of [F2]. Since $g$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, its integral after multiplication by $x$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{J\,s}$. For each canonical term, $\varepsilon_0EA$ has units $\varepsilon_0E^2\,\mathrm{s}$ because $A$ has the units of $E$ times time by [F3]. From $[\varepsilon_0]=\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{C\,V^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$ and $1\,\mathrm{C\,V}=1\,\mathrm J$, $\varepsilon_0E^2$ has units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$; integration over volume again gives $\mathrm{J\,s}$. These are the units asserted in the Definition.

Retain the fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of [[def-em-fields]], the
energy density $u$ and Poynting vector $S$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]],
the laboratory region, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and its spatial
Euclidean structure of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the constants and units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and the partial derivatives $\partial_j$ of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Write $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ for the
position in the spatial chart, $\delta_{ij}$ for the Kronecker symbol
($\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise), $\lvert E\rvert^2=\langle E,E\rangle$
with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and
$\times$ for the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] in the frame
basis. Let $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\mu_0>0$ be the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Momentum density] The **electromagnetic momentum density** is the map
$g:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ defined by

$$g:=\frac{S}{c^2}=\varepsilon_0\,E\times B,$$

in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm s^{-1}$; the second equality uses
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

(b) [Maxwell stress tensor] The **Maxwell stress tensor** is the spatial
tensor field $\sigma$ on $\Omega\times I$ with components

$$\sigma_{ij}:=\varepsilon_0\Bigl(E_iE_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert E\rvert^2\Bigr)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\Bigl(B_iB_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert B\rvert^2\Bigr),$$

in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$; the indices range over
$\{1,2,3\}$ and repeated symbols are not summed here, every sum being written
explicitly. The tensor is **symmetric**, $\sigma_{ij}=\sigma_{ji}$ for all
$i,j$, by inspection of the displayed expression. Its divergence is the vector
field with components
$(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$, the partial
derivatives being taken at fixed $t$.

(c) [Momentum flux] The **momentum flux tensor** is $\Pi:=-\sigma$, with
$(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\Pi_{ij}$; then
$\operatorname{div}\Pi=-\operatorname{div}\sigma$ componentwise.

(d) [Orbital angular momentum density and its flux] Relative to the origin of
the spatial chart, the **orbital angular momentum density** is
$\ell:=x\times g$, with components $\ell_i=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}x_jg_k$,
and its **flux tensor** is the spatial tensor field $x\times\Pi$ with
components

$$(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}\,x_j\,\Pi_{k\ell}.$$

Here $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the Levi-Civita symbol, defined by
$\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ if $(i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(1,2,3)$,
$\epsilon_{ijk}=-1$ if it is an odd permutation, and $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$ if two
indices coincide, in the positively oriented basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The object
$\ell$ carries $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-1}$ and the components
of $x\times\Pi$ carry $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-2}=\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-1}$.

(e) [Origin] Both $\ell$ and $x\times\Pi$ depend on the origin of the spatial
chart: under a shift $x\mapsto x+a$ of the origin by a constant $a\in\mathbb R^3$
their values become $\ell+a\times g$ and $x\times\Pi+a\times\Pi$ respectively,
so the definition fixes one origin in the laboratory frame and every statement
about $\ell$ or $x\times\Pi$ is relative to that fixed origin.

(f) [Status] This item fixes objects and index conventions only. No balance
identity and no interpretation of $\sigma$ or $\Pi$ as force or momentum flux
is asserted here; every balance identity involving these objects is the content
of the separate theorem items of this page.

(g) [Quadratic character and singular support] All five objects are quadratic
in the fields $E,B$. For a locally integrable branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] the exclusions recorded in
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] apply to each of them: the products
$E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally
integrable, no product of distributions is defined, and the displayed formulas
then define the objects pointwise almost everywhere, the framework using them
only where the local integrability of the products is separately established.
No value is assigned at a point of singular source support.

(h) [No covariant object] No four-dimensional or covariant interpretation of
$(u,S,g,\sigma)$ is defined here; in particular $g$ is not identified with the
spatial components of a covariant momentum density.

conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining

item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant

$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), let $m\ge1$, and let
$X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be a random element with target
$(\mathbb R^m,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m))$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]).
Use the statistical one-based coordinate labels: for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$
write $v_i:=v(i-1)$ for $1\le i\le m$, so
$X_i(\omega)=X(\omega)(i-1)$. Each $X_i$ is a real random variable because
the coordinate projection $x\mapsto x(i-1)$ is continuous and therefore has
Borel preimages of Borel sets
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]).
For every integer $r\ge1$ and matrix
$A\in M_{r\times m}(\mathbb R)$, the notation $A_{ij}$ below means its
zero-based matrix entry
$A(i-1,j-1)$ for $1\le i\le r$ and
$1\le j\le m$; likewise $\Sigma_{ij}$ means the entry at $(i-1,j-1)$ in
the covariance matrix below in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]]. These
are labels for the root library's zero-based function entries, not a different
matrix convention. If $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is open, $h:U\to\mathbb R^r$
has all first partials at $a\in U$, and $A=Jh(a)$, then $A_{ij}$ in this
notation is $\partial_{j-1}h_{i-1}(a)$, with the zero-based Jacobian
convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].
Assume $X$ is **square-integrable**:
$$E\bigl[|X|^2\bigr]=\sum_{i=1}^{m}E\bigl[X_i^2\bigr]<+\infty ,$$
where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
Its **mean vector** is
$$\mu=E[X]:=\bigl(E[X_1],\dots,E[X_m]\bigr)\in\mathbb R^m ,$$
the coordinates being the expectations of
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Its **covariance matrix** is the
$m\times m$ real matrix of [[def-matrix-space]]
$$\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}(X):=\bigl(\Sigma_{ij}\bigr)_{i,j=1}^{m},\qquad \Sigma_{ij}:=E\bigl[(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)\bigr]\in\mathbb R .$$
For the random vector $X$ the entries $\Sigma_{ij}$ are also written
$\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$, and $\Sigma_{ii}=\operatorname{Var}(X_i)$.

### Well-definedness and elementary properties

**Integrability of the entries.** Square-integrability gives
$E[X_i^2]<+\infty$ for each $i$. Since the underlying measure is a
probability measure, the elementary inequality
$$|X_i|\le \tfrac12\bigl(1+X_i^2\bigr)$$
gives $E|X_i|\le\tfrac12(1+E[X_i^2])<+\infty$ by monotonicity and
homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); hence $X_i$
is integrable and $\mu_i=E[X_i]$ is finite
([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]). Also
$$(X_i-\mu_i)^2\le2X_i^2+2\mu_i^2,$$
so $X_i-\mu_i$ is square-integrable; the probability-space inequality
$$|X_i-\mu_i|\le\tfrac12\bigl(1+(X_i-\mu_i)^2\bigr)$$
then makes it integrable as well. Finally
$$|(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)|\le \tfrac12\bigl((X_i-\mu_i)^2+(X_j-\mu_j)^2\bigr),$$
and the right-hand side is integrable by additivity, monotonicity and
homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]],
[[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); hence every
$\Sigma_{ij}$ is a finite real number.

**Symmetry.** For all $i,j$ the real numbers $(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)$ and
$(X_j-\mu_j)(X_i-\mu_i)$ are equal pointwise, so $\Sigma_{ij}=\Sigma_{ji}$;
thus $\Sigma^{\mathsf T}=\Sigma$.

For $M\in M_{m\times m}(\mathbb R)$ and $z\in\mathbb R^m$, write
$$z^{\mathsf T}Mz:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}z_iM_{ij}z_j.$$
For a real symmetric $m\times m$ matrix $M$, **positive semidefinite** means
$z^{\mathsf T}Mz\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^m$, and **positive definite**
means $z^{\mathsf T}Mz>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^m$. For a real
random variable $Z$, **almost surely constant** means that $Z=c$ outside a
measurable $\mathbb P$-null set for some $c\in\mathbb R$
([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).

**Positive semidefiniteness.** Let $z=(z_1,\dots,z_m)\in\mathbb R^m$. The
random variable $W:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ is a finite linear combination of
square-integrable random variables, hence square-integrable, and bilinearity
of covariance ([[lem-variance-and-covariance-identities-for-random-variables]])
gives
$$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=\sum_{i,j=1}^{m}z_iz_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j) =\operatorname{Cov}(W,W)=\operatorname{Var}(W) =E\bigl[(W-E[W])^2\bigr]\ge0 ,$$
the inequality holding because $(W-E[W])^2\ge0$ pointwise and expectation is
monotone ([[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]). If
$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=\operatorname{Var}(W)=0$, Chebyshev's inequality gives
$\mathbb P(|W-E[W]|\ge1/r)=0$ for every integer $r\ge1$; the union of these
events is $\{W\ne E[W]\}$, so $W=E[W]$ almost surely
([[cor-chebyshev-inequality-for-random-variables]]). Conversely, if $W=c$
almost surely, invariance of the integral under almost-everywhere equality
gives $E[W]=c$ and $E[(W-E[W])^2]=0$
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). Hence
$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=0$ exactly when $W$ is almost surely constant, and
$\Sigma$ is positive definite exactly when for every $z\ne0$ the random
variable $\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ fails to be almost surely constant.

No independence hypothesis is used anywhere in this definition; $\Sigma$
records the pairwise covariances of the coordinates.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

diagonal products $|Z_j|^2$ are integrable by the given finite second moment,

$|Z_1\overline{Z_2}|=|Z_1||Z_2|\le(|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2)/2$
pointwise. Hence each entry $\mathbb E[Z_i\overline{Z_j}]$ is a finite complex
expectation under [F1]–[F2], so $\Gamma(\rho)$ is well-defined.

=\mathbb E[\overline{Z_i\overline{Z_j}}]
=\overline{\mathbb E[Z_i\overline{Z_j}]}=\overline{\Gamma_{ij}}$;
the diagonal entries are real and nonnegative. Therefore
$\Gamma^\dagger=\Gamma$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), let $m\ge1$, and let
$X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be a random element with target
$(\mathbb R^m,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m))$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]).
Use the statistical one-based coordinate labels: for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$
write $v_i:=v(i-1)$ for $1\le i\le m$, so
$X_i(\omega)=X(\omega)(i-1)$. Each $X_i$ is a real random variable because
the coordinate projection $x\mapsto x(i-1)$ is continuous and therefore has
Borel preimages of Borel sets
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]).
For every integer $r\ge1$ and matrix
$A\in M_{r\times m}(\mathbb R)$, the notation $A_{ij}$ below means its
zero-based matrix entry
$A(i-1,j-1)$ for $1\le i\le r$ and
$1\le j\le m$; likewise $\Sigma_{ij}$ means the entry at $(i-1,j-1)$ in
the covariance matrix below in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]]. These
are labels for the root library's zero-based function entries, not a different
matrix convention. If $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is open, $h:U\to\mathbb R^r$
has all first partials at $a\in U$, and $A=Jh(a)$, then $A_{ij}$ in this
notation is $\partial_{j-1}h_{i-1}(a)$, with the zero-based Jacobian
convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].
Assume $X$ is **square-integrable**:
$$E\bigl[|X|^2\bigr]=\sum_{i=1}^{m}E\bigl[X_i^2\bigr]<+\infty ,$$
where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
Its **mean vector** is
$$\mu=E[X]:=\bigl(E[X_1],\dots,E[X_m]\bigr)\in\mathbb R^m ,$$
the coordinates being the expectations of
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Its **covariance matrix** is the
$m\times m$ real matrix of [[def-matrix-space]]
$$\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}(X):=\bigl(\Sigma_{ij}\bigr)_{i,j=1}^{m},\qquad \Sigma_{ij}:=E\bigl[(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)\bigr]\in\mathbb R .$$
For the random vector $X$ the entries $\Sigma_{ij}$ are also written
$\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$, and $\Sigma_{ii}=\operatorname{Var}(X_i)$.

### Well-definedness and elementary properties

**Integrability of the entries.** Square-integrability gives
$E[X_i^2]<+\infty$ for each $i$. Since the underlying measure is a
probability measure, the elementary inequality
$$|X_i|\le \tfrac12\bigl(1+X_i^2\bigr)$$
gives $E|X_i|\le\tfrac12(1+E[X_i^2])<+\infty$ by monotonicity and
homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); hence $X_i$
is integrable and $\mu_i=E[X_i]$ is finite
([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]). Also
$$(X_i-\mu_i)^2\le2X_i^2+2\mu_i^2,$$
so $X_i-\mu_i$ is square-integrable; the probability-space inequality
$$|X_i-\mu_i|\le\tfrac12\bigl(1+(X_i-\mu_i)^2\bigr)$$
then makes it integrable as well. Finally
$$|(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)|\le \tfrac12\bigl((X_i-\mu_i)^2+(X_j-\mu_j)^2\bigr),$$
and the right-hand side is integrable by additivity, monotonicity and
homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]],
[[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); hence every
$\Sigma_{ij}$ is a finite real number.

**Symmetry.** For all $i,j$ the real numbers $(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)$ and
$(X_j-\mu_j)(X_i-\mu_i)$ are equal pointwise, so $\Sigma_{ij}=\Sigma_{ji}$;
thus $\Sigma^{\mathsf T}=\Sigma$.

For $M\in M_{m\times m}(\mathbb R)$ and $z\in\mathbb R^m$, write
$$z^{\mathsf T}Mz:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}z_iM_{ij}z_j.$$
For a real symmetric $m\times m$ matrix $M$, **positive semidefinite** means
$z^{\mathsf T}Mz\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^m$, and **positive definite**
means $z^{\mathsf T}Mz>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^m$. For a real
random variable $Z$, **almost surely constant** means that $Z=c$ outside a
measurable $\mathbb P$-null set for some $c\in\mathbb R$
([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).

**Positive semidefiniteness.** Let $z=(z_1,\dots,z_m)\in\mathbb R^m$. The
random variable $W:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ is a finite linear combination of
square-integrable random variables, hence square-integrable, and bilinearity
of covariance ([[lem-variance-and-covariance-identities-for-random-variables]])
gives
$$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=\sum_{i,j=1}^{m}z_iz_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j) =\operatorname{Cov}(W,W)=\operatorname{Var}(W) =E\bigl[(W-E[W])^2\bigr]\ge0 ,$$
the inequality holding because $(W-E[W])^2\ge0$ pointwise and expectation is
monotone ([[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]). If
$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=\operatorname{Var}(W)=0$, Chebyshev's inequality gives
$\mathbb P(|W-E[W]|\ge1/r)=0$ for every integer $r\ge1$; the union of these
events is $\{W\ne E[W]\}$, so $W=E[W]$ almost surely
([[cor-chebyshev-inequality-for-random-variables]]). Conversely, if $W=c$
almost surely, invariance of the integral under almost-everywhere equality
gives $E[W]=c$ and $E[(W-E[W])^2]=0$
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). Hence
$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=0$ exactly when $W$ is almost surely constant, and
$\Sigma$ is positive definite exactly when for every $z\ne0$ the random
variable $\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ fails to be almost surely constant.

No independence hypothesis is used anywhere in this definition; $\Sigma$
records the pairwise covariances of the coordinates.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and $\omega>0$, let $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$,
and let $(E,B)$ be the plane-wave pair of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on
the whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with phase
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$. Suppose the amplitude conditions of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] hold, so that $k\cdot e=0$ and
$b=k\times e/\omega$. By that theorem, if the pair is nonzero then it also
satisfies the dispersion relation $|k|=\omega/c$, while the zero pair is
permitted for every $k\ne0$ and $\omega>0$, both on and off this dispersion
relation. This item classifies the polarization of that class of transverse
plane waves; it adds no field-theoretic content.

Write $e=a+id$ with the real vectors $a=\operatorname{Re}e$ and
$d=\operatorname{Im}e$ of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]],
applied componentwise in $\mathbb C^3$; since $k$ is real and $k\cdot e=0$, the
real and imaginary parts of this complex equation give
$\langle k,a\rangle=\langle k,d\rangle=0$. Put $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, $|\cdot|$ and $\times$ be the inner product, norm
and cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Then:

(a) [Trace] At every fixed $x$ one has
$E(x,t)=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ with $\theta=\theta(x,t)$. The curve
$\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$, $\gamma(\theta):=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$,
lies in the transverse plane
$k^\perp=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:\langle k,v\rangle=0\}$; it is the image of the unit
circle $S^1=\{(u_1,u_2)\in\mathbb R^2:u_1^2+u_2^2=1\}$ under the $\mathbb R$-linear
map $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$; it is $2\pi$-periodic in the phase parameter
$\theta$ and satisfies $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$, while the map
$t\mapsto E(x,t)$ has time period $T=2\pi/\omega$. The curve $\gamma$ is
called the **polarization trace** at $x$; it does not depend on $x$, so the
classification below is the same at every point.

(b) [Classification] Exactly one of the following three cases holds.

(i) **Linear polarization**: $\dim_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$.
When $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=1$, the trace is a nontrivial closed
segment in that span, traversed twice per period; when $a=d=0$, the trace is
the single point $\{0\}$ and $(E,B)$ is the zero wave.

(ii) **Circular polarization**: $|a|=|d|>0$ and $\langle a,d\rangle=0$. The
trace is the circle of radius $|a|$ in $k^\perp$, and $|E(x,t)|=|a|$ for all
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(iii) **Elliptical (nondegenerate, noncircular) polarization**:
$\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$ and not (ii). Here a **nondegenerate ellipse centred at $0$** in a real plane $P$ means
the set $L(S^1)$ for a real-linear isomorphism $L:\mathbb R^2\to P$.
The trace is such an ellipse in $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$, and the
origin lies in the relative interior of the enclosed region
$L(\{u\in\mathbb R^2:|u|\le1\})$ in that plane. If in addition $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, the
parametrization is along principal axes and the semiaxis lengths are $|a|$ and
$|d|$; the general principal-axis computation is not asserted by this item.

(c) [Handedness] For $a,d\in k^\perp$, the cross product $a\times d$ is
orthogonal to $a$ and to $d$
([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), hence parallel
to $k$; define the **helicity sign**
$H:=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle\in\mathbb R$, whose sign is taken in the
order of [[def-real-order]]. One has $H=0$ exactly in the linear case (i), and
$H\ne0$ otherwise. This library calls the polarization **right-handed** when
$H<0$ and **left-handed** when $H>0$. Geometrically, $H<0$ means that at fixed
$x$ the electric vector rotates clockwise as seen by an observer facing the
incoming wave (looking along $-\hat k$), and $H>0$ means counterclockwise;
here the screen orientation is fixed by any positive orthonormal triad
$(u,v,\hat k)$, with $u$ to the right and $v$ up for that observer.
Equivalently, $\langle E(x,t)\times\partial_tE(x,t),\hat k\rangle=\omega H$ for
every $(x,t)$. The names "right" and "left" handedness are conventional and
both conventions occur in the literature, so later statements in this library
use only the sign of $H$.

(d) [Status] This is a classification definition. It introduces the trace,
the three cases and the sign $H$, and asserts no field equation, no
propagation, energy or empirical content. The magnetic amplitude enters only
through the two amplitude conditions $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$
recalled above; the definition covers the zero wave, both on and off the
dispersion relation, and no non-plane or non-transverse field is classified.

### Well-definedness and conventions

The real vectors $a,d$ are well defined by the componentwise real and
imaginary parts of $e$; because $k$ is real, taking real and imaginary parts of
$k\cdot e=\sum_jk_j(a_j+id_j)$ gives $\langle k,a\rangle=0$ and
$\langle k,d\rangle=0$, so $a,d\in k^\perp$ and $\gamma$ takes values in
$k^\perp$. The trace formula in (a) is Euler's formula
$\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of [[thm-eulers-formula]] together with
the field arithmetic on the right-hand side of
$E=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a+id)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\bigr)
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta)+i(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)\bigr)$
and the real-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$: the real part is
$a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$, while the imaginary part is not a field. Since
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$ and $\omega>0$, at fixed $x$ the map
$t\mapsto\theta$ is a bijection onto $\mathbb R$; hence the set traced by
$E(x,t)$ as $t$ varies is the full image $\gamma(\mathbb R)$, independently of
$x$, and $\gamma$ is $2\pi$-periodic with $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$
because $\cos$ and $\sin$ shift by a sign under $\theta\mapsto\theta+\pi$. The
time period is $T=2\pi/\omega$, the least positive $s$ with
$\theta(x,t+s)=\theta(x,t)-2\pi$ for all $(x,t)$; it is distinct from the
phase-parameter period $2\pi$ of $\gamma$.

For the classification, "exactly one of the three cases holds" is checked
case by case: if $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$ then (i); otherwise
$\dim=2$, and either $|a|=|d|>0$ with $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, which is (ii),
or not, which is (iii). In case (i) with $\dim=1$, write $d=\lambda a$ with
$a\ne0$ (or symmetrically $a=\mu d$); then
$\gamma(\theta)=(\cos\theta-\lambda\sin\theta)a$, whose image is the segment
$\{sa:|s|\le\sqrt{1+\lambda^2}\}$ in $\mathbb R a$, traversed once in each direction between successive extrema of the scalar
factor (each such phase interval has length $\pi$). In case (ii),
expanding with the bilinearity of the inner product
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) gives
$|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2-2u_1u_2\langle a,d\rangle=|a|^2$
whenever $|a|=|d|$, $\langle a,d\rangle=0$ and $u_1^2+u_2^2=1$, so the image
of the unit circle under $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is contained in the
circle of radius $|a|$ in the plane $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; conversely,
for every $v$ in that plane with $|v|=|a|$ the coordinates
$u_1=\langle v,a\rangle/|a|^2$ and $u_2=-\langle v,d\rangle/|d|^2$ satisfy
$u_1^2+u_2^2=1$ and $u_1a-u_2d=v$, because $a/|a|$ and $d/|d|$ are orthonormal
and $v=\langle v,a/|a|\rangle(a/|a|)+\langle v,d/|d|\rangle(d/|d|)$; hence the
trace is exactly that circle. In case (iii) the vectors $a,d$
are linearly independent, so $T:(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is a linear
isomorphism of $\mathbb R^2$ onto the two-dimensional plane
$\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; the image of the closed unit disk under $T$ is a
compact convex subset with nonempty interior in that plane, the image of the
open disk is its nonempty interior, and the image of the unit circle is its
boundary, so the trace is a nondegenerate ellipse centred at
$0=T(0)$ with the origin in the relative interior of that enclosed region.
The trace itself is its boundary and has empty interior in the plane. If moreover
$\langle a,d\rangle=0$, then along the principal axes $a,d$ the parametrization
$u_1a-u_2d$ has the stated axis lengths because the two summands are
orthogonal: $|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2$; no computation of
principal axes for general $a,d$ is used or claimed.

For (c), the cross product $a\times d$ is orthogonal to both factors and
alternating ([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), and the real Gram identity
[[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]] says
$|a\times d|^2>0$ exactly when $a,d$ are linearly independent. Thus
$a\times d=0$ holds exactly when $a$ and $d$ are linearly dependent, that is,
in case (i); then $H=0$. Otherwise $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$, and
since $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\subseteq k^\perp$ are both two-dimensional,
they are equal; being orthogonal to $a$ and $d$, the vector $a\times d$ is
orthogonal to $k^\perp$, whose orthogonal complement in $\mathbb R^3$ is the
line $\mathbb R k$, so $a\times d=\mu k$ for a real $\mu$ and
$H=\mu|k|\ne0$. For the rotation identity, differentiating
$E=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ along $t$ with $\partial_t\theta=-\omega$ gives
$\partial_tE=\omega(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)$, so
$E\times\partial_tE
=\omega(a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta)\times(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)
=\omega\bigl((\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)a\times d
+\cos\theta\sin\theta(a\times a-d\times d)\bigr)=\omega\,a\times d$
by bilinearity and alternation, and taking the inner product with $\hat k$
gives the displayed identity. As a concrete check of the convention, take
$\hat k=e_3$ with the positive orthonormal screen triad $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, so
that $e_1$ points right and $e_2$ up for the observer looking along $-e_3$;
then $e=e_1-ie_2$ has $a=e_1$, $d=-e_2$,
$E(0,t)=\cos(\omega t)e_1-\sin(\omega t)e_2$ (clockwise), and
$H=\langle e_1\times(-e_2),e_3\rangle=-1<0$, consistently with the
right-handed naming. This fixes the sign convention of the cited treatment:
the source writes $E_0=\alpha-i\beta$ and calls the polarization right-handed
if and only if $\beta=\hat k\times\alpha$, which under $a=\alpha$,
$d=-\beta$ is $H=-|\alpha|^2<0$ in the circular case.

Finally, all amplitudes $e,b$ and vectors $k,a,d$ are constant and all
quantities above are computed from them by the operations of the cited items;
no limit, no integral and no field equation is used, and the definition is at
the level of classification only.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty, bounded, connected open set with smooth boundary, meaning each boundary point has Euclidean coordinates in which $\Omega$ is one side of a smooth graph. Use Euclidean coordinates $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$, let $\delta=\sum_{i=1}^3dx^i\otimes dx^i$, write $\partial_i=\partial/\partial x^i$, and set $\Delta=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i^2$. A multi-index is $\beta=(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3)\in\mathbb N_0^3$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$; write $|\beta|=\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3$ and $D^\beta=\partial_1^{\beta_1}\partial_2^{\beta_2}\partial_3^{\beta_3}$. Fix $0<\alpha<1$, a real function $S\in C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $S\geq0$, and a real dimensionless parameter $\varepsilon$. For a real function $g$ on $\overline\Omega$, define

$$[g]_{0,\alpha}:=\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|g(x)-g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha},\qquad \|g\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}:=\sup_{\overline\Omega}|g|+[g]_{0,\alpha},$$

and let $C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ consist of the continuous functions with finite displayed norm. Define $C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ to consist of functions whose derivatives through order $2$ on $\Omega$ extend continuously to $\overline\Omega$ and whose norm

$$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}:=\sum_{|\beta|\leq2}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta u|+\sum_{|\beta|=2}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha}$$

is finite, where $\beta$ is a multi-index. Write $X:=\{u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$, with its inherited norm, and $Y:=C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$. The bounded-domain charged conformal problem is to find $u\in X$ such that $\psi:=1+u>0$ on $\overline\Omega$ and

$$-8\Delta\psi=2\varepsilon^2 S\psi^{-3}\quad\hbox{in }\Omega,\qquad \psi|_{\partial\Omega}=1.$$

In the conformal-seed specialization $\bar h=\delta$, $\bar A=0$, $\tau=0$, and $\Lambda=0$ (so $h=\psi^4\delta$ and $K=0$), the initial data are time-symmetric, meaning their second fundamental form is $K=0$. The scalar equation is the Hamiltonian constraint from the conformal electrovacuum transformation when $S=|\bar E_0|_\delta^2+|\bar B_0|_\delta^2$. Here $\bar E_0,\bar B_0:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ are independently prescribed contravariant Euclidean vector fields, each the restriction of a smooth map on an open neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, and divergence-free means $\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i\bar E_0^i=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i\bar B_0^i=0$ on $\Omega$ in these Cartesian coordinates. The actual barred seed fields are $\bar E=\varepsilon\bar E_0$ and $\bar B=\varepsilon\bar B_0$. In geometric length coordinates, $\psi,\varepsilon$ are dimensionless, $\bar E_0,\bar B_0$ have units of inverse length, and $S$ has units of inverse length squared. This is a specialization with prescribed fields; the general problem allows any nonnegative $S\in C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$. The definition does not assert existence, uniqueness, a momentum constraint, or an asymptotically Euclidean or puncture solution.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For the problem of *Bounded-domain charged conformal problem*, there are $\rho>0$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, and $C<\infty$ such that for each $|\varepsilon|<\varepsilon_0$ there is exactly one solution $u_\varepsilon\in X$ with $\|u_\varepsilon\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}<\rho$. The corresponding $\psi_\varepsilon=1+u_\varepsilon$ satisfies $\psi_\varepsilon\geq1$ on $\overline\Omega$. If $v\in X$ is the unique solution of $-8\Delta v=2S$ in $\Omega$, $v=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, then

$$\|u_\varepsilon-\varepsilon^2v\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\leq C|\varepsilon|^4.$$

The constants may depend on $\Omega,\alpha,S$, and the uniqueness is only in the fixed neighborhood $\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}<\rho$; no global uniqueness, asymptotically Euclidean solution, puncture solution, or non-CMC result is asserted. The $O(\varepsilon^4)$ statement means the displayed bound for all $|\varepsilon|<\varepsilon_0$.

Let $\Sigma$ be a nonempty oriented smooth three-manifold without boundary. Let $\bar h$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, let $\psi\in C^\infty(\Sigma,(0,\infty))$, let $\bar E,\bar B$ be smooth contravariant vector fields, let $\bar A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor with $\bar h^{ij}\bar A_{ij}=0$, let $\tau\in C^\infty(\Sigma,\mathbb R)$, and let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be constant. Let $c,G,\mu_0>0$ and $\kappa=8\pi G/c^4$ be the parameters of the inherited SI-to-geometric dictionary, and set $\alpha=\sqrt{\kappa/(2\mu_0)}>0$. Define

$$h:=\psi^4\bar h,\qquad K:=\frac{\tau}{3}h+\psi^{-2}\bar A,\qquad E:=\psi^{-6}\bar E,\qquad B:=\psi^{-6}\bar B.$$

The fields $E$ and $B$ are geometric-normalized spatial vectors: in length coordinates their components have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Their SI-convention counterparts are $e:=\alpha^{-1}E$ and $b:=\alpha^{-1}B$. In length coordinates, metric components and $\psi$ are dimensionless, $\tau$ and the covariant components of $\bar A$ and $K$ have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$, and $\Lambda$ has units $\mathrm m^{-2}$. The tuple $(\Sigma,\bar h,\psi,\bar A,\tau,\bar E,\bar B,\Lambda)$ with these induced fields is called conformal electrovacuum seed data. This definition imposes no divergence, Hamiltonian, or momentum equation and asserts no existence, uniqueness, or spacetime development.

Use the smooth conformal seed data defined in this development on an oriented smooth three-manifold, and let $D$ and $\bar D$ be the Levi-Civita connections of $h=\psi^4\bar h$ and $\bar h$. Define $\Delta_{\bar h}\psi:=\bar h^{ij}\bar D_i\partial_j\psi$, with the Euclidean convention $\Delta=\sum_i\partial_i^2$ in Cartesian coordinates. Use the spatial curvature sign and scalar-curvature contraction fixed for induced data in the preceding Gauss-Codazzi convention. Let $e=\alpha^{-1}\psi^{-6}\bar E$ and $b=\alpha^{-1}\psi^{-6}\bar B$ be the SI-convention vector fields associated with the inherited constrained electrovacuum initial-data convention. Then the two Maxwell divergence constraints are equivalent to

$$\bar D_i\bar E^i=0,\qquad \bar D_i\bar B^i=0,$$

and the SI Hamiltonian constraint in that definition is equivalent to

$$-8\Delta_{\bar h}\psi+\bar R\,\psi-|\bar A|_{\bar h}^2\psi^{-7}+\left(\frac{2}{3}\tau^2-2\Lambda\right)\psi^5-2\left(|\bar E|_{\bar h}^2+|\bar B|_{\bar h}^2\right)\psi^{-3}=0.$$

Here $\bar R$ is the scalar curvature of $\bar h$ in the stated convention, and the barred norms use $\bar h$ to raise and lower indices. The exact vector divergence identities are $D_iE^i=\psi^{-6}\bar D_i\bar E^i$ and $D_iB^i=\psi^{-6}\bar D_i\bar B^i$. The separate momentum constraint remains

$$D^jK_{ji}-D_i\tau=-2\psi^{-6}(\bar E\times_{\bar h}\bar B)_i,$$

where the cross product on the right is lowered with $\bar h$. In particular, if $K=0$ and $\bar E\times_{\bar h}\bar B=0$, the momentum equation holds. The transformed scalar equation alone does not impose the momentum constraint and gives no elliptic existence theorem.

Let $\Sigma$ be a nonempty, smooth, oriented three-manifold without boundary. Let $h$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, let $K$ be a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor, and let $e,b$ be smooth vector fields tangent to $\Sigma$. For data induced on an embedded spacelike slice $i:\Sigma\hookrightarrow M$, let $n$ be its future unit normal, let $F$ be the smooth two-form of [[def-emg-electrovacuum-cauchy-system]], and define spatial covectors $\mathcal E,\mathcal B\in\Omega^1(\Sigma)$ by $\mathcal E(X):=F(X,n)$ and $\mathcal B(X):=-({\star_gF})(X,n)$ for $X\in T\Sigma$. Identify these with vector fields using the positive metric $h$: $e:=\sharp_h\mathcal E$ and $b:=\sharp_h\mathcal B$, so in any coordinates $e^i=h^{ij}\mathcal E_j$ and $b^i=h^{ij}\mathcal B_j$. Equivalently, $\mathcal E$ is the restriction of the observer electric covector $E/c$ and $\mathcal B$ the restriction of the observer magnetic covector $B$ of [[lem-emg-observer-field-decomposition]]. For an abstract data tuple not assumed to come from $F$, $e,b$ are simply the specified tangent vector fields. This fixes the convention without adding a potential or an existence assumption.

For the observer-covector comparison above, the smooth normal along $\Sigma$ has local smooth ambient extensions by [[lem-gr-spacelike-hypersurface-normal-and-second-fundamental-form]]; shrinking and normalizing an extension gives an observer congruence to which [[lem-emg-observer-field-decomposition]] applies. The restrictions $\mathcal E,\mathcal B$ depend only on $n|_\Sigma$, so they are independent of the chosen extension.

Write $h^{ij}$ for the inverse matrix to $h_{ij}$ and use $h$ to raise every spatial index. Let $D$ and $R(h)$ denote the Levi-Civita connection and scalar curvature of $h$, set $\tau:=h^{ij}K_{ij}$ and $|K|_h^2:=h^{ik}h^{j\ell}K_{ij}K_{k\ell}$, and choose the induced spatial orientation so $\operatorname{vol}_g=\theta^0\wedge\operatorname{vol}_h=-n^\flat\wedge\operatorname{vol}_h$ in a positively oriented normal coframe with $\theta^0(n)=1$. Define the spatial cross product by $h(e\times_hb,w)=\operatorname{vol}_h(e,b,w)$ for each tangent vector $w$.

For the fixed parameters $(\kappa,\Lambda,\mu_0)$ of [[def-emg-electrovacuum-cauchy-system]], the tuple $(\Sigma,h,K,e,b)$ is **constrained electrovacuum initial data** when

$$D_ie^i=0,\qquad D_ib^i=0,$$

$$R(h)+\tau^2-|K|_h^2=2\Lambda+\frac{\kappa}{\mu_0}\bigl(|e|_h^2+|b|_h^2\bigr),$$

$$D^jK_{ji}-D_i\tau=-\frac{\kappa}{\mu_0}(e\times_hb)_i.$$

Here the last display is an equality of covectors. The scalar-curvature form is the Gauss-Codazzi form of the normal projections in [[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]]; the sign and $K$ convention are those of [[def-gr-spacelike-initial-data-and-constraints]] and [[def-emg-electrovacuum-cauchy-system]]. This definition asserts no existence or uniqueness of a spacetime development.

For the periodic high-regularity class, use the dimensionless coordinate $\theta^i$ and length coordinate $X^i=L_0\theta^i$ of [[def-emg-periodic-high-sobolev-state]], for a fixed $L_0>0$. The arrays $h_{ij}$ and $K_{ij}$ are the length-coordinate covariant components with $h_{ij}\in H^{s+1}$ and $K_{ij}\in H^s$. The Sobolev components of $e,b$ are $e_A=h(e,\mathsf e_A)$ and $b_A=h(b,\mathsf e_A)$ in the canonical positively oriented $h$-orthonormal frame $\mathsf e_A$ specified there; thus $e_A,b_A\in H^s$. If $\mathsf e_A=E_A^i\partial_{X^i}$, their coordinate components are $e^i=E_A^i e_A$ and $b^i=E_A^i b_A$. The coefficients $E_A^i$ are smooth functions of the positive matrix $h_{ij}$; on the compact range of each such metric, [[lem-gr-smooth-composition-and-commutator-estimates]] puts them in $H^{s+1}$ and [[lem-gr-periodic-sobolev-algebra]] makes the coordinate components $H^s$ as well.

For these representatives define the spatial connection coefficients by $\Gamma(h)^k{}_{ij}=\tfrac12h^{k\ell}(\partial_{X^i}h_{j\ell}+\partial_{X^j}h_{i\ell}-\partial_{X^\ell}h_{ij})$, with $\partial_{X^i}=L_0^{-1}\partial_{\theta^i}$. On coordinate vector components put $D_i e^j=\partial_{X^i}e^j+\Gamma(h)^j{}_{ik}e^k$ and $D_i b^j=\partial_{X^i}b^j+\Gamma(h)^j{}_{ik}b^k$; on the covariant tensor $K$ put $D_iK_{jk}=\partial_{X^i}K_{jk}-\Gamma(h)^\ell{}_{ij}K_{\ell k}-\Gamma(h)^\ell{}_{ik}K_{j\ell}$. Define $R(h)$ by $R^a{}_{bij}=\partial_{X^i}\Gamma(h)^a{}_{jb}-\partial_{X^j}\Gamma(h)^a{}_{ib}+\Gamma(h)^a{}_{ic}\Gamma(h)^c{}_{jb}-\Gamma(h)^a{}_{jc}\Gamma(h)^c{}_{ib}$, followed by the Ricci and scalar contractions of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Sobolev embedding gives $h\in C^{s-1}$ and $K,e,b\in C^{s-2}$; the uniform positive lower eigenvalue makes $h^{-1}$ well defined, and the smooth-composition and algebra suppliers give $\Gamma(h)\in H^s$, $R(h)\in H^{s-1}$, and $D K,D e,D b\in H^{s-1}$. Since $s\ge5$, these constraint terms have continuous representatives, and their displayed equalities mean pointwise equality of those representatives. In the SI interpretation, $K$ and $D$ carry one inverse-length factor, $R(h)$ and $\Lambda$ carry inverse-length squared, and the orthonormal components $e_A,b_A$ have units tesla; the factors $\kappa/\mu_0$ give matching units in the constraints. No numerical parameter values are assigned here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded smooth domain and choose $R>0$ with $\Omega\subset(-R,R)^3$. Write $H^1_0(\Omega)$ for the $H^1$ closure of the compactly supported smooth functions. Then $\|v\|_{L^2}\le2R\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. A function $u\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$ represents an element of $H^1_0(\Omega)$ if and only if $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $L$ and its form $a$ be as in [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. **Homogeneous problem.** Given $F\in H^{-1}(\Omega)$ ([[def-h-minus-one-as-the-dual-of-h-one-zero]]), a **weak solution** of $Lu=F$ with zero boundary values is a class $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1_0(\Omega).$$ **Inhomogeneous problem.** Additionally assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for the trace supplier, and let $n\ge2$ and $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]), let $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega):=W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$ in the boundary scale of [[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]] and let $T$ be the trace operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. A weak solution with boundary data $g$ is a class $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $Tu=g$ and $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. The defining identities are identities between functionals on the $H^1_0$ classes, so they are independent of the chosen almost-everywhere representatives of $u$, of the coefficients and of the data ([[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); the boundary condition is imposed through the trace of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]], never by pointwise evaluation. The Dirichlet condition is imposed by $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ in the homogeneous problem and by $Tu=g$ in the inhomogeneous problem; testing against $v\in H^1_0$ expresses the weak equation and does not by itself impose boundary data; the integrals are the ones proved absolutely convergent in [[lem-elliptic-form-is-well-defined-and-bounded]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded
$C^{k+2}$ domain, $n\ge2$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$k\ge0$, let $L,a$ be as in
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with
$a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega)$, $b^i,c\in W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ and all
coefficient derivatives bounded, and let $f\in H^k(\Omega)$. If
$u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $Lu=f$ with zero boundary values
([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]), then
$u\in H^{k+2}(\Omega)$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}(\Omega)}\le C\big(\|f\|_{H^k(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\big),$$
with $C$ depending only on $n,k,\Omega$ and the coefficient bounds. The
derivative gain is exactly two orders; the boundary regularity required at
order $k$ is $C^{k+2}$, the coefficient regularity one order above the data
order, and the companion page records the sharp two-derivative example. For
$k=0$ the theorem is
[[thm-global-h-two-dirichlet-regularity]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$ with $kp>n$. Then there is $C(n,p,k,\Omega)$ with
$$\|uv\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\|v\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u,v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)),$$
so $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ is a Banach algebra; the constants and the conclusion may depend on the choice of equivalent Sobolev norm only through $C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p<\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then the set of restrictions
to $\Omega$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ is dense in
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|\varphi|_\Omega-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$.

The exponent range is $1\le p<\infty$; the result asserts no density in the
$W^{k,\infty}$ norm, and it does not hold on arbitrary open sets, as the
companion examples page shows.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: The base fields are smooth and $\partial_i\bar E_0^i=\partial_i\bar B_0^i=0$, so the source in [F1] is the constant $S=a^2$, and scaling them by $\varepsilon$ preserves their zero divergences. The units are consistent: $a^2$ and $\Delta$ have units of inverse length squared, while $\psi$ and $\varepsilon$ are dimensionless.

On $B_R(0)$, define $v(x):=\frac{a^2}{24}(R^2-|x|^2)$. It vanishes on $\partial B_R$, and $\Delta |x|^2=6$ in $\mathbb R^3$, so $-8\Delta v=-8(-6a^2/24)=2a^2=2S$. By uniqueness of the zero-boundary solution in [F2], this is the coefficient in the branch expansion.

Smoothness bootstrap, initial gain. Set $u=u_\varepsilon=\psi_\varepsilon-1$ and $f=(\varepsilon^2a^2/4)\psi_\varepsilon^{-3}$, so $-\Delta u=f$ and $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. The branch gives $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ and $\psi_\varepsilon\ge1$. The identities $\partial_i(\psi^{-3})=-3\psi^{-4}\partial_i\psi$ and $\partial_{ij}(\psi^{-3})=12\psi^{-5}(\partial_i\psi)(\partial_j\psi)-3\psi^{-4}\partial_{ij}\psi$ follow from [F11] and the product rule and show that $f\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$, with bounded derivatives through order two, hence $f\in H^2(\Omega)$ by integration by parts against compactly supported tests. By [F6], $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. Its classical equation tested against $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ gives the weak identity; continuity of both sides in the $H^1$ test norm and the defining density of $C_c^\infty$ in $H^1_0$ extend it to every test in $H^1_0$. Applying [F8] with $m=2$ yields $u\in H^4(\Omega)$.

Smoothness bootstrap, composition and iteration. Fix an integer $m\ge4$ and suppose $\psi=1+u\in H^m(\Omega)$. Its continuous range is a compact interval $J\subset[1,\infty)$ by [F2] and [F9]. To verify $\psi^{-3}\in H^m$, use [F10] to choose smooth restrictions $\psi_n\to\psi$ in $H^m$; [F9] gives uniform convergence, so for all sufficiently large $n$ the values of $\psi_n$ lie in one compact interval $J'\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $J$. For each smooth $q$ with values in $J'$, repeated application of the total chain and product rules [F11] expresses every $D^\beta(q^{-3})$, $|\beta|\le m$, as a finite sum of bounded factors $G^{(r)}(q)$, $G(s)=s^{-3}$, times products $\prod_jD^{\gamma_j}q$ with $|\gamma_j|\ge1$ and $\sum_j|\gamma_j|=|\beta|$. Each product is in $L^2$ with a bound controlled by $\|q\|_{H^m}$: derivatives of order at most $m-2$ lie in $H^2$ or a higher Sobolev space and hence in $L^\infty$ by [F9]; a factor of order $m$ can occur only alone and is in $L^2$; a factor of order $m-1$ occurs at most once, lies in $H^1\subset L^6$, and any remaining factor has total derivative order at most one and lies in $L^\infty$. Thus $q\mapsto G'(q)$ is uniformly bounded in $H^m$ on the bounded smooth approximants and their line segments. The same difference identity applied to $G'$ shows $t\mapsto G'(\psi_\ell+t(\psi_n-\psi_\ell))$ is continuous in $H^m$, so its displayed integral exists as a Banach-valued Riemann integral. The identity $G(\psi_n)-G(\psi_\ell)=(\psi_n-\psi_\ell)\int_0^1G'(\psi_\ell+t(\psi_n-\psi_\ell))\,dt$, together with the Banach-algebra bound [F9], shows $G(\psi_n)$ is Cauchy in $H^m$. Its uniform limit is $G(\psi)$, proving $\psi^{-3}\in H^m$. Hence $f\in H^m$; [F8] gives $u\in H^{m+2}$. Starting with $m=4$ and repeating for $m=4,6,8,\ldots$ proves $u\in H^{2j}(\Omega)$ for every sufficiently large integer $j$. The same embeddings imply $u\in H^r(\Omega)$ for every finite integer $r$, and then $u\in C^k(\overline\Omega)$ for every $k$, so $\psi_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega)$.

Verification of the full constraints. On the oriented manifold without boundary $\Sigma=\Omega$, take the conformal seed data $\bar h=\delta$, $\bar A=0$, $\tau=0$, $\Lambda=0$, $\bar E=\varepsilon a e_1$, and $\bar B=0$. Smoothness and positivity of $\psi_\varepsilon$ follow from steps 3.1–4.1 and [F2], so [F3] defines smooth $h,K,E,B$ and gives $K=0$. The Maxwell constraints hold because $\partial_i\bar E^i=\partial_i\bar B^i=0$ by step 1.1 and the barred metric is Euclidean. Since $\bar R=0$ and $|\bar E|_\delta^2=\varepsilon^2a^2$, the transformed Hamiltonian constraint [F4] is exactly $-8\Delta\psi_\varepsilon=2\varepsilon^2a^2\psi_\varepsilon^{-3}$, the branch equation. Its transformed momentum equation has zero left side because $K=\tau=0$ and zero right side because $\bar E\times_\delta\bar B=0$. Thus all four constraints in [F5] hold. The data are smooth constrained time-symmetric data on this fixed ball; the Dirichlet boundary value is prescribed, and the proof makes no claim of an isolated asymptotically flat black hole or any other boundary-value problem.
