supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $Y$ be a dense linear subspace of $H$ that is itself
a Hilbert space continuously embedded in $H$ (for instance $Y=D(A_0)$ with the
graph norm of a self-adjoint $A_0$), let $T>0$, and let $A(t)$ for
$t\in[0,T]$ be an operator with $D(A(t))=Y$, self-adjoint as an operator on $H$,
such that $t\mapsto A(t)$ belongs to $C^1([0,T];\mathcal B(Y,H))$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). Put $L:=\sup_t\|A'(t)\|_{\mathcal B(Y,H)}$.
Then:

(a) *Existence and uniqueness of a strong propagator.* There is a family
$U(t,s)$, $0\le s\le t\le T$, of unitary operators on $H$ with:
$U(s,s)=I$; $U(t,s)U(s,r)=U(t,r)$; $(t,s)\mapsto U(t,s)\xi$ continuous on
$\{s\le t\}$ for each $\xi\in H$; $U(t,s)Y=Y$ with
$\|U(t,s)y\|_Y\le C_T\|y\|_Y$ for a constant $C_T$ independent of
$(s,t)\in[0,T]^2$; and for every $y\in Y$ the map $t\mapsto U(t,s)y$ is $C^1$
in $H$ with
$$i\,\partial_tU(t,s)y=A(t)U(t,s)y,\qquad s\le t\le T.$$

(b) *Uniqueness.* If $V(t,s)$ is another family of bounded linear operators on $H$ with the same strong equation
on $Y$, $V(s,s)=I$ and $\sup_{r}\|V(r,s)y\|_{H}<\infty$, then $V=U$.

(c) *Equations for the reverse and adjoint.* $U(t,s)Y=Y$ for all $0\le s\le t\le T$
and $U(s,t):=U(t,s)^{-1}$ satisfies $i\partial_sU(s,t)y=A(s)U(s,t)y$ for
$y\in Y$; $U(t,s)^*=U(s,t)$. Equivalently, differentiating the second
argument of the forward propagator gives $i\partial_sU(t,s)y=-U(t,s)A(s)y$.
The domain maps are jointly strongly continuous in $Y$.

The theorem is stated for the abstract family $A$; a physical generator is
obtained by $A=H_{\mathrm{energy}}/\hbar$ after choosing a time unit.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d\ge1$, let $U\in C^2(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R)$, and let $M$ be real symmetric positive definite. Set
$$H(q,p)=U(q)+\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p,\qquad F(q,p)=(M^{-1}p,-\nabla U(q)).$$
Assume Countable Choice. Call this vector field **complete** when the solution through every $(q,p)$ exists for all $t\in\mathbb R$. If $F$ is complete, it has a unique global $C^1$ flow $\Phi_t$, which conserves $H$ and satisfies
$$\det D\Phi_t(q,p)=1\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$
Thus it preserves phase-space Lebesgue volume. Completeness is an explicit hypothesis. In particular, if $\nabla U$ is globally $L$-Lipschitz, then $F$ is globally Lipschitz with constant $C=\max\{\|M^{-1}\|_F,L\}$, so the global-existence and stability corollaries apply and
$$\|\Phi_t(z)-\Phi_t(w)\|_2\le e^{C|t|}\|z-w\|_2.$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let U⊂R^n be open and Y:U→R^n be C¹. There is a unique maximal flow Φ on an open domain
D⊂R×U containing {0}×U, and Φ is jointly C¹. Its time slices are local C¹
diffeomorphisms with inverse Φ_{−t}; $\partial_t\Phi=Y(\Phi)$ and $D_p\Phi$ is the
unique solution V of $V′=DY(\Phi)V$, V(0)=I. Each regular point has a C¹ flow box. If Y
is C², Φ and those flow boxes are C²; the second state variation W satisfies
$W′=DY(\Phi)W+D²Y(\Phi)[Ve_i,Ve_j]$, W(0)=0. Individual trajectories of a C¹ field are
C² in time. A trajectory remaining in a compact K⊂⊂U cannot have a finite maximal
endpoint. These Euclidean conclusions use no full AC or DC.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$, $d$, and $P$ satisfy [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]], with constant rank $r$. Write $U(r)=\{g\in\mathbb C^{r\times r}:g^*g=gg^*=I_r\}$ for the unitary group. The curvature of the projected connection $\nabla=P\,d$, as an endomorphism-valued two-form on $\mathbb C^d$, is
$$F=P(dP\wedge dP)P.$$
For any local $C^2$ orthonormal frame $V:U\to\mathbb C^{d\times r}$ with $V^*V=I_r$ and $P=VV^*$, its connection matrix $A=V^*dV$ is anti-Hermitian and its curvature matrix is $F_{\mathrm{fr}}=dA+A\wedge A=V^*FV$. If $V'=Vg$ for a $C^2$ map $g:U\to U(r)$, then $A'=g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg$ and $F'_{\mathrm{fr}}=g^{-1}F_{\mathrm{fr}}g$. Along every $C^2$ path, Kato transport is unitary and intertwines the endpoint projectors.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a compact boundaryless oriented smooth surface, let $d\geq1$, and let $P:\Sigma\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ family of rank-one orthogonal projections. Let $E_P\to\Sigma$ be the complex line bundle with fibers $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$, let $\nabla=P\,d$, and let $F=P(dP\wedge dP)P$ be the curvature of this projected connection. Then
$$\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F=\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle\in\mathbb Z.$$
Here $c_1(E_P)$ is the first integral Chern class of the underlying topological complex line bundle, and $[\Sigma]$ is the fundamental class for the stated orientation.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector
space, and let $k\geq0$. A **smooth $V$-valued differential $k$-form** on
$M$ is a family of alternating $k$-linear maps

$$\alpha_p:(T_pM)^k\longrightarrow V$$

such that $\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a scalar smooth $k$-form in the sense of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]] for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Equivalently,
for one (and hence every) basis $(v_1,\ldots,v_r)$ of $V$, the unique
components in $\alpha=\sum_i v_i\alpha^i$ all belong to $\Omega^k(M)$.

For such an $\alpha$, its **componentwise exterior derivative** is the unique
$V$-valued $(k+1)$-form $d_V\alpha$ characterized by

$$\lambda\circ d_V\alpha=d(\lambda\circ\alpha)$$

for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Indeed, in a basis with dual basis
$(\lambda^1,\ldots,\lambda^r)$, set

$$d_V\alpha=\sum_i v_i\,d\alpha^i,\qquad \alpha^i=\lambda^i\circ\alpha.$$

The scalar formula defining $d$ is real-linear term by term
[[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]], and its
output is a smooth form
[[lem-the-invariant-exterior-derivative-formula-is-c-infinity-multilinear]].
Thus the displayed construction has the stated characterization. It is
independent of the chosen basis because linear functionals separate points of
$V$, and the characterization also proves uniqueness.

The two smoothness descriptions are equivalent in both directions: testing
all $\lambda$ includes the dual basis components, while every
$\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a fixed real linear combination of the components in
one basis. If $M$ is empty, these assignments and identities are vacuous. If
$V=0$, there is only the zero-valued form and its derivative is zero; if
$\dim V=1$, the definition is exactly the scalar definition after choosing
one nonzero basis vector. No metric, nondegeneracy, manifold boundary, or
endpoint is involved. A single finite basis exists by finite-dimensionality;
the definition is basis-independent and chooses no basis or family, so no
choice axiom is used.

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a compact boundaryless oriented smooth surface, let $d\geq1$, and let $P:\Sigma\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ family of rank-one orthogonal projections. Let $E_P\to\Sigma$ be the complex line bundle with fibers $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$, let $\nabla=P\,d$, and let $F=P(dP\wedge dP)P$ be the curvature of this projected connection. Then
$$\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F=\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle\in\mathbb Z.$$
Here $c_1(E_P)$ is the first integral Chern class of the underlying topological complex line bundle, and $[\Sigma]$ is the fundamental class for the stated orientation.

neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector
space, and let $k\geq0$. A **smooth $V$-valued differential $k$-form** on
$M$ is a family of alternating $k$-linear maps

$$\alpha_p:(T_pM)^k\longrightarrow V$$

such that $\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a scalar smooth $k$-form in the sense of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]] for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Equivalently,
for one (and hence every) basis $(v_1,\ldots,v_r)$ of $V$, the unique
components in $\alpha=\sum_i v_i\alpha^i$ all belong to $\Omega^k(M)$.

For such an $\alpha$, its **componentwise exterior derivative** is the unique
$V$-valued $(k+1)$-form $d_V\alpha$ characterized by

$$\lambda\circ d_V\alpha=d(\lambda\circ\alpha)$$

for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Indeed, in a basis with dual basis
$(\lambda^1,\ldots,\lambda^r)$, set

$$d_V\alpha=\sum_i v_i\,d\alpha^i,\qquad \alpha^i=\lambda^i\circ\alpha.$$

The scalar formula defining $d$ is real-linear term by term
[[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]], and its
output is a smooth form
[[lem-the-invariant-exterior-derivative-formula-is-c-infinity-multilinear]].
Thus the displayed construction has the stated characterization. It is
independent of the chosen basis because linear functionals separate points of
$V$, and the characterization also proves uniqueness.

The two smoothness descriptions are equivalent in both directions: testing
all $\lambda$ includes the dual basis components, while every
$\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a fixed real linear combination of the components in
one basis. If $M$ is empty, these assignments and identities are vacuous. If
$V=0$, there is only the zero-valued form and its derivative is zero; if
$\dim V=1$, the definition is exactly the scalar definition after choosing
one nonzero basis vector. No metric, nondegeneracy, manifold boundary, or
endpoint is involved. A single finite basis exists by finite-dimensionality;
the definition is basis-independent and chooses no basis or family, so no
choice axiom is used.

Write $n=(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta)$ and use
$$\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Direct multiplication of the displayed matrices gives $\sigma_j^2=I$ and $\sigma_j\sigma_k+\sigma_k\sigma_j=0$ for $j\ne k$, while each $\sigma_j$ has trace zero. Hence $(n\cdot\sigma)^2=(n_x^2+n_y^2+n_z^2)I=I$ and $\operatorname{tr}(n\cdot\sigma)=0$, so $P_+$ is a rank-one orthogonal projector. On the northern chart, $u_N=(\cos(\theta/2),e^{i\phi}\sin(\theta/2))^T$ is a unit frame and $A_N=u_N^*du_N=i(1-\cos\theta)d\phi/2$, giving $dA_N=(i/2)\omega$. On the southern chart $u_S=e^{-i\phi}u_N$ is regular, and $A_S=A_N-i\,d\phi=-i(1+\cos\theta)d\phi/2$, so $dA_S=(i/2)\omega$ there as well. By [F1], these local calculations identify the global curvature trace as $\operatorname{tr}F_+=(i/2)\omega$.

Use orientation-preserving disk coordinates to identify each $D^2$ with $\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|\leq1\}$ oriented by $dx\wedge dy$. The explicit collar is $(q,t)\mapsto(1-t)q$, where $q=e^{i\theta}\in S^1$ and $t=1-r\geq0$ is inward radial distance. Since $dx\wedge dy=r\,d\theta\wedge dt$, the induced boundary orientation at $t=0$ is increasing $\theta$ (counterclockwise). Define $h(s)=e^{-1/s}$ for $s>0$ and $h(s)=0$ for $s\leq0$. For $0\leq t\leq\epsilon/2$ set $\chi_0(t)=h(t)/(h(t)+h(\epsilon/2-t))$, and for $t\geq\epsilon/2$ set $\chi_0(t)=1$. Every derivative of $h$ vanishes at $0$, so $\chi_0$ is smooth, flat at $0$, positive for $t>0$, at most $1$, and equal to $1$ near $\epsilon$; hence $\int_0^\epsilon\chi_0(t)\,dt<\epsilon$. Put $b(t)=h(t-\epsilon/4)h(3\epsilon/4-t)$, a nonnegative smooth function supported in $[\epsilon/4,3\epsilon/4]$ with positive integral, and define $\chi=\chi_0+c b$ where $c=(\epsilon-\int_0^\epsilon\chi_0)/\int_0^\epsilon b>0$. Then $\chi$ is positive for $t>0$, flat at $0$, equals $1$ near $\epsilon$, and has integral $\epsilon$. Set $\rho(t)=\int_0^t\chi(s)\,ds$. Thus $\rho(0)=\rho'(0)=\rho''(0)=0$, $\rho'(t)>0$ for $t>0$, and $\rho(t)=t$ near $\epsilon$. Replace $f_j(q,t)$ by $f_j(q,\rho(t))$ in each collar. This preserves area integral: the pullback coefficient is multiplied by $\rho'(t)$, and substitution $s=\rho(t)$ gives the original integral. Now form $X=D_0^2\cup_{S^1}(-D_1^2)$ by gluing the standard boundary circles with the identity; the first disk has orientation $dx\wedge dy$, the second has its negative, and their induced boundary orientations are opposite. Use the signed collar coordinates $s=t$ on the first disk and $s=-t$ on the second as seam charts; together with the two disk interiors they define the smooth structure on $X$. Both sides have orientation $d\theta\wedge ds$. The modified maps have the same boundary trace and all normal derivatives through order two vanish at the seam, while their tangential derivatives through order two agree there. They therefore glue to a $C^2$ map $g:X\to S^2$. The double is compact, smooth and boundaryless, and its chosen orientation gives $\int_Xg^*\omega=\int_{D^2}f_0^*\omega-\int_{D^2}f_1^*\omega$.

The projector $P_+\circ g$ is $C^2$ and rank one. Its projected curvature is $g^*F_+$: applying [F1] to $P_+\circ g$, the chain rule and [F4] give $d(P_+\circ g)=g^*dP_+$ and preserve the ordered wedge product. Thus [F2] gives
$$-\frac1{4\pi}\left(\int_{D^2}f_0^*\omega-\int_{D^2}f_1^*\omega\right)=\frac{i}{2\pi}\int\operatorname{tr}F_{P_+\circ g}\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the coefficient is $-1/(4\pi)$ because $i\cdot i=-1$. Rearranging proves the stated $4\pi$ period. This is a topological ambiguity statement for the same boundary loop; no physical observation is involved.

derivations.claim: We use real-parameter differentiation in the finite orthonormal basis supplied by [F1]. For a complex scalar $f=a+ib$ with real components, its derivative is $a'+ib'$: convergence of the complex difference quotient is equivalent to convergence of its two real coordinates, since $|x|,|y|\le|x+iy|\le|x|+|y|$. Expanding $(a+ib)(c+id)=(ac-bd)+i(ad+bc)$ transfers [F11] to complex scalar products, and conjugation differentiates by conjugating the derivative. Finite sums then give the scalar-vector and matrix product rules entry by entry, and $(M^*)'=(M')^*$. These entry derivatives are the finite-dimensional vector or operator derivatives: in an orthonormal basis the squared vector norm is the finite sum of squared coordinate moduli, while for a $d\times d$ matrix $A$, each coordinate of $Ax$ has modulus at most $d\max_{j,k}|A_{jk}|\,\|x\|$ by the finite triangle inequality and $|x_k|\le\|x\|$. Thus $\|Ax\|^2\le d^3(\max_{j,k}|A_{jk}|)^2\|x\|^2$. Thus entrywise difference-quotient remainders tending to zero also tend to zero in the corresponding norm. Direct calculation for each displayed Pauli matrix gives $\sigma_i^*=\sigma_i$, $\sigma_i^2=I$, $\operatorname{tr}\sigma_i=0$, and $\det\sigma_i=-1$. With $c=\cos(t/2)$ and $s_t=\sin(t/2)$, direct $2\times2$ matrix calculations and the Pythagorean identity [F8] give $A_i(t)^*A_i(t)=(c^2+s_t^2)I=I$ and $\det A_i(t)=c^2+s_t^2=1$, so each $A_i(t)$ lies in $SU(2)$. Its entries are differentiable by [F9]. The addition formulas [F10] and $\sigma_i^2=I$ give $A_i(t+h)=A_i(t)A_i(h)$ for each $i$, and [F9] gives $A_i(0)=I$; thus each map $t\mapsto A_i(t)$ is a homomorphism from $(\mathbb R,+)$ to $SU(2)$. For $i=z$, the Euler formula [F7] and parity [F8] give $A_z(t)=\operatorname{diag}(\exp(-it/2),\exp(it/2))$. Set $U(t):=D(A_z(t))$. Since $D$ is a differentiable representation, $U$ is differentiable, $U(t+h)=U(t)U(h)=U(h)U(t)$, and the generator convention gives $U'(0)=-iJ_z$. Differentiating the two products with respect to $h$ at $0$ yields $U'(t)=U(t)(-iJ_z)=(-iJ_z)U(t)$.

By [F1], the irreducibility hypothesis leaves one spin-$s$ block, with orthonormal basis $v_k$, $k=0,\ldots,2s$, and $J_zv_k=(s-k)v_k$. Write $\mu_k=s-k$ and $u_k(t)=U(t)v_k$. Step 1.1 gives $u_k'(t)=-i\mu_k u_k(t)$. From [F5] and [F6], the scalar map $t\mapsto\exp(i\mu_k t)$ has derivative $i\mu_k\exp(i\mu_k t)$: its difference quotient at $t$ factors as $\exp(i\mu_k t)(\exp(i\mu_k h)-1)/h$ and the second factor tends to $i\mu_k$. The coordinate product rule established in step 1.1 gives $\frac{d}{dt}(\exp(i\mu_k t)u_k(t))=0$. To justify constancy, write this vector in the fixed finite orthonormal basis of [F1]. Every real and imaginary coordinate has zero derivative on $\mathbb R$ and is continuous (its increment is its difference quotient times the real increment). For arbitrary $a<b$, apply [F12] separately to these real coordinate functions on $[a,b]$; each has equal endpoint values. All coordinates, and hence the vector, are therefore constant on $\mathbb R$ and equal $v_k$ at $t=0$. Consequently $U(t)v_k=\exp(-i\mu_k t)v_k$.

Put $N=2s\in\mathbb N_0$. For every $k=0,\ldots,2s$, $2(s-k)=N-2k$ is an integer and [F5], [F7] give $\exp(-i2\pi(s-k))=\exp(-i\pi N)\exp(i2\pi k)=(-1)^N$. Indeed, $\exp(-i\pi)=-1$ follows from $\exp(i\pi)=-1$ and $\exp(-i\pi)\exp(i\pi)=\exp(0)=1$; also $\exp(i2\pi)=\exp(i\pi)^2=1$. Repeated use of [F5] gives the displayed integer powers. Thus step 1.2 implies $U(2\pi)v_k=(-1)^{2s}v_k$ for every basis vector.

By the diagonal form in step 1.1 and [F7], $A_z(2\pi)=\operatorname{diag}(\exp(-i\pi),\exp(i\pi))=-I$. Hence $D(-I)=U(2\pi)$; step 1.3 evaluates this operator on an orthonormal basis and proves $D(-I)=(-1)^{2s}I_V$.

By [F2], every $R\in SO(3)$ has exactly two lifts $W$ and $-W$. The representation law gives $D(-W)=D(-I)D(W)=(-1)^{2s}D(W)$ by step 2.1. The scalar has modulus one by [F7], so the projective class $[D(W)]\in PU(V)$ is independent of the lift. If $R_1=\rho(W_1)$ and $R_2=\rho(W_2)$, then $W_1W_2$ lifts $R_1R_2$, and $[D(W_1W_2)]=[D(W_1)][D(W_2)]$; hence the ray map is a homomorphism. The map is continuous: on any evenly covered neighborhood for $\rho$, its local section $s$ is continuous and the descended map there is $q\circ D\circ s$, a composition of continuous maps.

If $s$ is integer, $(-1)^{2s}=1$, so $D(W)$ is independent of the lift; defining $\widetilde D(R)=D(W)$ gives a unitary representation because products of lifts lift the product, as in step 3.1, and it is continuous by the same local-section argument. If $s$ is half-integer, $(-1)^{2s}=-1$, so the two lifts $I$ and $-I$ of the identity have images $I_V$ and $-I_V$; these differ since $V\ne\{0\}$. Therefore $D$ cannot factor as a unitary representation through $\rho$, although its projective class from step 3.1 does factor.

Work with finite-dimensional system and environment spaces $H_S=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_E=\mathbb C^m$, where $d,m\geq1$, using the ordered tensor product $H_S\otimes H_E$ with the system factor first. A system or environment state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one; these state matrices are dimensionless. At the initial time, for every allowed system state $\rho$, adopt the joint preparation $\rho\otimes\eta$, where the fixed environment state $\eta$ does not depend on $\rho$. For each $t\geq0$, choose a declared unitary $U_t$ on $H_S\otimes H_E$, meaning $U_t^*U_t=U_tU_t^*=I$, with $U_0=I$. The reduced system dynamics is the map $\Phi_t(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left(U_t(\rho\otimes\eta)U_t^*\right)$, where for the fixed product basis the finite partial trace has entries $(\operatorname{Tr}_E R)_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{j=1}^mR_{(\alpha,j),(\beta,j)}$. This assignment excludes initially correlated joint states. It imposes no one-parameter group, continuity, or semigroup law on $U_t$.

A time-homogeneous finite GKSL model may instead be selected as a separate approximation: choose a fixed finite-dimensional Hamiltonian matrix $H=H^*$ in joules, a constant $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, and finitely many jump matrices $L_a$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, and use $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ for $t\geq0$ with $\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_a\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right)$. Each application must state its rates and physical regime. Selecting this approximation is not a consequence of the finite unitary reduction, and this postulate claims no weak-coupling or reservoir limit.

Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d\ge1$. For a matrix $X$ define $|X|=(X^*X)^{1/2}$ by finite Hermitian functional calculus and define its trace norm by $\|X\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}|X|$. This is a complete norm on the finite-dimensional matrix space. Write $\|Y\|:=\sup\{\|Yv\|:\|v\|\le1\}$ for the operator norm induced by the Hilbert-space norm. For all matrices $X,Y$,
$$
\|YX\|_1\le\|Y\|\|X\|_1,\qquad \|XY\|_1\le\|Y\|\|X\|_1,\qquad |\operatorname{Tr}X|\le\|X\|_1.
$$
For unitary $U$, $\|UXU^*\|_1=\|X\|_1$.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a finite GKSL generator on $M_d(\mathbb C)$, $d\geq1$, with the units and conventions of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]]. For a bounded operator $A$ on a complex Banach space, write $e^{tA}:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}t^nA^n/n!$ for the operator-norm convergent series of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]]. Then $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ is a finite channel for every $t\geq0$. The family satisfies $T_0=\operatorname{id}$, $T_{t+s}=T_t\circ T_s$, and is norm-continuous. Time is measured in seconds; no negative-time channel or physical bath limit is asserted.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

derivations.claim: Write $E_{jk}=|j\rangle\langle k|$, $j,k\in\{0,1\}$, so $I=E_{00}+E_{11}$. In this basis, $H=\operatorname{diag}(0,\hbar\omega)$, $L=\sqrt\gamma E_{01}$, and $L^*L=\gamma E_{11}$. Direct multiplication in [F1] gives $\mathcal L(E_{00})=0$, $\mathcal L(E_{11})=\gamma(E_{00}-E_{11})$, $\mathcal L(E_{01})=(i\omega-\gamma/2)E_{01}$, and $\mathcal L(E_{10})=(-i\omega-\gamma/2)E_{10}$.

The matrix space is finite-dimensional and complete by [F2]. The trace-ideal estimate [F4] applied to the finitely many left and right multiplications in [F1] bounds $\|\mathcal L(X)\|_1$ by a finite constant times $\|X\|_1$, so $\mathcal L$ is bounded; [F2] therefore gives $e^{t\mathcal L}=\sum_{n\geq0}t^n\mathcal L^n/n!$. Put $D=E_{00}-E_{11}$. Step 1.1 gives $\mathcal L(D)=-\gamma D$ and $\mathcal L(E_{11})=\gamma D$; induction therefore gives $\mathcal L^n(E_{11})=\gamma(-\gamma)^{n-1}D$ for $n\geq1$. Summing this scalar series using [F3] and the real-extension clause [F7] yields $e^{t\mathcal L}(E_{11})=E_{11}+(1-e^{-\gamma t})D$, including $\gamma=0$ because both the added coefficient and every positive power term then vanish. Also step 1.1 gives $\mathcal L^n(E_{00})=0$ for $n\geq1$, while the two coherence matrix units are eigenvectors, so [F3] gives $e^{t\mathcal L}(E_{01})=e^{(i\omega-\gamma/2)t}E_{01}$ and $e^{t\mathcal L}(E_{10})=e^{(-i\omega-\gamma/2)t}E_{10}$. Applying these four identities linearly to $\rho(0)=\sum_{j,k}\rho_{jk}(0)E_{jk}$ gives all four formulas in the Statement.

By [F5] and [F6], the full evolution map is completely positive and trace-preserving for $t\geq0$, so it carries each initial density matrix to a density matrix. These formulas are deductions within the selected approximation and assert no microscopic bath limit.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, an integer $r\ge1$, and an action scale
$\hbar>0$. Inner products are linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Use the Fock-to-Schrödinger unitary
$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\to L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ of
[[lem-nrqmx-finite-mode-fock-schr-identification]]. In Schrödinger coordinates
define the self-adjoint quadratures
$$Q_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(\sqrt\hbar\,x_j)\mathcal U,\qquad P_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j})\mathcal U,$$
where $x_j$ is the real multiplication operator on its maximal domain. Fix the
angular-frequency Fourier unitary by
$$[\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}f](k)=(2\pi)^{-r/2}\int_{\mathbb R^r}e^{-ik\cdot x}f(x)\,dx\quad(f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)),$$
and define $-i\partial_{x_j}:=\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}^{-1}M_{k_j}\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}$, where $M_{k_j}$ is multiplication by $k_j$ on its maximal domain. Their common Schwartz core satisfies
$$[Q_j,Q_k]=[P_j,P_k]=0,\qquad [Q_j,P_k]=i\hbar\delta_{jk}I.$$
Write $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$ and
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
The Weyl unitary labelled by $z=(q_1,p_1,\ldots,q_r,p_r)$ is the unitary
whose grouped-coordinate formula, with $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_r)$ and
$p=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)$, is
$$[W(z)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
It obeys $W(z)W(z')=e^{-i\hbar z^TJz'/2}W(z+z')$ and is regular and
irreducible. By the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem, every
nonzero irreducible regular Weyl system with this finite phase space and this
same nonzero central parameter is unitarily equivalent to it.

A density operator is a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Its quadrature second moments are finite when, for
one (equivalently every) spectral expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ with $w_n>0$,
$\sum_nw_n\|R_j\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for every $j$. For such a state define
$$d_j=\sum_nw_n\langle R_j\psi_n,\psi_n\rangle,\qquad V_{jk}=\operatorname{Re}\sum_nw_n \langle(R_j-d_jI)\psi_n,(R_k-d_kI)\psi_n\rangle.$$
These quantities are independent of the chosen orthonormal eigenbasis in
each eigenspace. The state is Gaussian when its Weyl characteristic function
has the form
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho W(z))= \exp\!\left(i z^Td-\tfrac12z^TVz\right)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}),$$
with real $d$ and real symmetric $V$. Here $R_j$ has units
$\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, each Weyl label has units
$1/\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, and $V$ has units of action. No finite particle
number truncation is used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(V,\omega)$ be a finite-dimensional real
symplectic vector space of dimension $2n$, let $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ be
nonzero, and let $W:V\to U(\mathcal H)$ be a nonzero irreducible regular
Weyl system with

$$W(v)W(w)=e^{-i\lambda\omega(v,w)/2}W(v+w).$$
Then $W$ is unitarily equivalent to the Schrödinger Weyl system on $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$, so there is exactly one unitary-equivalence class of irreducible regular Weyl systems with the fixed parameter $\lambda$. In a symplectic basis the model is
$$\big(W_\lambda(q,p)f\big)(x)=e^{i\lambda p\cdot(x-q/2)}f(x-q),$$
for $\omega((q,p),(q',p'))=q\cdot p'-p\cdot q'$. The statement assumes finite-dimensional phase space, irreducibility, strong continuity, and a fixed nonzero central parameter. It makes no claim about algebraic modules, nonregular representations, $\lambda=0$, or infinitely many modes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\in\mathbb N_0$, let $(V,\omega)$ be a real vector space of dimension $2n$ with a nondegenerate alternating bilinear form, let $\lambda\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space. A unitary operator on $\mathcal H$ means a bijective complex-linear isometry. Suppose $W:V\to U(\mathcal H)$ satisfies $W(0)=I$ and

$$W(v)W(w)=e^{-i\lambda\omega(v,w)/2}W(v+w)\qquad(v,w\in V),$$

is regular in the sense that $t\mapsto W(tv)\xi$ is norm-continuous for every $v\in V$ and $\xi\in\mathcal H$, and is irreducible in the sense that its only closed invariant subspaces are $\{0\}$ and $\mathcal H$. Choose a symplectic basis identifying $(V,\omega)$ with $\mathbb R^n\oplus\mathbb R^n$ and $\omega((q,p),(q',p'))=q\cdot p'-p\cdot q'$. Then $W$ is unitarily equivalent, meaning that there is a unitary map $U:\mathcal H\to L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ intertwining the two Weyl actions, to the Schrödinger system

$$\bigl(W_\lambda(q,p)f\bigr)(x)=e^{i\lambda p\cdot(x-q/2)}f(x-q)$$

on $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$. Consequently, there is exactly one unitary-equivalence class of nonzero irreducible regular Weyl systems with this fixed finite-dimensional phase space and parameter. No conclusion is asserted for infinite-dimensional phase spaces, nonregular systems, or zero central parameter.

Let $r\ge1$, $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_r\\-I_r&0\end{pmatrix}$, and
$$\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)=\{S\in M_{2r}(\mathbb R):S^TJ_0S=J_0\}.$$
Every $S\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ is a finite product of matrices
of the following three types and their inverses:
$$U_X=\begin{pmatrix}I&X\\0&I\end{pmatrix},\quad L_Y=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\Y&I\end{pmatrix},\quad D_A=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\0&A^{-T}\end{pmatrix},$$
where $X,Y$ are real symmetric and $A$ is real invertible. Partial Fourier
rotations, which act by $(q_j,p_j)\mapsto(-p_j,q_j)$ on any selected set of
coordinates and fix the others, are also products of these matrices.
In addition, for every $S$ there is a product $G$ of these generators such
that the upper-left block of $SG$ is invertible.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$, for $r\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$,
define the Weyl unitaries in grouped label order $(q,p)\in\mathbb R^r\oplus
\mathbb R^r$ by
$$[W(q,p)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
For $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}$, every
$T\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ has a unitary $M_T$ such that
$$M_T^*W(z)M_T=W(Tz)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}).$$
Any two such unitaries differ by a scalar of modulus one. The covariance
identity holds on all of $L^2$; the corresponding unbounded quadrature
identities hold on the common transported Schwartz domain. This is an
individual existence and phase-uniqueness result; it does not identify the
global topology or kernel of a continuously chosen implementer family.

Use the finite-mode conventions, including their Axiom of Choice assumption, of the finite-mode symplectic-data definition. Let $r\ge1$, $\hbar>0$, and put $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_r\\-I_r&0\end{pmatrix}$. In grouped order $(q,p)$, write
$$S=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}\in M_{2r}(\mathbb R),\qquad A,B,C,D\in M_r(\mathbb R),\qquad S^TJ_0S=J_0,$$
and assume its upper-right block $B$ is invertible. Define
$$R_g:=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)^T.$$
Fix a compact interval $I=[0,T]$ with $T>0$. For each $j\in\{1,2\}$, let $K_j:I\to M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ have Lebesgue-integrable entries in grouped order and satisfy $K_j(t)=K_j(t)^T$ for every $t$. Let $S_j:I\to M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ be absolutely continuous with $S_j(0)=I_{2r}$, $\dot S_j(t)=J_0K_j(t)S_j(t)$ almost everywhere, and $S_j(T)=S$. Define the real symmetrically ordered quadratic operator on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ by
$$H_{j,t}:=\frac14\sum_{a,b=1}^{2r}(K_j)_{ab}(t)((R_g)_a(R_g)_b+(R_g)_b(R_g)_a),$$
with no linear or scalar term. Assume $U_j:I\to\mathcal U(L^2(\mathbb R^r))$ is a path of unitary Schwartz automorphisms with $U_j(0)=I$ such that, for each $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$, the path $t\mapsto U_j(t)f$ is absolutely continuous in every Schwartz seminorm and satisfies
$$i\hbar\,\partial_tU_j(t)f=H_{j,t}U_j(t)f$$
almost everywhere. Here a unitary Schwartz automorphism is a unitary on $L^2$ whose restriction is a continuous linear bijection of $\mathcal S$ with continuous inverse, and the Schwartz seminorms are $p_{\alpha,\beta}(f)=\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$ for multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$. Absolute continuity of each trajectory means the usual finite disjoint-interval condition for its increments in every seminorm. These hypotheses include piecewise-smooth Hamiltonian paths.
Then
$$U_2=U_1\quad\text{or}\quad U_2=-U_1.$$
The same conclusion holds after multiplying both propagators by a fixed
normalized quadratic propagator, provided the resulting endpoint lies in a
chart with invertible upper-right block.

Use the finite-mode conventions, including their Axiom of Choice assumption, of the finite-mode symplectic-data definition. Let $r\ge1$, $\hbar>0$, and put $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_r\\-I_r&0\end{pmatrix}$. In grouped order $(q,p)$, write
$$S=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}\in M_{2r}(\mathbb R),\qquad A,B,C,D\in M_r(\mathbb R),\qquad S^TJ_0S=J_0,$$
and assume its upper-right block $B$ is invertible. Define
$$R_g:=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)^T.$$
Fix a compact interval $I=[0,T]$ with $T>0$. For each $j\in\{1,2\}$, let $K_j:I\to M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ have Lebesgue-integrable entries in grouped order and satisfy $K_j(t)=K_j(t)^T$ for every $t$. Let $S_j:I\to M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ be absolutely continuous with $S_j(0)=I_{2r}$, $\dot S_j(t)=J_0K_j(t)S_j(t)$ almost everywhere, and $S_j(T)=S$. Define the real symmetrically ordered quadratic operator on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ by
$$H_{j,t}:=\frac14\sum_{a,b=1}^{2r}(K_j)_{ab}(t)((R_g)_a(R_g)_b+(R_g)_b(R_g)_a),$$
with no linear or scalar term. Assume $U_j:I\to\mathcal U(L^2(\mathbb R^r))$ is a path of unitary Schwartz automorphisms with $U_j(0)=I$ such that, for each $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$, the path $t\mapsto U_j(t)f$ is absolutely continuous in every Schwartz seminorm and satisfies
$$i\hbar\,\partial_tU_j(t)f=H_{j,t}U_j(t)f$$
almost everywhere. Here a unitary Schwartz automorphism is a unitary on $L^2$ whose restriction is a continuous linear bijection of $\mathcal S$ with continuous inverse, and the Schwartz seminorms are $p_{\alpha,\beta}(f)=\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$ for multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$. Absolute continuity of each trajectory means the usual finite disjoint-interval condition for its increments in every seminorm. These hypotheses include piecewise-smooth Hamiltonian paths.
Then
$$U_2=U_1\quad\text{or}\quad U_2=-U_1.$$
The same conclusion holds after multiplying both propagators by a fixed
normalized quadratic propagator, provided the resulting endpoint lies in a
chart with invertible upper-right block.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $r\ge1$, fix a positive real action-scale parameter
$\hbar>0$, and let $H=\mathbb C^r$ with orthonormal basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$, and let $\mathcal F_s(H)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^{\otimes_s n}$
be the bosonic Fock space with vacuum $\Omega$ and creation and annihilation
operators $a_j^*,a_j$ from
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For
$N=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in\mathbb N_0^r$, set
$$|N\rangle:=\prod_{j=1}^r\frac{(a_j^*)^{n_j}}{\sqrt{n_j!}}\Omega.$$
Let $g_N(x)=\prod_{j=1}^r g_{n_j}(x_j)$ be the normalized product Hermite
function from [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-multidimensional-oscillator-completeness]].
Then $(|N\rangle)_N$ and $(g_N)_N$ are complete orthonormal families, and the
map $\mathcal U|N\rangle=g_N$ extends uniquely to a unitary
$$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r).$$
On the algebraic finite-particle span, $\mathcal U a_j\mathcal U^{-1}$ and
$\mathcal U a_j^*\mathcal U^{-1}$ are respectively
$(x_j+\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ and $(x_j-\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ on product
Hermite functions. In particular the quadratures
$$Q_j=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j+a_j^*),\qquad P_j=-i\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j-a_j^*)$$
act there as multiplication by $\sqrt\hbar x_j$ and as
$-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j}$, respectively. These are core identities;
they do not assert that a finite number cutoff preserves the canonical
commutation relations.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $d\ge1$. For each $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ put $K_j^y:=L^2(\mathbb R,dy_j)$ and take a copy $(g^{(j)}_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of the Hermite family of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $K_j^y$. Define the left-associated completed tensor products by $\mathcal K_1^y:=K_1^y$ and $\mathcal K_r^y:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^y\widehat\otimes K_r^y$ for $2\le r\le d$. Let $\Theta_y^{(1)}:K_1^y\to L^2(\mathbb R,dy_1)$ be the identity; recursively, for $2\le r\le d$, let

$$\Theta_y^{(r)}:=\Theta_{r-1,1}^y\circ\bigl(\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}\bigr):\mathcal K_r^y\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy),$$

where $\Theta_{r-1,1}^y:L^2(\mathbb R^{r-1},dy)\widehat\otimes K_r^y\to L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy)$ is the two-factor Euclidean product unitary of [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]], and $\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}$ is the bounded tensor map of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Thus $\Theta_y^{(r)}$ is a specified unitary, with $\Theta_y^{(r)}(u\otimes v)(y',y_r)=\Theta_y^{(r-1)}u(y')v(y_r)$ almost everywhere. For $N=(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d$, set $G_N^{y,1}:=g^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{y,r}:=G_N^{y,r-1}\otimes g^{(r)}_{n_r}$; define $g_N:=\Theta_y^{(d)}G_N^{y,d}\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$.

Let $\varphi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N^d$ list the multi-indices by increasing total degree $M=\sum_jn_j$ and, within each finite level, in lexicographic order. By [[thm-stars-and-bars]] each level is finite and the levels exhaust $\mathbb N^d$, so this specifies a bijection. All sums indexed by $\mathbb N^d$ below are taken in this order; nonnegative sums equivalently mean the supremum of finite subsums.

The functions $g_N$ have smooth product representatives from the recursive construction. These representatives are unique: a continuous difference that is nonzero at a point remains nonzero on a ball of positive Lebesgue measure. The coordinate derivatives in (b) and (c) are taken on these representatives and their scaled products.

Then:

(a) $(g_N)_{N\in\mathbb N^d}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$: $\langle g_N,g_M\rangle=\delta_{NM}$ and every $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$ has $f=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\langle f,g_N\rangle g_N$ with $\|f\|^2=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2$, the sum being the supremum over finite subfamilies ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]);

(b) with the eigenvalues $\lambda_N:=\sum_{j=1}^d(2n_j+1)=2M+d$, $M:=\sum_jn_j$, let $A_d$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $e_m:=g_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $\lambda_{\varphi(m)}$. Then $A_d$ is self-adjoint with

$$A_dg_N=\lambda_Ng_N,\qquad D(A_d)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\lambda_N^2|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(A_d)=\{2M+d:M\in\mathbb N\}$$

(the spectrum by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]); the algebraic span of the $g_N$ is a core, and on that span

$$A_d=\sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(-\partial_{y_j}^2+y_j^2\bigr)$$

as operators, the $j$-th summand acting in the $j$-th coordinate;

(c) for real $m_j,\omega_j,\hbar>0$ put $\ell_j:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_j\omega_j)}$ and let $D_j:K_j^y\to K_j^x:=L^2(\mathbb R,dx_j)$ be the one-dimensional unitary of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]]. Define $\mathcal K_1^x:=K_1^x$ and $\mathcal K_r^x:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^x\widehat\otimes K_r^x$ for $2\le r\le d$, and define $\Theta_x^{(1)}$ and $\Theta_x^{(r)}$ by the same recursion as $\Theta_y^{(r)}$, using the two-factor Euclidean product unitaries on the $x$-coordinate spaces. Let $\mathcal D_1:=D_1$ and recursively $\mathcal D_r:=\mathcal D_{r-1}\otimes D_r:\mathcal K_r^y\to\mathcal K_r^x$; each $\mathcal D_r$ is unitary by [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Put $D_d:=\Theta_x^{(d)}\mathcal D_d(\Theta_y^{(d)})^{-1}:L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx)$. For $N\in\mathbb N^d$, define $G_N^{x,1}:=D_1g^{(1)}_{n_1}=:\psi^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{x,r}:=G_N^{x,r-1}\otimes\psi^{(r)}_{n_r}$; then $\psi_N:=D_dg_N=\Theta_x^{(d)}G_N^{x,d}$. Let $H$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $\psi_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $E_{\varphi(m)}$, where $E_N:=\hbar\sum_{j=1}^d\omega_j(n_j+\frac12)$. Then $H$ is self-adjoint with

$$H\psi_N=E_N\psi_N,\qquad D(H)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_N E_N^2|\langle f,\psi_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(H)=\overline{\{E_N:N\in\mathbb N^d\}},$$

the span of the $\psi_N$ is a core, and on that core

$$H=\sum_{j=1}^d\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_j}\partial_{x_j}^2+\frac{m_j\omega_j^2}{2}x_j^2\Bigr);$$

(d) if $\omega_1=\cdots=\omega_d=\omega$, then $\sigma(H)=\{\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2):M\in\mathbb N\}$, and the eigenvalue $\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2)$ has multiplicity

$$\bigl|\{(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d:n_1+\cdots+n_d=M\}\bigr|=\binom{M+d-1}{d-1};$$

in particular for $d=3$ the multiplicity is $(M+1)(M+2)/2$ ([[thm-stars-and-bars]]). All parameters are positive real numbers; no physical interpretation is asserted.

derivations.claim: Reorder interleaved coordinates by the fixed permutation $P(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)$, and write $R_g:=PR$ and $W_g(w)=W(P^Tw)$ for grouped labels. Then $J_0=PJP^T$ and $S_g=PSP^T$ obeys $S_g^TJ_0S_g=J_0$. Apply [F3] directly to the grouped Weyl system on $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ with label matrix $S_g^T$; this matrix is symplectic because $S_g^TJ_0S_g=J_0$ also implies $S_gJ_0S_g^T=J_0$. Since $S_g^TP=PS^T$, converting labels back gives $$M_S^*W(z)M_S=M_S^*W_g(Pz)M_S=W_g(S_g^TPz)=W(S^Tz).$$ Differentiating the bounded one-parameter Weyl identity on the common Schwartz core gives $M_S^*RM_S=SR$. For the rest of the proof abbreviate $R_g$ to $R$ and $S_g$ to $S$, so $R$, $K$, and $J_0$ all use grouped order.

Use exactly the endpoint definition and trajectory class in the Statement, on arbitrary compact intervals $[0,T]$ with $T>0$. Reordering by the fixed permutation of step 1.1 sends $K$ to $PKP^T$ and preserves entrywise integrability, reality and symmetry, so [F4] constructs and uniquely determines these evolutions in grouped order with $H_t=\tfrac14\sum_{j,k}K_{jk}(t)(R_jR_k+R_kR_j)$ and no linear or scalar term. The operator acts on the common Schwartz space, and each trajectory is absolutely continuous in every seminorm and solves the equation almost everywhere. Concatenation gives products: first evolve by $U_2$ on $[0,T_2]$, then evolve by $U_1$ on $[0,T_1]$ with initial vector $U_2(T_2)f$, obtaining endpoint $U_1(T_1)U_2(T_2)$. The concatenated coefficient is integrable and symmetric on $[0,T_2+T_1]$, and the two absolutely continuous trajectories match at the join. The reversed evolution $U(T-t)U(T)^{-1}$ starts at $I$, ends at $U(T)^{-1}$, and is generated almost everywhere by $-H_{T-t}$, whose symmetric coefficient is again integrable. Thus inverses also belong to the set. By [F4], each endpoint implements the symplectic solution $\dot S=J_0K(t)S$. If two matrices had the same implementing unitary, differentiating their Weyl covariances on Schwartz space would give $(S-S')R=0$. Applied to the vacuum, $Q_kg_0=\sqrt{\hbar/2}g_{e_k}$ and $P_kg_0=i\sqrt{\hbar/2}g_{e_k}$ by [F6]; the reality of the rows forces both their position and momentum coefficients to vanish. Thus the endpoint is unique. For two lifts, $\pi(M_1M_2)=\pi(M_1)\pi(M_2)$ by conjugating the quadratures, so $\pi$ is a homomorphism.

Every generator from [F2] is a path endpoint of a homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonian. A symmetric shear is joined to the identity by scaling its symmetric block, and a partial Fourier rotation is joined by varying the oscillator angle. If $\det A>0$, polar decomposition writes $A=OP$ with $O\in SO(r)$ and $P$ positive definite. The path $P_t=(1-t)I+tP$ stays positive definite, and an orthogonal matrix in $SO(r)$ is a product of plane rotations, each joined to the identity by varying its angle. These paths connect the coordinate change to the identity. If $\det A<0$, factor one coordinate reflection from a positive-determinant change; that reflection is a $\pi$ oscillator rotation on that mode. This gives a piecewise-smooth symplectic path for each generator. Along any such path $S_t$, the matrix $X_t=\dot S_tS_t^{-1}$ satisfies $X_t^TJ_0+J_0X_t=0$; hence $K_t=-J_0X_t$ is symmetric and $\dot S_t=J_0K_tS_t$. The symmetrically ordered quadratic with matrix $K_t$ therefore has this classical endpoint. Thus [F2] supplies, for every $S$, a product of normalized quadratic propagators whose endpoint is $S$, proving $\pi$ is onto. The one-parameter paths also show that each such product belongs to the identity component of $\operatorname{Mp}$.

If $M_1,M_2$ implement the same $S$, then [F3] makes $M_2M_1^*=\lambda I$ for some $|\lambda|=1$. For any other representation $W'$ in [F1], choose a unitary $V$ with $VW'(z)V^*=W(z)$ by the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem. Then $M'_S=V^*M_SV$ is unitary and $$M_S'^*W'(z)M'_S=V^*M_S^*W(z)M_SV=W'(S^Tz).$$ Conjugating the phase-uniqueness statement by $V$ proves the same result in that representation.

If two normalized lifts lie over the same grouped matrix $S$, the Gaussian determinant calculation in [F5] makes them differ by sign. This already holds for every $S$: the matrix $A+iB$ used there is invertible by symplecticity, including when either real block is singular. In particular it supplies the required invertible-$B$ chart argument without an imported Maslov-index parity formula. Thus every fiber has at most two elements.

The identity has two distinct lifts. The constant zero Hamiltonian gives $I$. On the first mode (and as the identity on the other modes if $r>1$), take the canonical Schwartz evolution of $H=\hbar(N+1/2)$ constructed in [F4]. For each Hermite vector, $e^{-it(n+1/2)}|n\rangle$ solves the same Schrödinger equation with that initial vector, so uniqueness in [F4] identifies $U(t)|n\rangle=e^{-it(n+1/2)}|n\rangle$. Its classical endpoint is the identity at $t=2\pi$, because its Hamilton equations are $\dot Q=P$, $\dot P=-Q$ and make one full rotation, while by [F6] $$U(2\pi)|n\rangle=e^{-2\pi i(n+1/2)}|n\rangle=-|n\rangle$$ for every $n$. Completeness of the Hermite basis gives $U(2\pi)=-I$. For any $S$, choose a normalized lift $\widetilde M_S$ supplied by step 2.1. Then $\widetilde M_S$ and $-\widetilde M_S$ are two distinct lifts; step 2.3 proves there are no others. The kernel is exactly $\{I,-I\}$.

Fix $S_0$ and a normalized lift $M_0$. On a matrix neighborhood $\mathcal B$ of $S_0$ small enough that $SS_0^{-1}$ lies in the local neighborhood of [F4], put $\sigma(S)=L(SS_0^{-1})M_0$. The parameter path $(Y,A,X)\mapsto(\tau Y,I+\tau(A-I),\tau X)$ in [F4] joins each local factor lift to $I$ smoothly, with homogeneous quadratic logarithmic generator. Thus the local factors are endpoints of the piecewise-smooth subclass of the integrable class defining this group, so $\sigma(S)$ belongs to $\operatorname{Mp}$ and has endpoint $S$. Conversely the construction of [F4] writes any integrable-coefficient propagator endpoint as a finite product of these same local lifts. Hence allowing the broader integrable temporal class in the parity lemma introduces no additional endpoint operators or phases. It depends continuously on $S$, as does its inverse, pointwise in the Schwartz topology: the explicit chirp and linear-coordinate factors have uniformly bounded seminorm estimates on compact parameter neighborhoods, and the Fourier factors are fixed continuous maps. These estimates also justify continuity when composing such a varying local factor with a varying Schwartz vector. Step 3.1 shows every lift over $S$ is exactly $\sigma(S)$ or $-\sigma(S)$.

The endpoint map is continuous for the specified operator topology, without assuming joint continuity of arbitrary Schwartz-operator composition. For each row $j$ and mode $k$, covariance and [F6] give $\langle R_jMg_0,Mg_{e_k}\rangle=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(S_{j,Q_k}+iS_{j,P_k})$, where the pairing is linear in its first argument. On the left $R_j$ is continuous on Schwartz space, its inclusion into $L^2$ is continuous, and only the two fixed input vectors $g_0,g_{e_k}$ are used. Thus every real matrix entry of $\pi(M)$ is continuous. Over $\mathcal B$, the scalar $\varepsilon(M):=\langle Mg_0,\sigma(\pi(M))g_0\rangle$ is continuous, takes exactly the values $+1,-1$, and distinguishes the two lifts since $\|g_0\|=1$. Therefore the two inverse images $\varepsilon^{-1}(1)$ and $\varepsilon^{-1}(-1)$ in $\pi^{-1}(\mathcal B)$ are disjoint open sheets; on each, $\pi$ and $\pm\sigma$ are continuous inverse maps onto $\mathcal B$. This proves the two-fold covering in the given topology.

The same charts make the set a topological group. Locally its elements are $\varepsilon\sigma(S)$. Products and inverses of their explicit finite-parameter factors depend continuously on the matrix parameters and on each Schwartz vector, by the uniform seminorm bounds in step 4.1; their endpoint matrices multiply and invert continuously. The sign relative to a local section at the resulting endpoint is recovered by the continuous vacuum pairing in step 5.1. Hence multiplication and inversion are continuous in these charts, which have precisely the operator topology by step 5.1. Finally every defining normalized path is continuous in that topology by [F4], including its inverse path, so it joins its endpoint to $I$. Consequently the group is path connected. Together with step 3.1 this proves the connected double cover with kernel $\{I,-I\}$ and its defining unitary action, retaining the unrestricted phase ambiguity only for arbitrary individual Weyl implementers.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\omega=2\pi/T$, $\hbar>0$, and let $H:\mathbb R\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ be $C^1$, $T$-periodic, and Hermitian at every time. On $\mathscr H_T=L^2((0,T),dt;\mathbb C^d)$ define
$$D(K)=\{f=(f_1,\ldots,f_d): f_a\in H^1(0,T)\text{ for every }a,\ f(0)=f(T)\},\qquad (Kf)(t)=H(t)f(t)-i\hbar f'(t).$$
Here each $H^1(0,T)$ function is represented by its unique absolutely continuous representative, so endpoint values are its traces, and $f'$ is its componentwise weak derivative. Then $K$ is self-adjoint on exactly $D(K)$. Choose $v_j$ and $\varepsilon_j$ from [[thm-nrqmx-finite-floquet-normal-form]], so $H_Fv_j=\varepsilon_jv_j$ and $P(t)$ is its periodic unitary. The functions
$$\phi_{jn}(t)=T^{-1/2}e^{in\omega t}P(t)v_j\qquad(1\le j\le d,\ n\in\mathbb Z)$$
form an orthonormal basis of $\mathscr H_T$ and satisfy $K\phi_{jn}=(\varepsilon_j+n\hbar\omega)\phi_{jn}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[def-countable-choice]]). Let $0<L<\infty$ and $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$. Put
$D_\theta:=\{u\in H^1(0,L):u^*(L)=e^{i\theta}u^*(0)\},\qquad
P_\theta u:=-i\,Du,$
with $H^1$ and the trace $u^*$ of [[def-nrqm-intervals-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]
and [[lem-nrqm-intervals-integration-by-parts]] clause (b). Then:

(a) $D_\theta$ is dense in $L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, $P_\theta$ is symmetric and
self-adjoint;

(b) the functions
$\varphi_n(x):=\frac{1}{\sqrt L}e^{i(2\pi n+\theta)x/L}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z)$
form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, each
$\varphi_n\in D_\theta$, and $P_\theta\varphi_n=\kappa_n\varphi_n$ with
$\kappa_n:=\frac{2\pi n+\theta}{L};$
the eigenvalues $\kappa_n$ are simple and
$\sigma(P_\theta)=\{\kappa_n:n\in\mathbb Z\}$;

(c) $P_\theta$ is the unique self-adjoint extension of the symmetric operator
$P_\theta$ restricted to the finite linear span of the $\varphi_n$, and its
domain is exactly
$D_\theta=\Bigl\{\sum_nc_n\varphi_n:\sum_n\kappa_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix integers $d\ge1$, $b,N\ge0$, and real numbers $\hbar>0$, $\omega>0$, and $\tau>0$. Let $H_k\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ for $-b\le k\le b$ satisfy $H_{-k}=H_k^*$; set $H_k=0$ when $|k|>b$. Thus $H(t)=\sum_{k=-b}^{b}H_ke^{ik\omega t}$ is a finite Fourier polynomial with period $T=2\pi/\omega$. Put $q=(2N+1)d$. Let $S_\tau$ be a caller-supplied total classical routine on $\{M\in M_q(\mathbb C):M=M^*\}$ whose declared interface, on input $M$, returns real numbers $\widetilde\lambda_1,\ldots,\widetilde\lambda_q$, an orthonormal basis $x_1,\ldots,x_q$ of standard $\mathbb C^q$, and residuals $r_j=\|Mx_j-\widetilde\lambda_jx_j\|\le\tau$ for $1\le j\le q$. This algorithm returns that finite record unchanged and does not independently certify its residual claims.

The algorithm takes $(d,b,N,\hbar,\omega,(H_k)_{|k|\le b},\tau,S_\tau)$ and returns a matrix $K_N$ and the eigensolver's output record:

1. Order the Fourier indices as $-N,-N+1,\ldots,N$ and allocate a $(2N+1)d$ by $(2N+1)d$ block matrix.

2. For each ordered pair $n,m\in\{-N,\ldots,N\}$, assign the $d$ by $d$ block
$$ (K_N)_{nm}:=H_{n-m}+n\hbar\omega\,\delta_{nm}I_d,$$
where $\delta_{nm}=1$ if $n=m$ and $0$ otherwise.

3. Set $R:=S_\tau(K_N)$ by one call, then return $(K_N,R)$.

derivations.claim: For $-N\le m\le N$ and $v\in\mathbb C^d$, $e_m(t)v=T^{-1/2}e^{im\omega t}v$ is smooth and periodic, so it lies in $D(K)$ by [F1]. Multiplication by $H(t)$ gives $\sum_kT^{-1/2}e^{i(m+k)\omega t}H_kv$; its coefficient in harmonic $n$ is $H_{n-m}v$. The derivative term is $-i\hbar\,\partial_t(e_m v)=m\hbar\omega e_m v$, which contributes only when $n=m$. Thus $\Pi_NK(e_m v)$ has $n$th coefficient $(H_{n-m}+n\hbar\omega\delta_{nm}I_d)v$.

For every pair $n,m$, [F3] gives $(K_N)_{nm}^*=H_{n-m}^*+n\hbar\omega\delta_{nm}I_d=H_{m-n}+m\hbar\omega\delta_{mn}I_d=(K_N)_{mn}$, since $H_{-k}=H_k^*$ and the diagonal term is present only when $n=m$. Hence $K_N$ is Hermitian.

The coefficient just computed is precisely the block assigned by [F3] in row $n$, column $m$. Since the ordered Fourier basis spans $\mathcal S_N$, equality of all its matrix blocks proves that $K_N$ is exactly the matrix of $\Pi_NK|_{\mathcal S_N}$.

There are $(2N+1)^2$ ordered pairs $(n,m)$, each assignment fills one finite $d$ by $d$ block, so the block assembly terminates after exactly that many assignments. By step 1.2, $K_N$ is Hermitian, and it has dimension $q=(2N+1)d$; hence it is in the domain of the total routine $S_\tau$ in [F4]. The algorithm makes one call $R:=S_\tau(K_N)$ after assembly, and totality gives a returned finite record. Thus the complete procedure is well-defined and terminates. This exact compression and termination argument proves no convergence as $N\to\infty$, spectral accuracy, or residual claim beyond the routine's stipulated interface.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space, with inner product linear in its first variable, and let $A:D(A)\subseteq H\to H$ be densely defined, self-adjoint, and nonnegative, meaning $\langle Au,u\rangle\ge0$ for every $u\in D(A)$. Here self-adjoint means equality with the Hilbert-space adjoint, including equality of domains. A projection-valued measure (PVM) on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ is a map $E:\Sigma\to\mathcal B(H)$ such that every $E(S)$ is a bounded orthogonal projection ($E(S)^2=E(S)=E(S)^*$), $E(\varnothing)=0$, $E(X)=I$, $E(S\cap T)=E(S)E(T)$, and $E(\bigcup_n S_n)u=\sum_nE(S_n)u$ in norm for each disjoint sequence $(S_n)$ and each $u\in H$. On a locally compact Hausdorff Borel space, such a PVM is regular when each finite scalar measure $\mu_u(S):=\langle E(S)u,u\rangle$ is inner regular on Borel sets and outer regular by open supersets. Then $I+A:D(A)\to H$ is bijective. Its inverse $B:=(I+A)^{-1}$ is a bounded positive (meaning $\langle Bx,x\rangle\ge0$ for all $x\in H$) self-adjoint injection with $\|B\|\le1$ and dense range $D(A)$. For a bounded operator, its spectrum $\sigma(B)$ is the set of complex $z$ for which $B-zI$ has no bounded two-sided inverse. Let $E_B$ be the regular spectral PVM on the Borel subsets of the nonempty compact set $\sigma(B)$ satisfying $B=\int_{\sigma(B)}b\,dE_B(b)$. Then $\sigma(B)\subseteq[0,1]$ and $E_B(\{0\})=0$. Define $\phi(b)=b^{-1}-1$ for $b\in\sigma(B)\setminus\{0\}$ and, for every Borel $S\subseteq[0,\infty)$, define

$$E_A(S):=E_B(\{b\in\sigma(B)\setminus\{0\}:\phi(b)\in S\}).$$

This is a PVM on the Borel subsets of $[0,\infty)$. For each $u\in H$ put $\mu_u(S):=\langle E_A(S)u,u\rangle$. The unbounded integral $\int_{[0,\infty)}\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda)$ denotes the operator $T_A$ with domain

$$D(T_A):=\left\{u\in H:\int_{[0,\infty)}\lambda^2\,d\mu_u(\lambda)<\infty\right\}$$

and action

$$T_Au:=\lim_{N\to\infty}\Phi_{E_A}(\lambda\mathbf1_{[0,N]})(u),$$

where $\Phi_{E_A}(g)$ is the bounded Borel PVM integral of $g$. Then $A=T_A$ and hence

$$A=\int_{[0,\infty)}\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda),\qquad D(A)=\left\{u\in H:\int_{[0,\infty)}\lambda^2\,d\langle E_A(\lambda)u,u\rangle<\infty\right\}.$$

For every bounded Borel function $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb C$, $f(A):=\Phi_{E_A}(f)$ is bounded, satisfies $\|f(A)\|\le\sup_{\lambda\ge0}|f(\lambda)|$, and obeys $\|f(A)u\|^2=\int|f|^2\,d\mu_u$. The condition $E_B(\{0\})=0$ does not assert that $0\notin\sigma(B)$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: On $H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with standard basis $(e_n)_{n\ge1}$ define $D(A)=\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\ge1}n^2|x_n|^2<\infty\}$ and $(Ax)_n=nx_n$. Finite sequences lie in $D(A)$ and are dense. For $x\in D(A)$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F2] gives $\sum n|x_n|^2\le(\sum n^2|x_n|^2)^{1/2}(\sum|x_n|^2)^{1/2}<\infty$, so $\langle Ax,x\rangle=\sum n|x_n|^2\ge0$ and $A$ is nonnegative.

The operator is self-adjoint. If $y\in D(A^*)$, there is $z\in\ell^2$ with $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle$ for every finite sequence $x$; choosing $x=e_n$ gives $z_n=ny_n$, so $\sum n^2|y_n|^2=\|z\|^2<\infty$ and $y\in D(A)$. Conversely, if $y\in D(A)$ then $z=(ny_n)\in\ell^2$ satisfies the adjoint identity for every $x\in D(A)$: both inner-product series converge by [F2] because $Ax,y,x,z\in\ell^2$, and their terms agree. Thus $D(A^*)=D(A)$ and $A^*=A$.

The inverse of $I+A$ is the bounded diagonal operator $B e_n=(n+1)^{-1}e_n$. Indeed for any $x\in\ell^2$, $y_n=x_n/(n+1)$ satisfies $\sum n^2|y_n|^2\le\sum|x_n|^2$, and $(I+A)y=x$. The operator $B$ is positive and injective, but it is not bounded below because $\|Be_n\|=(n+1)^{-1}\to0$ for unit vectors $e_n$. The vector $y=(1/n)_{n\ge1}$ belongs to $\ell^2$: for $n\ge2$, $n^{-2}\le(n-1)^{-1}-n^{-1}$, so $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}\le2$. It is not in $\operatorname{Ran}B$, since $Bx=y$ would require $x_n=(n+1)/n>1$ for every $n$, which is not square-summable. Hence $B$ is not surjective and $0\in\sigma(B)$.

Define $E_B(S)x=\sum_{n:(n+1)^{-1}\in S}x_ne_n$ for Borel $S\subseteq\sigma(B)$. Its values are orthogonal coordinate projections, and the coordinate definition gives $E_B(\varnothing)=0$, $E_B(\sigma(B))=I$, and $E_B(S)E_B(T)=E_B(S\cap T)$. For disjoint Borel $S_k$, each coordinate $n$ occurs in at most one projection, so the partial sums $\sum_{k\le N}E_B(S_k)x$ converge in $\ell^2$ to $E_B(\bigcup_kS_k)x$: the squared norm of the omitted coordinates is a tail of the convergent nonnegative series $\sum_n|x_n|^2$. Thus $E_B$ is strongly countably additive. It integrates the coordinate function to $B$, because its integral acts diagonally by $(n+1)^{-1}$ on each $e_n$. For every $x$, its finite scalar measure is $\mu_x(S):=\langle E_B(S)x,x\rangle=\sum_{n:(n+1)^{-1}\in S}|x_n|^2$. On $(\mathbb R^d,\gamma_{C_1})\times(\mathbb R^d,\gamma_{C_2})$, the sum map $(y,z)\mapsto y+z$ has characteristic function
$$\int e^{iu\cdot(y+z)}\,d(\gamma_{C_1}\times\gamma_{C_2}) =\exp(-u^TC_1u/2)\exp(-u^TC_2u/2) =\exp[-u^T(C_1+C_2)u/2].$$
The product measure exists by [F3], the integrand is bounded and therefore integrable, and [F4] justifies the iterated integral/product factorization. Since $C_1+C_2$ is positive semidefinite, [F2] and [F5] identify the pushforward under addition as $\gamma_{C_1+C_2}$. This includes singular and zero covariances.

The function $(x,y,z)\mapsto f(x+y+z)$ is nonnegative and Borel. Apply [F6] to integrate first in $y$ and then in $z$; the resulting iterated integral equals the integral against the product law of $(y,z)$. By step 1.1 its pushforward under addition is $\gamma_{C_1+C_2}$. Therefore
$$\int\left(\int f(x+z+y)\,d\gamma_{C_1}(y)\right)d\gamma_{C_2}(z) =\int f(x+w)\,d\gamma_{C_1+C_2}(w),$$
including the value $+\infty$. By [F1] this is exactly $T_{C_2}(T_{C_1}f)(x)=T_{C_1+C_2}f(x)$.

For finite nonnegative Borel $V$, [F1] gives $\exp[-V_{C_1}(x)]=T_{C_1}(e^{-V})(x)$ and the corresponding identity after applying $C_2$. Substituting $f=e^{-V}$ into step 2.1 proves the stated potential-weight identity. Since the normalized Gaussian integrals are expectations under probability laws, no determinant factor occurs. derivations.claim: For each $n\ge1$, define the product-test map $J_n:S_d^{\otimes_{\rm alg}n}\to S_{d,n}$ by $J_n(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)$ and linear extension; the product of Schwartz functions is a Schwartz function. Set $J_0(c)=c$ and, for $a\in T_d$, define $Q_S(a):=\omega_S(\Theta a\,a)$. Fix a finite positive-time polynomial $a=\sum_{j=0}^{N}a_j$, with each $a_j$ a finite sum of degree-$j$ product tests. Expanding concatenation and the moment functional gives the finite sum $Q_{S^\lambda}(a)=\sum_{j,k=0}^{N}\langle S^\lambda_{j+k},J_{j+k}((\Theta a_j)a_k)\rangle .$ Every test in this finite sum is fixed independently of $\lambda$, so [A2] gives $Q_{S^\lambda}(a)\to Q_S(a)$. By [A1], every value $Q_{S^\lambda}(a)$ is a nonnegative real number. Since $[0,\infty)$ is closed in $\mathbb C$, its limit $Q_S(a)$ is also a nonnegative real number. As $a$ was arbitrary, $S$ is reflection positive.

Fix one Euclidean isometry $\gamma(x)=Rx+b$ and one order-$n$ test $\Phi$. The pullback $\Phi\mapsto\Phi\circ(\gamma^{-1})^{\times n}$ is continuous on Schwartz space: the chain rule writes each derivative as a finite linear combination of derivatives of $\Phi$ evaluated at the inverse affine image, and each polynomial weight in $x$ becomes a finite sum of polynomial weights in the new variable with fixed coefficients. Thus each transformed Schwartz seminorm is bounded by finitely many original seminorms. If every $S^\lambda_n$ is invariant under this fixed pullback, [A2] applied to both $\Phi$ and its pullback passes the equality to $S_n$. A permutation of argument blocks is a coordinate permutation and preserves the same seminorms exactly, so the same limit argument passes permutation symmetry. Step 1.1 uses only a fixed finite number of orders and tests; it supplies neither a uniform-in-$n$ bound nor a limit as a translation parameter tends to infinity, so it proves no order-uniform growth or clustering claim.
