For $\kappa\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, the **Casimir Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov connection** on the trivial vector bundle $F_n(\mathbb C)	imes V	o F_n(\mathbb C)$ is

$$
abla^{\mathrm{KZ}}_\kappa:=d-\kappa^{-1}\sum_{i<j}\Omega_{ij}\eta_{ij}.$$

Here a connection on this trivial bundle is a complex-linear operator on smooth $V$-valued sections satisfying $
abla(fs)=df\otimes s+f
abla s$ for every smooth scalar function $f$ and section $s$. The associated quadratic Casimir is $C_B:=\sum_a x_ax^a$ in the universal enveloping algebra; with the Killing-form convention above it is central, and $\Omega_{ij}$ is its tensor-level Casimir counterpart.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra. Let $\kappa:\mathfrak g\times\mathfrak g\to\mathbb R$ be a symmetric bilinear form that is invariant, meaning
$$\kappa([U,V],W)=\kappa(U,[V,W])\qquad(U,V,W\in\mathfrak g).$$
No nondegeneracy, positivity, simplicity, or compactness assumption is imposed. Put $S^1=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ and $\mathcal L\mathfrak g=C^\infty(S^1,\mathfrak g)$, with pointwise bracket $[X,Y](\theta)=[X(\theta),Y(\theta)]_{\mathfrak g}$. For $Y\in\mathcal L\mathfrak g$, write $Y'=\partial_\theta Y$ in the indicated periodic coordinate.

A Lie-algebra $2$-cocycle for the trivial scalar action is an alternating bilinear map $\omega:\mathcal L\mathfrak g\times\mathcal L\mathfrak g\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\omega([X,Y],Z)+\omega([Y,Z],X)+\omega([Z,X],Y)=0.$$
Define the candidate current cocycle and its candidate central-term bracket by
$$\omega(X,Y)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\kappa(X(\theta),Y'(\theta))\,d\theta,\qquad \widehat{\mathcal L\mathfrak g}=\mathcal L\mathfrak g\oplus\mathbb R,$$
$$[(X,a),(Y,b)]=([X,Y],\omega(X,Y)).$$
The real coordinates $a,b$ are central coordinates and do not enter the right-hand side. A one-dimensional central extension means a short exact sequence of Lie algebras $0\to\mathbb R\to\widehat{\mathcal L\mathfrak g}\to\mathcal L\mathfrak g\to0$ whose kernel is central. The proposition on this page verifies that the displayed operation has this Lie-algebra structure. The normalization is fixed as written; no integer level, integration to a loop group, or representation-theoretic existence or unitarity follows from this definition.

For the finite-dimensional real Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, invariant symmetric form $\kappa$, smooth loop algebra $\mathcal L\mathfrak g$, and bilinear form $\omega$ defined in [[def-qftx-loop-current-cocycle]], the form $\omega$ is alternating and satisfies
$$\omega([X,Y],Z)+\omega([Y,Z],X)+\omega([Z,X],Y)=0\qquad(X,Y,Z\in\mathcal L\mathfrak g).$$
Consequently the candidate bracket on $\widehat{\mathcal L\mathfrak g}$ is a Lie bracket and gives a one-dimensional central extension of $\mathcal L\mathfrak g$ by $\mathbb R$.

Let $k$ be a field and let $\mathcal C$ be a locally finite $k$-linear abelian rigid monoidal category whose tensor product is $k$-bilinear. For each object $Y$ write $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(Y):=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(Y,Y)$. The tensor unit $\mathbf1$ is assumed to satisfy $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf1)\cong k$ as $k$-algebras. Here rigid means every object has left and right duals with evaluation and coevaluation maps satisfying the two snake identities. Equip $\mathcal C$ with a braiding $c_{Y,Z}:Y\otimes Z\to Z\otimes Y$, natural in $Y,Z$, satisfying the two hexagon identities with the associator $\alpha$. Fix $X\in\mathcal C$, put $P_0(X)=\mathbf1$, $P_1(X)=X$, and recursively put $P_{m+1}(X)=P_m(X)\otimes X$.

For any object $Y$, let $\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal C}(Y)$ be the group under composition of those $g\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(Y)$ for which some $h\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(Y)$ satisfies $g\circ h=h\circ g=\operatorname{id}_Y$.

For each $n\ge2$ and $1\le i<n$, let $Q_{n,i}(X)$ be the parenthesized product $\bigl(P_{i-1}(X)\otimes(X\otimes X)\bigr)\otimes P_{n-i-1}(X)$, with the unit factors at either end removed by the fixed unitors when an exponent is zero. Choose a canonical rebracketing isomorphism $\rho_{n,i}:P_n(X)\to Q_{n,i}(X)$ made from associators, unitors, and their inverses, without permuting the ordered tensor factors. Define

$$B_i^X:=\rho_{n,i}^{-1}\circ\bigl(\operatorname{id}_{P_{i-1}(X)}\otimes c_{X,X}\otimes\operatorname{id}_{P_{n-i-1}(X)}\bigr)\circ\rho_{n,i}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(P_n(X)).$$

The family $B_i^X$ is independent of the chosen canonical rebracketing path and determines a homomorphism $\varrho_n:B_n\to\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal C}(P_n(X))$, where $B_n$ is the braid group with positive generator $\sigma_i$ sent to $B_i^X$. These are exact algebraic morphisms.

**Physical interpretation boundary.** A physical adiabatic-exchange interpretation needs additional model data; the categorical data below supply none of the analytic or physical data. Here $\mathcal H$ is a complete complex inner-product space, with inner product linear in its first variable. For each dimensionless $s\in[0,1]$, let $K(s):\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$ be self-adjoint on a specified common dense domain $\mathcal D$. For a densely defined operator $K$, its adjoint $K^*$ is defined by $y\in\mathcal D(K^*)$ exactly when some $z\in\mathcal H$ satisfies $\langle Kx,y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle$ for every $x\in\mathcal D(K)$, with $K^*y=z$; self-adjoint means $\mathcal D(K^*)=\mathcal D$ and $K^*x=Kx$ there. The spectrum $\sigma(K)$ is the set of $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ for which $K-\lambda I$ has no bounded, everywhere-defined inverse.

For each $s$, supply a projection-valued measure $E_s$ on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R$: each $E_s(A)$ is an orthogonal projection, $E_s(\mathbb R)=I$, and for pairwise disjoint Borel sets $A_j$, $E_s(\bigcup_j A_j)x=\sum_jE_s(A_j)x$ with norm convergence for every $x\in\mathcal H$. Require $E_s$ to represent $K(s)$ as its spectral integral: with $\mu_{s,x}(A):=\langle E_s(A)x,x\rangle$, the domain is $\mathcal D=\{x\in\mathcal H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,d\mu_{s,x}(\lambda)<\infty\}$ and $K(s)x=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_s(\lambda)x$ there. For a Borel set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R$, define its spectral projection by $P(s):=E_s(\Omega)$. Require $\operatorname{ran}P(s)$ to be finite-dimensional and $\operatorname{dist}(\Omega,\sigma(K(s))\setminus\Omega)\ge\gamma>0$ uniformly in $s$, where $\operatorname{dist}(A,B):=\inf\{|a-b|:a\in A,\ b\in B\}$ and $\inf\varnothing:=+\infty$.

Require $s\mapsto P(s)$ to be continuously differentiable in operator norm. Its ranges then form a finite-rank Hermitian vector bundle $E\to[0,1]$, meaning the locally trivial bundle with fiber $E_s:=\operatorname{ran}P(s)$ and the inner product inherited from $\mathcal H$. A Hermitian connection on $E$ is a complex-linear covariant derivative $\nabla_s$ on continuously differentiable sections satisfying $\nabla_s(f\psi)=f'\psi+f\nabla_s\psi$ and $\partial_s\langle\psi,\phi\rangle=\langle\nabla_s\psi,\phi\rangle+\langle\psi,\nabla_s\phi\rangle$. Its parallel transport $W(s,0):E_0\to E_s$ is the map obtained by solving $\nabla_s\psi(s)=0$ along the interval.

Supply a family of unitary operators $U_\varepsilon(s,0):\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$, where unitary means surjective and inner-product-preserving, with $U_\varepsilon(0,0)=I$ and $U_\varepsilon(s,0)\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal D$. Require for each $x\in\mathcal D$ that $s\mapsto U_\varepsilon(s,0)x$ is differentiable in Hilbert norm and satisfies $i\varepsilon\partial_sU_\varepsilon(s,0)x=K(s)U_\varepsilon(s,0)x$; all conditions ensuring this propagator exists are part of the model data. Here $\varepsilon>0$ is an energy scale and the slow-evolution regime means $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. A linear operator $A$ on $\mathcal H$ is bounded when $\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\|Ax\|<\infty$; this supremum is its operator norm $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. The added data must include a bound $r(\varepsilon)\to0$ such that

$$\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\|U_\varepsilon(s,0)P(0)-\iota_sW(s,0)P(0)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le r(\varepsilon),$$

where $\iota_s:E_s\hookrightarrow\mathcal H$ is inclusion. In a physical realization, $K(s)$, $\gamma$, and $\varepsilon$ have the model's energy units; no numerical values are fixed here. The categorical data do not assert an experimental realization.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a complex finite semisimple rigid tensor category with simple unit $\mathbf 1$ and a finite set $I$ of isomorphism classes of simple objects. Fix a braiding $c$ and a ribbon twist $\theta$. The induced pivotal map is $j_X=u_X\theta_X:X\to X^{\vee\vee}$, where $u$ is the Drinfeld morphism of [[thm-a-braided-rigid-category-has-a-drinfeld-morphism]]. Throughout this pair we use the associated spherical pivotal structure: $j$ is part of the data, and sphericality means $\dim_j(X)=\dim_j(X^\vee)$ for every object, as in [[def-spherical-structure]]. Its trace is $\operatorname{tr}_j(f)=\operatorname{Tr}_L(j_Xf)$ for $f\in\operatorname{End}(X)$.

Write $0$ for the unit label and $i^*$ for the dual of $i$. Put $N_{ij}^k=\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}(k,i\otimes j)$, $d_i=\operatorname{tr}_j(1_i)$, and $s_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}_j(c_{j,i}c_{i,j})$. Define $D^2=\sum_{i\in I}d_i^2$. The unnormalized Hopf-link matrix is $s=(s_{ij})$. The ribbon fusion category is **modular** when $s$ is invertible. When $D^2\ne0$, either square root $D$ defines the normalized matrix $S=s/D$; for a modular category, [[lem-modular-hopf-matrix-squared]] proves this nonvanishing. No positivity of the general $d_i$ or of $D$ is assumed.

Let $\ell\ge3$, $q=e^{\pi i/\ell}$, and let $\mathcal C_\ell$ be the standard ribbon semisimplification of finite-dimensional integrable type-1 tilting modules for Lusztig's divided-power $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, using the positive-trace quantum ribbon convention. Then $\mathcal C_\ell$ is modular, with simples $a=0,\ldots,\ell-2$, dimensions $d_a=\sin((a+1)\pi/\ell)/\sin(\pi/\ell)$, twists $\theta_a=q^{a(a+2)/2}$, and

$$s_{ab}=\frac{\sin((a+1)(b+1)\pi/\ell)}{\sin(\pi/\ell)},\qquad S_{ab}=\sqrt{\frac2\ell}\sin\frac{(a+1)(b+1)\pi}{\ell}.$$

In a braided rigid monoidal category there is a natural isomorphism

$$u_X:X\to X^{\vee\vee},$$

called the **Drinfeld morphism** (or **Drinfeld isomorphism**), defined by

$$X\xrightarrow{1_X\otimes\operatorname{coev}_{X^\vee}}X\otimes X^\vee\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{c_{X,X^\vee}\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^\vee\otimes X\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_X\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^{\vee\vee}.$$

Write

$$d_{X,Y}:X^{\vee\vee}\otimes Y^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{\sim}(X\otimes Y)^{\vee\vee}$$

for the monoidal comparison of the double-dual functor. Then

$$d_{X,Y}\circ(u_X\otimes u_Y)=u_{X\otimes Y}\circ c_{Y,X}\circ c_{X,Y}.$$

Thus $u$ need not be monoidal: the double braiding is precisely its
monoidality obstruction.

derivations.claim: Let $(x_a),(x^a_{\mathrm{bas}})$ be $B_{\mathrm{bas}}$-dual bases. By [F1], $(x_a,(2h^\vee)^{-1}x^a_{\mathrm{bas}})$ are $B_{\mathrm{Kill}}$-dual, so their Casimir tensors satisfy $\Omega_{\mathrm{Kill}}=(2h^\vee)^{-1}\Omega_{\mathrm{bas}}$.

The current extension in [F3] satisfies Jacobi and has central kernel by [F4]. Extending its real bracket complex-bilinearly preserves skew-symmetry and Jacobi, since each is a finite polynomial identity in the structure constants; restriction to the Laurent-mode subalgebra preserves the same identities. Thus the central extension used for the affine module input is a Lie algebra.

For $J_m(x)=xe^{-im\theta}$, the cocycle in [F3] gives $\omega(J_m(x),J_n(y))=-in\delta_{m+n,0}B_{\mathrm{bas}}(x,y)=im\delta_{m+n,0}B_{\mathrm{bas}}(x,y)$. Replacing $K$ by $K_{\mathrm{aff}}=iK$ yields the stated mode bracket. Also $d=i\partial_\theta$ sends $J_m(x)$ to $mJ_m(x)$. On noncentral terms the derivation identity is the equality $m+n=m+n$; on the central term both sides agree because it is supported on $m+n=0$, where the total degree is zero. Thus $d$ is a derivation and $[d,K_{\mathrm{aff}}]=0$, fixing the affine mode and central-level conventions used by the Definition.

[F5] supplies the braid-action interface only under its stated rigid monoidal category and coherence hypotheses. [F8] identifies the Drinfeld morphism used in the pivotal map of [F6], which separately fixes the ribbon and modular data conventions. These inputs specify what a comparison must preserve; neither statement asserts an equivalence with the KZ local system, so the Definition reserves an equivalence proof as a separate theorem obligation.

The two KZ one-form coefficients agree exactly when $\kappa_{\mathrm{Kill}}^{-1}(2h^\vee)^{-1}=\kappa_{\mathrm{bas}}^{-1}$. Substituting [F2] and $\kappa_{\mathrm{bas}}=k+h^\vee$ gives $\kappa_{\mathrm{Kill}}=(k+h^\vee)/(2h^\vee)$, the conversion recorded in the Definition.

The actual theorem [F7] proves modularity only for its stated $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ quotient and conventions. That category-specific result supplies the concrete modular input named in the Definition, but does not identify its ribbon exchanges with the WZW/KZ monodromy or establish factorization.

derivations.claim:
By [F3], the bounded linear isometry $\Omega_+$ has a bounded Hilbert
adjoint. For any $z$ in a Hilbert space,
$\|z\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|(z,x)|$: Cauchy–Schwarz gives the upper bound, and
if $z\ne0$ the choice $x=z/\|z\|$ attains it. For $y\in\mathcal H$, the
adjoint identity and [F2] therefore give
$\|\Omega_+^*y\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|(\Omega_+^*y,x)|
=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|(y,\Omega_+x)|\le\|y\|$, since $\|\Omega_+x\|=\|x\|$.
Therefore
$\|Sx\|=\|\Omega_+^*\Omega_-x\|\le\|\Omega_-x\|=\|x\|$ for every
$x\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}$, so $S$ is a contraction.

By [F3], the bounded maps $\Omega_\pm$ and $S$ have bounded Hilbert
adjoints with the stated adjoint identities. For either isometry $\Omega$,
the adjoint identity gives
$(x,\Omega^*\Omega y)=(\Omega x,\Omega y)=(x,y)$ for all $x,y$; nondegeneracy
therefore gives $\Omega^*\Omega=I$. For $P=\Omega\Omega^*$ the same identity
gives $(Px,y)=(\Omega^*x,\Omega^*y)=(x,Py)$, so $P^*=P$, and
$\Omega^*\Omega=I$ gives $P^2=P$. Also $P$ fixes each $\Omega x$ and its
image is contained in $\operatorname{Ran}\Omega$, so $P$ is the orthogonal
projection onto the closed range. If
$\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+=\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_-=:R$, both products
are the same projection $P_R$. For all $x,z\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}$,
$(Sx,z)_{\mathrm{as}}=(\Omega_-x,\Omega_+z)_{\mathcal H}
=(x,\Omega_-^*\Omega_+z)_{\mathrm{as}}$, so uniqueness of the adjoint gives
$S^*=\Omega_-^*\Omega_+$. It follows that
$S^*S=\Omega_-^*P_R\Omega_-=\Omega_-^*\Omega_-=I$ and
$SS^*=\Omega_+^*P_R\Omega_+=\Omega_+^*\Omega_+=I$, so $S$ is unitary.

Conversely, suppose $S$ is unitary and put
$P_+=\Omega_+\Omega_+^*$. By [F3] and step 1.2 this is a bounded
orthogonal projection.
For each $x$,
$\|P_+\Omega_-x\|=\|\Omega_+^*\Omega_-x\|=\|Sx\|=\|x\|
=\|\Omega_-x\|$. For an orthogonal projection $P$, the identity
$\|Py\|=\|y\|$ implies
$\|y\|^2=\|Py\|^2+\|(I-P)y\|^2$ and hence $(I-P)y=0$; therefore
$\Omega_-x\in\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+$ for every $x$, proving
$\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_-\subseteq\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+$. Since $S$
is onto, for every $z\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}$ choose $x$ with $Sx=z$.
Then $\Omega_+z=\Omega_+Sx=P_+\Omega_-x=\Omega_-x$, which gives the reverse
range inclusion. Thus the ranges coincide.

An abstract polymer model consists of an at most countable set $\Gamma$ (finite or in bijection with $\mathbb N$), a reflexive symmetric relation $\sim$ on $\Gamma$ (so $\gamma\sim\gamma$ and $\gamma\sim\eta$ implies $\eta\sim\gamma$), and an activity function $z:\Gamma\to\mathbb C$. Its elements are called polymers, and $\gamma\sim\eta$ means that the two polymers are incompatible. A subset $X\subseteq\Gamma$ is compatible when no two distinct elements of $X$ are related by $\sim$. For real and natural summands, finite-index sums and products are enumeration-independent. For complex summands, define a finite sum or product by any enumeration and repeated addition or multiplication in $\mathbb C$; associativity and commutativity make the result independent of the enumeration. The empty sum is $0$ and the empty product is $1$. For each finite $V\subseteq\Gamma$, define the finite-volume partition polynomial

$$Z_V(z):=\sum_{\substack{X\subseteq V\\X\text{ compatible}}}\ \prod_{\gamma\in X}z_\gamma,$$

where the empty subset contributes $1$.

Write $[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $\binom{[n]}2:=\{\{i,j\}:i,j\in[n],\ i\ne j\}$. A simple graph on $[n]$ is a pair $([n],E)$ with $E\subseteq\binom{[n]}2$; a path is a finite vertex list with distinct vertices and each consecutive pair an edge. A graph is connected when every two vertices are joined by a path. A cycle is a vertex list $(v_0,\ldots,v_k)$ with $k\geq3$, $v_k=v_0$, $v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}$ distinct, and each consecutive pair an edge; a tree is a connected simple graph with no cycle. For $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ be the set of connected simple graphs on $[n]$ and let $\mathcal T_n$ be the set of trees on $[n]$. The set $[n]$ is finite; its power set is finite, so its subset $\binom{[n]}2$ is finite; the power set of that edge set is finite as well. Each simple graph on $[n]$ is determined by an edge set in this last power set, so $\mathcal C_n$ and $\mathcal T_n$ are finite.

For an ordered tuple $(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)\in\Gamma^n$, put $f_{ij}:=-\mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_i\sim\gamma_j\}}$ and define the connected coefficient

$$U_n(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n):=\sum_{G\in\mathcal C_n}\ \prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}f_{ij}.$$

For $n=1$, $\mathcal C_1$ contains the one-vertex graph and the empty edge product equals $1$. These are finite polynomial and coefficient definitions; they assert no convergence.

A **finite simple graph** is an ordered pair $G=(V,E)$ in which $V$ is a finite
set and

$$E\subseteq [V]^2:=\{\,\{u,v\}\subseteq V: u\ne v\,\}.$$

The elements of $V=V(G)$ are the **vertices** and the elements of $E=E(G)$ are
the **edges**. Thus every edge has two distinct endpoints, there are no loops,
and an unordered pair of vertices occurs as at most one edge. Finiteness and the
notation $|V|$ and $|E|$ are those of [[def-finite-cardinality]].

When no qualifier is present, the word **graph** has this meaning.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$, there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$. Induction (The principle of mathematical induction): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ (The von Neumann naturals form a Peano system) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
(Zero and one under multiplication) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
(Cancellation for multiplication by a nonzero factor). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ (Addition is cancellative). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
(Multiplication is associative, Multiplication is commutative) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional (Multiplication of natural numbers), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ take values in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ (The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined). Its **partial sums** are the unique sequence $(s_n)$ in $[0,+\infty]$ satisfying

$$s_0=0,\qquad s_{n+1}=s_n+a_n.$$

To apply The recursion theorem with a fixed successor function, use the state space $\mathbb N\times[0,+\infty]$ and the self-map $T(n,s)=(n+1,s+a_n)$, starting from $(0,0)$. Recursion gives a unique state sequence; induction makes its first coordinate $n$, and its second coordinates are exactly the unique $(s_n)$ satisfying the displayed recurrence. Addition of two nonnegative extended reals is always defined, including when either is $+\infty$. The sequence $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing, and its **nonnegative extended sum** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n\in[0,+\infty],$$

whose existence follows from completeness of the extended real line (Every subset of $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, agreeing with the real supremum and infimum on nonempty sets bounded in $\mathbb{R}$). More generally, for $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$\sum_{k\ge m}a_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{m+j}.$$

Finite sums use the same recursion: $\sum_{k<n}a_k=s_n$, so the empty sum at $n=0$ is $0$. A double sum such as $\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}$ means that the inner nonnegative extended sum is formed first and the resulting nonnegative extended sequence is then summed.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), in particular an ordered field
(Ordered field) and a field (Field), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
(Addition of natural numbers).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
(The recursion theorem). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** (The principle of mathematical induction). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
The recursion theorem, so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order (Order on the natural numbers); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
(Addition is commutative) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
(Addition is cancellative) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $S$ be a finite set, $n := \lvert S\rvert$ (The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and
let $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_i$ for $a(i)$.
Choose a bijection $\varphi : n \to S$, which exists because $S \approx n$
(Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$), and set

$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i := \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}, \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i := \prod_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

the right-hand sides being the iterated operations of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion when the
values are real and of Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$ when they are natural.

**Independence of the enumeration, which is the content of the definition.** Let
$\varphi, \psi : n \to S$ be two bijections. Then $\pi := \varphi^{-1} \circ \psi$
is a bijection $n \to n$ (Injection, surjection, bijection), and
$a_{\psi(k)} = a_{\varphi(\pi(k))}$ for every $k < n$. Applying
A finite sum is unchanged by a permutation of its index range: $\sum_{k<n} a_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for every bijection $\pi : n \to n$ to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the
former whenever the index set is a natural number.

**(b) Reindexing along a bijection.** If $h : T \to S$ is a bijection of finite
sets, then $\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$, and likewise for
products. Indeed $\lvert T\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = n$ by transport
(The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and if $\varphi : n \to S$ is a bijection then
$h^{-1} \circ \varphi : n \to T$ is one, so
$\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{k<n} a_{h(h^{-1}(\varphi(k)))} = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$.

**(c) The empty index set and a constant summand.** $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$,
so $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 0$ and $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 1$ by
the base clause of the recursion. And for a constant $c$, clause (a) together
with the constant clause of Laws of finite sums and products in $\mathbb{N}$, and $\iota\big(\sum_{k<n} a_k\big) = \sum_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$
in $\mathbb{N}$, or clause 2 of Laws of finite sums and finite products in $\mathbb{R}$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in S} c = \lvert S\rvert \cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{N}), \qquad \sum_{i \in S} c = \iota(\lvert S\rvert)\cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}),$$

the second with $\iota$ written out because $\lvert S\rvert$ is a natural number
and not an element of $\mathbb{R}$ (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field).

Let $G$ be a graph. A **spanning tree** of $G$ is a spanning subgraph $T$ of $G$ that is a tree ([[def-subgraph-induced-subgraph-and-spanning-subgraph]], [[def-tree-forest-and-leaf]]). Equivalently,

$$V(T)=V(G),\qquad E(T)\subseteq E(G),$$

and $T$ is connected and acyclic.

The null graph has no spanning tree under the library convention that a tree is nonempty and connected.
A finite graph $G$ is connected if and only if it has a spanning tree.
Every finite graph has only finitely many spanning trees.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$.

- $m$ is a **maximum** (or *greatest element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $s \le m$
  for every $s \in S$.
- $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$
  for every $s \in S$.

A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then
$m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so
$m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy
axiom of an ordered field (Ordered field, Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)).
The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: The nonempty finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the listable ones proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $F$ be a field (Field) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
(The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann), The recursion theorem):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in Field, and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ (Field) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c, d \in F$.

1. **Translation invariance.** If $a < b$ then $a + c < b + c$.
2. **Adding inequalities.** If $a < b$ and $c < d$ then $a + c < b + d$.

derivations.claim: Fix $n\geq2$ and a tuple $(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)$, and let $H$ be the simple graph on $[n]$ whose edge $\{i,j\}$ is present exactly when $\gamma_i\sim\gamma_j$. By [F1], $U_n=\sum_{G\subseteq H,\ G\text{ connected}}(-1)^{|E(G)|}$. Here the complete graph on $[n]$ has edge set $\binom{[n]}2$, and $G\subseteq H$ means that $G$ has the same vertex set and $E(G)\subseteq E(H)$. Represent each edge $\{i,j\}$ with $i<j$ by $(i,j)$ and order these pairs lexicographically, first by $i$ and then by $j$; list the edges as $e_1<_{\rm lex}\cdots<_{\rm lex}e_m$ and assign rank $\rho(e_k)=k\cdot1_{\mathbb R}$. For a tree $T$, its rank sum is $\sum_{e\in E(T)}\rho(e)$. By [F8], each connected graph $G$ has a spanning tree; by [F9], its spanning trees form a finite nonempty set, so their finite real rank sums have a minimum. A tree has a unique path between any two vertices: connectedness gives a path, and two distinct paths would contain a cycle between their first divergence and next common vertex, contradicting acyclicity. Here is the cut and exchange argument used below. Let $f=\{u,v\}$ be an edge of a tree $T$. There is no $u$-$v$ path in $T-f$, since such a path together with $f$ would be a cycle in $T$. For any vertex $w$, the unique $T$-path from $u$ to $w$ either avoids $f$, or crosses $f$ from $u$ to $v$ and then has a suffix from $v$ to $w$ avoiding $f$. Thus every vertex is reachable from $u$ or from $v$ in $T-f$, but not both: reachability from both would concatenate to a $u$-$v$ walk avoiding $f$, and deleting repeated-vertex portions of a finite walk gives a path, contradicting the preceding observation. Vertices reachable from the same endpoint are joined by concatenating their endpoint paths and deleting repetitions. Hence $T-f$ has exactly two connected components, with vertex sets $C_u,C_v$, and no remaining tree edge crosses this partition; call it the cut of $f$. If $e=\{x,y\}\notin E(T)$ and $f$ lies on its unique $T$-path, then $x,y$ lie in opposite components, for otherwise a path in $T-f$ would contradict uniqueness of the $T$-path. Adding $e$ to $T-f$ joins the two components, so $T-f+e$ is connected. It is acyclic: a cycle would have to use $e$ since $T-f$ is acyclic, and removing $e$ from that cycle would give a path in $T-f$ between opposite components. Thus $T-f+e$ is a spanning tree on the same vertex set. Every path from one side of any such cut to the other has a crossing edge, by considering the first vertex at which its finite vertex list changes sides. The minimum-rank-sum spanning tree is unique: if distinct minimizing trees $T,S$ existed, take the least-ranked edge $e$ in their symmetric difference and, after swapping their names if needed, take $e\in T\setminus S$. Deleting $e$ from $T$ gives a cut crossed by the $S$-path between the endpoints of $e$; a crossing edge $f$ on that path lies in $S\setminus T$, and replacing $f$ by the earlier edge $e$ lowers the rank sum of $S$ by [F10], a contradiction. For a tree $T$, let $A(T)\subseteq\binom{[n]}2\setminus E(T)$ consist of the edges later than every edge on their unique $T$-path. If $G$ contains $T$ and a non-tree edge $e$ is earlier than a path edge $f$, then $T-f+e$ is a spanning tree of lower rank sum by [F10], so $T$ is not minimum. Conversely, if every non-tree edge of $G$ is later than every edge on its $T$-path, then for each $f\in T$ every other edge of $G$ crossing the cut made by deleting $f$ is later than $f$. Choose a minimum-rank-sum spanning tree $S$ of $G$, which exists by [F8]–[F9]. If $S$ omitted $f$, the $S$-path between the endpoints of $f$ crosses this cut at an edge $e$; adding $f$ to $S$ and deleting that path edge $e$ gives a spanning tree with lower rank sum by [F10], contradicting minimality of $S$. Hence $S$ contains every edge $f$ of $T$ and equals $T$: any additional edge would form a cycle with its $T$-path. Thus $T$ is the unique minimum tree of $G$ exactly when $T\subseteq G\subseteq T\cup A(T)$. Consequently, connected subgraphs of $H$ split into disjoint classes indexed by trees $T\subseteq H$, each class consisting of $T\cup A$ for $A\subseteq A(T)\cap E(H)$. The signed sum in one class is $(-1)^{n-1}(1-1)^{|A(T)\cap E(H)|}$, whose real absolute value is at most $1$. Applying the finite-sum triangle inequality from [F5, F7] to the class contributions gives $|U_n(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)|\leq\sum_{T\in\mathcal T_n}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}\mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_i\sim\gamma_j\}}$. For $n=1$ both sides equal $1$.

A rooted tree means a tree with one distinguished vertex; its height is the greatest number of edges in a path from that root. A size-$n$ labelled tree here has vertex set $[n]$, and in $S_\gamma^{(k)}$ its root is label $1$; removing the root separates it into child subtrees. For fixed root label $1$ of type $\gamma$, let $S_\gamma^{(k)}$ be the nonnegative sum over all such finite rooted labelled trees of height at most $k$, with all other vertex types summed over $\Gamma$, each non-root vertex of type $\eta$ weighted by $|z_\eta|$, each edge weighted by $\mathbf 1_{\{\eta\sim\eta'\}}$, and each size-$n$ sum divided by $(n-1)!$. The root has weight $1$, so $S_\gamma^{(0)}=1$. At height at most $k+1$, the root has $m$ child subtrees of height at most $k$. For ordered subtree sizes $n_1,\ldots,n_m$, assigning the $n-1$ labels to the ordered branch vertex sets contributes $(n-1)!/(n_1!\cdots n_m!)$. In each branch there are $n_j$ choices for its child-root label; with the fixed-root subtree sum normalized by $(n_j-1)!$, the factor $n_j(n_j-1)!/n_j!$ is $1$. The parent normalization $(n-1)!$ therefore leaves the product of the branch weights, and division by $m!$ removes the ordering of the branches. Therefore, as an identity of nonnegative countable sums, $S_\gamma^{(k+1)}=\sum_{m=0}^\infty\frac1{m!}(\sum_{\eta\sim\gamma}|z_\eta|S_\eta^{(k)})^m=\exp(\sum_{\eta\sim\gamma}|z_\eta|S_\eta^{(k)})$. If $\Gamma$ is infinite, its at-most-countability supplies a bijection with $\mathbb N$; if finite, use $\Gamma$ itself. Thus finite type and size cutoffs exhaust all choices, and increasing limits give the stated countable-sum identity. By [F2], $S_\gamma^{(0)}=1\leq e^{a_\gamma}$. If $S_\eta^{(k)}\leq e^{a_\eta}$ for every $\eta$, the assumed majorant [A1] gives $0\leq\sum_{\eta\sim\gamma}|z_\eta|S_\eta^{(k)}\leq a_\gamma$; [F3] then gives $S_\gamma^{(k+1)}\leq e^{a_\gamma}$. The nonnegative sums increase with $k$ and every finite tree has finite height, so their limit is the full rooted tree sum and is at most $e^{a_\gamma}$.

Apply the pointwise graph-to-tree bound of step 1.1 to each tuple in the definition of $R_\gamma$. All weights are nonnegative after taking absolute values, so summing over the countable polymer labels and then over $n$ preserves the inequality; the right side is the rooted tree sum bounded in step 1.2. Hence $R_\gamma\leq e^{a_\gamma}$.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer $n$. Congruence modulo $n$ is an equivalence relation on
$\mathbb Z$ by [[lem-congruence-is-an-equivalence-relation]]. The
**congruence class of $a$ modulo $n$** is

$$[a]_n:=\{\,b\in\mathbb Z:b\equiv a\pmod n\,\},$$

and the **integers modulo $n$** form the quotient set

$$\mathbb Z/n:=\{\,[a]_n:a\in\mathbb Z\,\}.$$

This is the quotient-set construction of [[def-equivalence-relation]]. By
[[lem-equivalence-classes-partition]], two classes are equal exactly when their
representatives are congruent:

$$[a]_n=[b]_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\equiv b\pmod n.$$

At $n=0$ each class is a singleton because congruence modulo $0$ is equality.
At $n=1$ there is one class, namely $\mathbb Z$ itself.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Every class in $\mathbb Z/n$
([[def-integers-modulo-n]]) contains exactly one integer $r$ with
$0\le r<n$. Consequently the map

$$r\longmapsto[r]_n\qquad(0\le r<n)$$

is a bijection from the von Neumann natural $n$ to $\mathbb Z/n$, and
$|\mathbb Z/n|=n$. This includes $n=1$, where the only representative is $0$.
For $n=0$, the map $a\mapsto[a]_0$ is a bijection $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/0$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, including $n=0$ and $n=1$. For classes in
$\mathbb Z/n$ ([[def-integers-modulo-n]]) define

$$[a]_n+[b]_n:=[a+b]_n,\qquad [a]_n[b]_n:=[ab]_n.$$

These are binary operations in the sense of [[def-binary-operation]]. Indeed,
if $[a]_n=[a']_n$ and $[b]_n=[b']_n$, then
$a\equiv a'\pmod n$ and $b\equiv b'\pmod n$, so

$$a+b\equiv a'+b'\pmod n,\qquad ab\equiv a'b'\pmod n$$

by [[lem-congruence-respects-integer-arithmetic]]. Thus the two displayed
classes do not depend on the representatives chosen.

For $n=0$, every class is a singleton and these operations reproduce integer
addition and multiplication under the bijection $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/0$. For
$n=1$, the quotient has one element, so $[0]_1=[1]_1$ and both operations are
the unique binary operation on a one-element set.

For every $n\in\mathbb N$, with addition and multiplication as in
[[def-addition-and-multiplication-modulo-n]]:

1. $(\mathbb Z/n,+,[0]_n)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), with
   $-[a]_n=[-a]_n$;
2. $(\mathbb Z/n,\cdot,[1]_n)$ is a commutative monoid
   ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]);
3. multiplication distributes over addition on both sides.

The assertions include $n=0$ and $n=1$. At $n=1$, the two distinguished
identities coincide because $[0]_1=[1]_1$.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $k,\ell\in\mathbb Z$. Then

$$\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}=\begin{cases}N,&k\equiv\ell\pmod N,\\\\ 0,&k\not\equiv\ell\pmod N.\end{cases}$$

At $N=1$ the congruence holds for all $k,\ell$ and the sum is $1$. The sum is the finite sum of the complex family $x\mapsto e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}$ over the von Neumann natural $N=\{0,\dots,N-1\}$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]), and $N$ on the right is the natural number $N$ read in $\mathbb C$ as the additive multiple $N\cdot1_{\mathbb C}$, that is, the value at $N$ of the canonical embedding $\mathbb N\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-integer-multiples-agree-with-canonical-natural]]).

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid and let all index sets below be finite.

1. If $h:T\to S$ is a bijection and $a:S\to M$, then $\sum_{t\in T}a_{h(t)}=\sum_{s\in S}a_s$.
2. If $S$ and $T$ are disjoint and $a:S\cup T\to M$, then $\sum_{u\in S\cup T}a_u=\sum_{s\in S}a_s+\sum_{t\in T}a_t$.
3. If $a:S\times T\to M$, then
   $$\sum_{(s,t)\in S\times T}a_{s,t}=\sum_{s\in S}\left(\sum_{t\in T}a_{s,t}\right)=\sum_{t\in T}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_{s,t}\right).$$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

$$\ker(\exp)=2\pi i\mathbb Z,$$
and $\exp z=\exp w$ exactly when $z-w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$, $\sin ^2x+\cos ^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. Wherever the displayed quotients are defined, $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, $\cot(-x)=-\cot x$, $\sec(-x)=\sec x$, $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$, $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$, and $1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $x\in\Lambda_{d,L}$ and put $a_j=\widetilde x_j$. By [F1]–[F2], the $j$th representative of $x+e_j$ is $a_j+1-L\epsilon_j$, where $\epsilon_j=1$ if $a_j=L-1$ and $0$ otherwise; the $j$th representative of $x-e_j$ is $a_j-1+L\eta_j$, where $\eta_j=1$ if $a_j=0$ and $0$ otherwise. All other representatives are unchanged. Substitution into the definition of $\chi_r$, followed by the exponential addition law and $\exp(2\pi i n)=1$ for integers $n$ from [F5], gives $\chi_r(x+e_j)=e^{2\pi i r_j/L}\chi_r(x)$ and $\chi_r(x-e_j)=e^{-2\pi i r_j/L}\chi_r(x)$. This also holds for $L=1$ and $L=2$.

For $r,s\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}^d$, finite-sum factorization [F4] and the conjugation identity [F8] give $\langle\chi_r,\chi_s\rangle=\prod_{j=1}^d L^{-1}\sum_{u=0}^{L-1}e^{2\pi i(r_j-s_j)u/L}$. By [F1], distinct canonical representatives are incongruent modulo $L$, so [F3] makes each factor $1$ when $r_j=s_j$ and $0$ otherwise. This is the inner-product identity stated above.

Substituting the shift identities of step 1.1 into $-\Delta$ gives $-\Delta\chi_r=\sum_{j=1}^d(2-e^{2\pi i r_j/L}-e^{-2\pi i r_j/L})\chi_r$. By [F6]–[F7], each coefficient equals $2-2\cos(2\pi r_j/L)=4\sin^2(\pi r_j/L)$, proving the eigenvalue formula.

For any $f:\Lambda_{d,L}\to\mathbb C$, set $\widehat f(r)=L^{-d}\sum_{y\in\Lambda_{d,L}}f(y)\overline{\chi_r(y)}$. By [F4] and [F8], the frequency sum factors as $\sum_r\chi_r(x)\overline{\chi_r(y)}=\prod_{j=1}^d\sum_{r_j=0}^{L-1}e^{2\pi i r_j(\widetilde x_j-\widetilde y_j)/L}$. The canonical-representative theorem [F1] and orthogonality [F3] make this product $L^d$ if $x=y$ in $\Lambda_{d,L}$ and $0$ otherwise. Therefore $\sum_r\widehat f(r)\chi_r(x)=L^{-d}\sum_y f(y)\sum_r\chi_r(x)\overline{\chi_r(y)}=f(x)$ for every $x$. If a linear combination $\sum_r c_r\chi_r$ vanishes, taking its inner product with $\chi_s$ and applying step 2.1 gives $c_s=0$ for each $s$, so the expansion is unique.

For every real $f$, the translations $x\mapsto x+e_j$ are bijections with inverses $x\mapsto x-e_j$, so reindexing the finite sums [F4] gives $\sum_xf(x)(-\Delta f)(x)=\sum_{j=1}^d\sum_x(f(x+e_j)-f(x))^2\ge0$. Thus $-\Delta$ is positive semidefinite; its matrix is symmetric because every shift term is paired with its inverse shift. For nonzero $f$, $$f^{\mathsf T}(m^2I+\kappa(-\Delta))f=m^2\sum_xf(x)^2+\kappa\sum_{j=1}^d\sum_x(f(x+e_j)-f(x))^2>0,$$ since $m^2>0$ and $\kappa>0$. By steps 2.2 and 3.1, the spanning functions $\chi_r$ satisfy the eigenvalue equations in the Statement, so the combined operator has the displayed eigenvalues.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized product Haar measure $dx$, with $dx(\mathbb T^d)=1$. Coordinates and time are dimensionless in the diffusive normalization $D=1$. For $r\in(0,1)$ set the mobility function $\chi(r):=r(1-r)$. For any finite interval $[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $\rho:[a,b]\times\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$ be a scalar density and let $j:[a,b]\times\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be a vector current. Require both fields to be smooth up to the time endpoints and periodic in space, and require that for some $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, $\varepsilon\le\rho(t,x)\le1-\varepsilon$ for every $(t,x)$. Call $(\rho,j)$ admissible when it also satisfies the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot j=0$. Define its dimensionless action by

$$\mathcal I_{[a,b]}(\rho,j):=\frac14\int_a^b\int_{\mathbb T^d}\frac{|j(t,x)+\nabla\rho(t,x)|^2}{\rho(t,x)(1-\rho(t,x))}\,dx\,dt.$$

This is the macroscopic fluctuation functional in the stated normalized SSEP coefficient convention. It is a definition of a functional and does not assert a microscopic path-space large-deviation principle or a probability estimate.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function, with images and preimages written $f[\,\cdot\,]$
and $f^{-1}[\,\cdot\,]$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). Conditions
(a), (b), (c), and (e) below are equivalent without choice, and each implies
(d). Assuming Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), all five are
equivalent. The authorized Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) suffices;
only its countable instance is used for the converse from (d).

- **(a)** $f$ is continuous at every point of $X$ in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$
  sense ([[def-metric-continuity]]).
- **(b)** $f^{-1}[V]$ is open in $X$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
  ([[def-metric-topology]]).
- **(c)** $f^{-1}[G]$ is closed in $X$ for every closed $G \subseteq Y$.
- **(d)** $f$ is **sequentially continuous**: whenever $x_k \to x$ in $(X,d_X)$,
  also $f(x_k) \to f(x)$ in $(Y,d_Y)$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]).
- **(e)** $f[\overline{A}] \subseteq \overline{f[A]}$ for every $A \subseteq X$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

**Where choice is used.** Only the implication (d) $\Rightarrow$ (e) uses a
choice principle, and it uses it only through
[[thm-metric-sequential-closure]], whose forward direction spends the Axiom of
Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The cycle
(a) $\Rightarrow$ (b) $\Rightarrow$ (c) $\Rightarrow$ (e) $\Rightarrow$ (a) and
the implication (a) $\Rightarrow$ (d) are choice free.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The real numbers) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Enumerate $X$ as $x_1,\dots,x_m$ and let $\Delta=\{\lambda\in[0,1]^m:\sum_j\lambda_j=1\}$. The set $\Delta$ is bounded. Its coordinate maps and sum map are continuous, since each coordinate inequality $|\lambda_j-\lambda'_j|\le\|\lambda-\lambda'\|_2$ follows from the norm formula [F9], while $|\sum_j(\lambda_j-\lambda'_j)|\le m\|\lambda-\lambda'\|_2$ follows from the real triangle inequality; hence $\Delta$, an intersection of their closed inverse images, is closed. By [F1], $\Delta$ is compact. For $\lambda,\lambda'\in\Delta$, the triangle inequality and coordinate bound give
$$\left\|\sum_j\lambda_jT(x_j)-\sum_j\lambda'_jT(x_j)\right\|_2\le\sum_j|\lambda_j-\lambda'_j|\,\|T(x_j)\|_2\le\|\lambda-\lambda'\|_2\sum_j\|T(x_j)\|_2,$$
so the map $\lambda\mapsto\sum_j\lambda_jT(x_j)$ is continuous. Thus [F2] makes its image $K$ compact; [F3] makes $K$ closed.

For every integer $n\ge1$, noninteriority of $\mu$ gives a point $p_n
otin K$ with $\|p_n-\mu\|_2<1/(2n)$. Since $K$ is closed, its complement is open, so some ball $B(p_n,ho_n)$ of radius $ho_n>0$ lies outside $K$. Choose $r_n>0$ smaller than both $ho_n$ and $1/n-\|p_n-\mu\|_2$. Density [F7] gives a rational vector $q_j\in B(p_n,r_n)$; then $q_j
otin K$ and $\|q_j-\mu\|_2<1/n$. Thus $J_n=\{j\in\mathbb N:q_j
otin K,\ \|q_j-\mu\|_2<1/n\}$ is nonempty; let $j_n$ be its least member and set $y_n=q_{j_n}$. This least-index construction uses no choice and $y_n	o\mu$.

For $z,z'\in K$, the triangle inequality gives $\|y_n-z\|_2\le\|y_n-z'\|_2+\|z-z'\|_2$, and exchanging $z,z'$ gives $\bigl|\|y_n-z\|_2-\|y_n-z'\|_2\bigr|\le\|z-z'\|_2$. Hence $z\mapsto\|y_n-z\|_2$ is continuous on $K$ in its Euclidean metric. The nonempty compact set $K$ therefore has a minimizer $z_n\in K$ by [F5]. It is unique: if distinct $z,z'\in K$ both minimize, convexity puts $(z+z')/2$ in $K$ and
$\|y_n-(z+z')/2\|_2^2=(\|y_n-z\|_2^2+\|y_n-z'\|_2^2)/2-\|z-z'\|_2^2/4$
is strictly smaller. For any $v\in K$ and $0<s\le1$, convexity gives $z_n+s(v-z_n)\in K$. Minimality then implies
$\|y_n-z_n\|_2^2\le\|y_n-z_n-s(v-z_n)\|_2^2$;
expanding the inner products, dividing by $s$, and letting $s\downarrow0$ gives
$(y_n-z_n)\cdot(v-z_n)\le0$.

Since $\mu\in K$, minimality gives $\|y_n-z_n\|_2\le\|y_n-\mu\|_2$, so the triangle inequality gives $\|z_n-\mu\|_2\le2\|y_n-\mu\|_2\to0$. Put $u_n=(y_n-z_n)/\|y_n-z_n\|_2$; the denominator is positive because $y_n\notin K$, and homogeneity of the norm gives $\|u_n\|_2=1$. Thus $(u_n)$ is bounded in the Euclidean metric; [F8] gives a subsequence $u_{n_j}$ converging to $u$. The reverse triangle inequality, obtained by applying the triangle inequality in both orders, gives $\bigl|\|u_{n_j}\|_2-\|u\|_2\bigr|\le\|u_{n_j}-u\|_2$, hence $\|u\|_2=1$. For every $v\in K$, step 3.1 gives $u_{n_j}\cdot(v-z_{n_j})\le0$. By [F10],
$$|u_{n_j}\cdot(v-z_{n_j})-u\cdot(v-\mu)|\le\|u_{n_j}-u\|_2\,\|v-z_{n_j}\|_2+\|u\|_2\,\|\mu-z_{n_j}\|_2\longrightarrow0,$$
since $z_{n_j}\to\mu$ and hence $(v-z_{n_j})$ is bounded. Passing to the limit gives $u\cdot(v-\mu)\le0$. Taking $v=T(x)\in K$ proves the claimed support inequality.

   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function, with images and preimages written $f[\,\cdot\,]$
and $f^{-1}[\,\cdot\,]$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). Conditions
(a), (b), (c), and (e) below are equivalent without choice, and each implies
(d). Assuming Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), all five are
equivalent. The authorized Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) suffices;
only its countable instance is used for the converse from (d).

- **(a)** $f$ is continuous at every point of $X$ in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$
  sense ([[def-metric-continuity]]).
- **(b)** $f^{-1}[V]$ is open in $X$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
  ([[def-metric-topology]]).
- **(c)** $f^{-1}[G]$ is closed in $X$ for every closed $G \subseteq Y$.
- **(d)** $f$ is **sequentially continuous**: whenever $x_k \to x$ in $(X,d_X)$,
  also $f(x_k) \to f(x)$ in $(Y,d_Y)$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]).
- **(e)** $f[\overline{A}] \subseteq \overline{f[A]}$ for every $A \subseteq X$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

**Where choice is used.** Only the implication (d) $\Rightarrow$ (e) uses a
choice principle, and it uses it only through
[[thm-metric-sequential-closure]], whose forward direction spends the Axiom of
Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The cycle
(a) $\Rightarrow$ (b) $\Rightarrow$ (c) $\Rightarrow$ (e) $\Rightarrow$ (a) and
the implication (a) $\Rightarrow$ (d) are choice free.
